lessons.title: Why Software Fails and the Principles of Testing
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother asks you to buy 2 kg of potatoes from the bazar. You are thinking about cricket, so you write "20 kg" on the list by mistake. The shopkeeper reads the list and loads 20 kg into a sack. At home everyone stares at the giant sack. Notice the three different things that happened: a human slip in your head, a wrong entry sitting quietly on the paper, and a visible problem when the list was actually used. Software fails in exactly this three-step way, and this whole course is about catching such problems before they reach real people.

Where this course stands: In Software Engineering you already met testing in a few lessons: error, fault and failure, the seven principles, test levels, a handful of black-box and white-box techniques, and quality models. Here we treat testing and quality assurance as a full discipline. We will go much deeper into each idea, add many new techniques, work through real numbers, and see how professional QA teams plan, automate, measure and improve. This first lesson rebuilds the foundation carefully, because every later lesson stands on it.

The first word, mistake or error: A mistake (also called an error) is a human action that produces a wrong result. A developer misreads a requirement, types less-than where less-than-or-equal was needed, forgets that a list can be empty, or copies code from an older project without checking its assumptions. Mistakes come from time pressure, tiredness, complex code, unclear requirements, poor communication and new technology. Mistakes happen in people's heads, not in the computer.

The second word, defect, fault or bug: A defect is the result of a mistake that sits inside a work product. It can be in code, but also in a requirement document, a design diagram, a test case or a configuration file. The words defect, fault and bug are used almost interchangeably in industry. A defect is like the "20 kg" written on the list: it is wrong, but nothing bad has happened yet. A defect can sleep in the code for years if the faulty line never runs.

The third word, failure: A failure is when the system, while running, does something different from what it should: wrong output, a crash, a frozen screen, a slow response, a security hole being exploited. A failure is the visible event. Here is the key chain: a mistake can introduce a defect, and when the defective code is executed under the right conditions, it can cause a failure. Not every defect causes a failure. If the bug is in a branch that only runs on 29 February, it stays hidden for years. Also, some failures are not caused by code defects at all: a power cut, radiation flipping a memory bit, or a faulty network cable can make correct software misbehave.

A tiny example in code: Suppose a shop gives a discount if a customer buys 5 or more items. The developer writes if (items > 5) give discount. The mistake was in thinking. The defect is the ">" sign. A customer buying 7 items gets the discount correctly, so no failure appears. A customer buying exactly 5 items gets no discount: that is the failure. A tester who only tried 7 items would believe everything was fine. This is why later lessons spend so much time on choosing good test inputs.

Root cause: The root cause is the earliest reason that led to the defect. In the example, the root cause might be that the requirement said "more than 4" in one place and "5 or more" in another, or that the developer was rushing. Fixing only the line of code removes this one defect; fixing the root cause (clear requirements, code reviews, better training) prevents a whole family of similar defects. Mature teams always ask "why did this happen?" and not just "where is the bug?"

Famous failure, Ariane 5: On 4 June 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket of the European Space Agency broke up less than a minute after launch. Software reused from the older Ariane 4 converted a 64-bit floating-point value related to horizontal velocity into a 16-bit signed integer. Ariane 5 flew faster than Ariane 4, the number did not fit, an exception was raised, and the guidance system shut down. The code had worked perfectly on Ariane 4. The lesson: software that is correct in one context can fail in another, and reused code must be tested again under the new conditions.

Famous failure, Mars Climate Orbiter: In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter. One piece of ground software produced thrust data in imperial units (pound-force seconds), while another part expected metric units (newton-seconds). The spacecraft went too close to Mars and was lost. Each team's code may have looked fine alone; the defect lived at the interface between them. That is exactly what integration testing, which we will study soon, is meant to catch.

Famous failure, Therac-25: In the mid-1980s the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine gave several patients massive radiation overdoses, and some of them died. Investigations found software race conditions and the removal of hardware safety interlocks that older models had, so the software alone was trusted to keep patients safe. This case is taught everywhere because it shows that in safety-critical systems poor testing and poor engineering cost human lives.

What testing is: Software testing is the process of evaluating a software product and related work products to find defects, to check that requirements are met, and to build confidence in quality, so that people can make informed decisions. Testing includes running the software (dynamic testing), but also reviewing documents and code without running anything (static testing). It also includes planning, designing test cases, preparing data, reporting and analysing results. Many beginners think testing is only "clicking around after the code is finished"; that is a small part of it.

Objectives of testing: Typical goals are to find defects and failures, to prevent defects by examining requirements and designs early, to verify that specified requirements are fulfilled, to validate that the system works as users and stakeholders expect, to build confidence in the level of quality, to reduce the risk of failures in production, and to comply with contractual, legal or regulatory requirements. Different projects weigh these goals differently. A bank's payment system and a student's hobby game do not need the same depth of testing.

Testing versus debugging: Testing shows that a failure exists, or finds a defect through review. Debugging is the development activity of finding the cause of a failure, analysing it, and fixing it. After the fix, testers run confirmation testing to check the defect is really gone, and regression testing to check the fix did not break anything else. Testers find and report; developers usually debug. In small teams the same person does both, but they are still different activities.

Principle 1, testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence: Tests can prove that bugs exist, but no amount of passing tests can prove a program has no bugs. If 500 tests pass, you know those 500 situations work. You do not know about the 501st. So we speak of reducing risk and building confidence, never of proving perfection.

Principle 2, exhaustive testing is impossible: Consider a form with just two fields, each accepting a whole number from 1 to 1000. All combinations are 1000 times 1000, which is one million tests, and that ignores invalid inputs, timing, devices and network conditions. Real software has astronomically more combinations. Instead of testing everything, we use risk analysis, test techniques and priorities to choose a small but smart set of tests.

Principle 3, early testing saves time and money: A wrong requirement caught in a review costs a conversation and an edited sentence. The same mistake found after release may need redesign, recoding, retesting, redeployment, customer support and lost reputation. This idea is often called shift-left: start testing activities, such as reviewing requirements, as early as possible in the lifecycle.

Principle 4, defects cluster together: A small number of modules usually contain most of the defects. Complex modules, recently changed code, code written in a hurry, or code by a new team member tend to be buggier. When testers notice a cluster, they spend more effort there. This is similar to the Pareto (80/20) idea, though the exact ratio varies from project to project.

Principle 5, tests wear out: If you run the same tests again and again, they eventually stop finding new defects, just like a pesticide used repeatedly stops killing insects that have become resistant. This is often called the pesticide paradox. Regression tests are still valuable for catching breakage, but to find new defects you must regularly review, update and add test cases and try new data and techniques.

Principle 6, testing is context dependent: Testing an air traffic control system, a mobile banking app such as a bKash-style wallet, an e-commerce site during a big sale, and a school's result website all need different approaches, techniques and depth. Safety-critical software needs formal techniques and strong coverage; a quick prototype might need only light exploratory testing.

Principle 7, absence-of-defects fallacy: Even if you find and fix many defects, the software can still be useless if it solves the wrong problem or is too hard to use. A perfectly bug-free ticket app that nobody can figure out is still a failure. Testing therefore includes validation: checking that the product meets real user needs, not only the written specification.

Real-life example, an exam result website: Every year when board results are published, millions of students try to check their results at the same moment. A result site may compute grades correctly (no functional defect) and still fail because it cannot handle the load. Here the defect may be in capacity planning or configuration rather than in the grade logic. Good testing would include performance testing with realistic numbers of users before result day, not just checking that one student's GPA is right.

Real-life example, a mobile wallet send-money feature: Imagine the limit for one transfer is 25,000 Taka. A developer writes amount < 25000 instead of amount <= 25000. A user sending exactly 25,000 Taka is rejected and calls customer care. The mistake was a slip, the defect is one character, and the failure appears only at the exact boundary. Testers who apply boundary value analysis, which we will study in lesson 7, would try 24,999, 25,000 and 25,001 and catch it before customers do.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up error, defect and failure. Remember: error is human, defect is in the work product, failure is observed during execution. Exams ask you to classify a scenario ("a programmer misunderstood the formula" is an error; "the formula in line 40 is wrong" is a defect; "the invoice shows the wrong total" is a failure). Another favourite is matching a situation to a principle, such as "the same regression suite has found nothing new for six months" (tests wear out) or "most bugs were in the payment module" (defect clustering). Also remember that testing and debugging are different activities.

Recap: Software fails because people make mistakes that create defects, and defects cause failures when the faulty code runs under the right conditions. Testing evaluates the product to find defects, reduce risk and build confidence, while debugging locates and fixes causes. Seven principles guide us: tests show presence not absence, exhaustive testing is impossible, test early, defects cluster, tests wear out, context matters, and a bug-free product can still be useless. Next we look at what quality really means and how QA, QC and testing differ.
key_points: A mistake (error) is a human action; it can create a defect (fault, bug) in a work product, which may cause a failure when executed.
Not every defect causes a failure, and some failures come from the environment rather than code.
Ariane 5, Mars Climate Orbiter and Therac-25 show reuse, interface and safety failures.
Testing finds defects, verifies and validates, builds confidence and reduces risk; debugging finds and fixes the cause.
Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence, and exhaustive testing is impossible.
Early testing saves money, defects cluster, and repeated tests wear out (pesticide paradox).
Testing is context dependent, and a defect-free product that does not meet user needs is still a failure.
lessons.tip: Whenever you read a news story about a software problem, try to name the error, the defect and the failure separately. This habit makes the vocabulary automatic before exams.
lessons.task: Think of one app you use daily (a ride-sharing app, a mobile wallet, a food delivery app). Write down one possible human mistake a developer could make, the defect it would create in the code, and the failure a user would actually see. Then write which of the seven principles would help catch it.

quiz.q: A developer misunderstood the tax rule and wrote the wrong formula on line 40. What is "the wrong formula on line 40"?
quiz.explain: The wrong formula sitting in the code is a defect; the misunderstanding was the error, and a wrong invoice would be the failure.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the principle "testing shows the presence of defects"?
options: Passing all tests proves the software is correct
Testing is only useful at the end of a project
Exhaustive testing is needed for confidence
Testing can reveal bugs but cannot prove that none remain
quiz.explain: Tests can show defects exist but can never prove their absence, so we talk about reducing risk.

quiz.q: A regression suite has run every night for a year and has found no new defects for months. Which principle explains this?
quiz.explain: Repeating the same tests stops finding new defects; tests must be reviewed and new ones added.

quiz.q: What was the core software problem in the Ariane 5 flight 501 failure?
options: A wrong unit of measurement between two teams
A race condition in a medical machine
Reused code converted a 64-bit floating-point value into a 16-bit integer that overflowed
The rocket ran out of memory because of too many tests
quiz.explain: Code reused from Ariane 4 overflowed when converting a larger velocity-related value on the faster Ariane 5.

quiz.q: Which activity is usually done by developers rather than testers?
options: Debugging to locate and fix the cause of a failure
quiz.explain: Debugging is a development activity; testers find and report failures and then confirm fixes.

lessons.title: Quality, QA vs QC, and the Psychology of Testing
lessons.content:
Think about a sweet shop that is famous for its roshogolla. How does it stay famous? The owner decides how the milk is chosen, how long the chhana is kneaded, how clean the kitchen must be, and trains every cook the same way. That is one kind of work. Then, before boxes go out, someone tastes a few pieces from each batch and throws away a batch that is too hard. That is a second kind of work. Software quality works the same way: one set of activities builds quality into the process, another checks the product. Mixing them up is one of the most common confusions in this field.

What quality means: There is no single magic definition, so it helps to know the classic ones. Philip Crosby described quality as conformance to requirements: the product does what was specified. Joseph Juran described it as fitness for use: the product actually serves the user's purpose. The ISO 9000 family describes quality as the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfils requirements. In practice we need both views. A product can match the written specification and still be unfit for use if the specification was wrong, and that is exactly the absence-of-defects fallacy from lesson 1.

Product quality characteristics: In Software Engineering you saw ISO/IEC 25010, the standard product quality model. Its widely taught edition lists eight characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability, each with sub-characteristics such as time behaviour, fault tolerance or testability. A newer revision renames a few and adds safety, but the idea is the same. For a tester, this list is a checklist of what to look at beyond "does the button work". Several later lessons, such as performance, security and accessibility testing, are about those non-functional characteristics.

Quality assurance (QA): QA is process-oriented and preventive. It asks: are we following good processes that make defects less likely? QA activities include defining development and testing processes, setting coding standards, organising training, running process audits, choosing tools, doing root cause analysis after incidents, and improving the process over time. QA is like the sweet shop owner's recipe and training. Importantly, QA is everybody's responsibility, not just one department's.

Quality control (QC): QC is product-oriented and corrective. It examines actual work products to find defects so they can be fixed. Testing is the biggest QC activity, but reviews of documents and code, inspections and acceptance checks are also QC. QC is like the person tasting pieces from each batch. QC gives information; somebody still has to act on it.

Where testing fits: Testing is a major form of quality control: it evaluates the product, both statically (reviews, static analysis) and dynamically (running it). Testing results also feed QA, because patterns in defects show where the process is weak. If 40 percent of defects come from unclear requirements, the QA response is a better requirements process, not just more testing. A simple way to remember: QA builds the right way of working, QC checks the things produced, and testing is the main tool QC uses.

A common job-title confusion: In many companies, including in Dhaka's software industry, the testing team is called "the QA team" and testers are called "QA engineers". That is a naming habit, not the textbook meaning. Most of their daily work is actually QC (testing), although good QA engineers also improve processes, review requirements and suggest standards. In an exam, stick to the definitions: QA is process, QC is product.

Verification and validation: These two words are related but different. Verification asks "are we building the product right?": does each work product conform to its specification? Validation asks "are we building the right product?": does it meet the real needs of users in their real environment? Reviewing a design against the requirements document is verification. Letting real shopkeepers use a billing app in their shop and seeing whether it helps them is validation. Both are needed, and both can happen throughout the lifecycle.

Cost of quality: Quality is not free, but poor quality costs more. The cost of quality model splits spending into four buckets. Prevention costs: training, process definition, good tools, requirement reviews. Appraisal costs: testing, inspections, audits, test environments. Internal failure costs: fixing defects found before release, rework, retesting, delays. External failure costs: defects found by customers, including support calls, patches, refunds, penalties and lost reputation. The first two are the cost of good quality; the last two are the cost of poor quality.

Worked example of cost of quality: Suppose a team spends 2 lakh Taka on prevention (training and reviews) and 6 lakh on appraisal (testing). They still find defects that cost 4 lakh to fix internally, and released defects cost 8 lakh in support, patches and refunds. Total cost of quality is 2 + 6 + 4 + 8 = 20 lakh. The cost of poor quality is 4 + 8 = 12 lakh, which is 60 percent of the total. If an extra 2 lakh in prevention cut external failures in half (to 4 lakh) and internal failures to 3 lakh, the new total would be 4 + 6 + 3 + 4 = 17 lakh: spending more early saved 3 lakh overall. The exact numbers vary by project, but the shape of this argument is why companies invest in prevention.

Why it matters even more for software: Software defects can be copied to millions of users at once. A defect in a mobile banking app affects every customer the same day. External failures can also include legal penalties and, in health or transport, harm to people. That is why mature organisations measure these costs and keep pushing work toward prevention and early appraisal.

Independence of testing: Authors are bad at finding their own mistakes, the same way you can read your own essay three times and miss a spelling error your friend spots immediately. Independent testers bring a different viewpoint, different assumptions and no emotional attachment to the code. Levels of independence, from lowest to highest, are commonly described as: the developer tests their own code; another developer or tester inside the same team; an independent test team inside the organisation; testers from the business or user side; and an external test organisation.

Independence has trade-offs: More independence finds different kinds of defects and is often required for safety-critical or regulated systems. But too much independence can cause isolation: testers far from the team learn about changes late, communication slows, and developers may lose the feeling of responsibility for quality ("the testers will catch it"). Modern Agile teams usually keep testers inside the team for fast feedback, while still having some independent checks, such as acceptance tests by business users.

The psychology of testing: Finding defects can feel like criticism. A developer who has worked late for a week does not enjoy hearing "your feature is broken". So how testers communicate matters a lot. Good practice: start with collaboration, not battle; describe the behaviour objectively ("when the amount is exactly 25,000 the transfer is rejected") instead of blaming people ("you wrote bad code"); remind everyone that the shared goal is a better product; and ask questions when you are unsure whether something is a defect.

Confirmation bias and other traps: Humans tend to look for evidence that confirms what they already believe. A developer who believes the code is correct designs tests that show it works, often choosing "happy path" inputs. A tester's job is the opposite mindset: to think about how things can go wrong. Other biases include assuming the system behaves like the last one you tested, and trusting information from people in authority without checking. Being aware of these traps is the first defence. Writing tests from the specification before looking at the code also helps.

The tester's mindset: Good testers are curious, sceptical in a friendly way, attentive to detail, and good communicators. They ask "what if?" constantly: what if the network drops mid-payment, what if the name has a Bangla character, what if two users book the last seat at the same moment. Developers usually have a constructive mindset focused on making things work. Both mindsets are valuable and the best teams combine them, sometimes in the same person.

Who owns quality: A healthy team treats quality as a shared responsibility. Product owners own clear acceptance criteria, developers own unit tests and clean code, testers own test design and independent evaluation, operations staff own monitoring, and managers own the time and budget that make all of this possible. When a team says "quality is the QA team's job", developers rush code over the wall, testers become a bottleneck, and defects pile up near the deadline. When everyone owns a piece, defects are caught where they are cheapest, and testers can spend their energy on the hard, risky areas instead of obvious slips.

Real-life example, a food delivery company: A Dhaka food delivery startup notices many complaints about wrong delivery charges. QC (testing) found and fixed several defects in the fee calculation, but new ones keep appearing. A QA review then finds the root cause: the pricing rules live in three different places, and each team updates them separately. The QA fix is a process and design change: one shared pricing service, a rule that every pricing change needs a review by a second person, and automated tests for every rule. Complaints drop because the process changed, not just because more bugs were caught.

Real-life example, a government land records portal: A team builds a portal that matches every requirement in the contract, and system testing passes (verification succeeded). But when officers in an upazila office use it, they find the forms assume fast internet and English typing, while their real work involves slow connections and Bangla names. Validation fails. Earlier user involvement, such as acceptance testing with real officers and prototypes reviewed in the field, would have exposed the gap before rollout.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Typical questions ask you to classify activities as QA or QC: "defining a code review process" is QA, "reviewing a specific module's code" is QC, "running system tests" is QC (testing), "auditing whether teams follow the test process" is QA. Another favourite: "are we building the product right?" is verification; "are we building the right product?" is validation. Cost of quality questions ask you to place items in the four buckets: training is prevention, testing is appraisal, rework before release is internal failure, customer refunds are external failure.

Recap: Quality means both conformance to requirements and fitness for use, and ISO/IEC 25010 gives a structured list of characteristics to check. QA improves the process and prevents defects; QC checks the product and finds them; testing is the main QC activity. Verification checks we built it right, validation checks we built the right thing. Cost of quality shows that prevention and early appraisal are usually cheaper than failures. Independent, well-communicating testers with a curious, sceptical mindset find more of what matters. Next we follow testing through the lifecycle, starting with unit and integration testing.
key_points: Quality is both conformance to requirements (Crosby) and fitness for use (Juran).
ISO/IEC 25010 lists product quality characteristics such as functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security and maintainability.
QA is process-oriented and preventive; QC is product-oriented and finds defects; testing is the main QC activity.
Verification: are we building the product right? Validation: are we building the right product?
Cost of quality has four buckets: prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure.
Independent testing finds different defects but too much independence causes isolation.
Testers should report behaviour objectively, avoid blame and watch for confirmation bias.
lessons.tip: For QA vs QC questions, ask one thing: is this activity about the way we work (QA) or about a specific thing we produced (QC)? That one question answers most exam items.
lessons.task: List ten activities from a project you know (for example: writing coding guidelines, testing the login page, a code review of one module, training new developers, fixing a bug a customer reported). Mark each as QA or QC, and for each cost, put it in one of the four cost-of-quality buckets.

quiz.q: Which activity is quality assurance (QA) rather than quality control (QC)?
options: Running system tests on the release build
Inspecting the code of the payment module
Defining a review process that every team must follow
Checking a sample of printed invoices for errors
quiz.explain: QA is about the process; defining how reviews are done is a process activity. The others examine specific products.

quiz.q: "Are we building the right product?" describes:
quiz.explain: Validation checks that the product meets real user needs; verification checks conformance to specifications.

quiz.q: Customer refunds and emergency patches after a release belong to which cost-of-quality category?
quiz.explain: Costs caused by defects found after release, by customers, are external failure costs.

quiz.q: A team spends 3 lakh on prevention, 5 lakh on appraisal, 2 lakh on internal failures and 10 lakh on external failures. What is the cost of poor quality?
quiz.explain: Cost of poor quality is internal plus external failure: 2 + 10 = 12 lakh (total cost of quality is 20 lakh).

quiz.q: Why are developers often weak at testing their own code?
options: They do not know the programming language
Testing tools do not allow developers to run tests
Confirmation bias and attachment make them look for proof that it works
Developers are not allowed to see requirements
quiz.explain: Authors tend to confirm their own assumptions and choose happy-path inputs; independent eyes see different problems.

lessons.title: Testing in the Lifecycle: Unit and Integration Testing
lessons.content:
Think about building a bus. Before the bus rolls out of the factory, engineers test each part on its own: the engine on a test bench, the brakes on a rig, every headlight bulb. Then they join parts and test the joins: does the engine actually turn the wheels through the gearbox, does the dashboard read the fuel sensor correctly? Only after that do they drive the whole bus on a test track, and finally the transport company takes it for a trial run on a real route. Software testing follows the same ladder, and the first two rungs, unit testing and integration testing, are where most defects should be caught.

Test levels, the big picture: A test level is a group of test activities organised and managed together, tied to a stage of development. The four classic levels are component (unit) testing, integration testing, system testing and acceptance testing. Each level has its own objectives, its own test basis (the documents tests are designed from), its own typical defects, its own environment and often its own people. This lesson covers the first two; the next lesson covers system and acceptance testing.

V-model recap: In Software Engineering you saw the V-model, which pairs each development stage on the left of the V with a test level on the right: requirements with acceptance testing, system specification with system testing, architectural design with integration testing, and detailed design with unit testing. The useful idea is that test planning and design for each level start as soon as its matching development document exists. Acceptance tests can be drafted while requirements are being written, long before code exists. That is early testing in action.

Testing in Agile: In Scrum or Kanban teams there is no long waterfall, but the levels still exist. Within one sprint, developers write unit tests, the team runs integration tests on every merge, system-level checks run on a staging environment, and the product owner accepts stories against acceptance criteria. All four levels happen in short loops instead of long phases. Testers work inside the team, attending refinement meetings, asking questions about stories and preparing tests in parallel with coding.

Shift-left: Shift-left means moving testing activities earlier: reviewing user stories for testability, writing acceptance criteria before coding, writing unit tests before or with the code, and running static analysis on every commit. The opposite idea, shift-right, means testing and monitoring in production, which we meet in the CI and DevOps lesson. Both are useful; shift-left reduces cost, shift-right catches what only real usage reveals.

Component (unit) testing, what it is: Component testing, usually called unit testing, tests the smallest separately testable pieces of software in isolation: a function, a method, a class, or a small module. The test basis is the detailed design, the code itself and the function's contract (what inputs it accepts and what it promises to return). Typical defects found are wrong calculations, incorrect logic in conditions, off-by-one errors in loops, wrong handling of null or empty inputs, and incorrect error handling.

Who does unit testing and how: Developers usually write unit tests, often with a framework from the xUnit family such as JUnit for Java or pytest for Python (lesson 18 goes deep). Unit tests run in milliseconds, so a project can have thousands of them and run them all on every change. Because a unit is tested alone, its dependencies, such as a database or a payment gateway, are replaced with test doubles like stubs and mocks (lesson 19). In test-driven development the unit test is written before the code.

A small unit-test example: Suppose a function deliveryFee(distanceKm) returns 30 Taka for up to 3 km, then 10 Taka for each additional km, rounded up. Good unit tests check 0 km (30), 3 km (30), 3.1 km (40, because the extra 0.1 km is rounded up to 1 km), 5 km (50) and a negative distance (should raise an error). Each test is a few lines: call the function, compare the result with the expected value. If someone later changes the rounding, these tests fail within seconds.

Integration testing, what it is: Units that pass alone can still fail together, just like the Mars Climate Orbiter software from lesson 1. Integration testing focuses on the interactions and interfaces between components or systems. The test basis is the software and system design, sequence diagrams, interface and API specifications, and workflows. Typical defects are wrong data formats or units, missing or wrong parameters, incorrect order of calls, wrong assumptions about who validates data, timing and concurrency problems, and failure handling between parts (what happens when the other side is down or slow).

Two kinds of integration: Component integration testing checks interactions between components inside one system, for example the order module calling the inventory module. It is usually done by developers and often automated in the CI pipeline. System integration testing checks interactions with other systems and external services, for example your e-commerce site talking to a payment gateway, an SMS provider or a courier's tracking API. System integration is harder because you do not control the other side: its test environment may be unavailable, slow or different from production.

Big bang integration: The simplest strategy is to build all components and integrate them at once, then test the whole thing. It needs no stubs or drivers, which sounds attractive. The problem is that when something fails, the defect could be anywhere among dozens of interfaces, so localising it is slow and painful. Big bang also delays integration testing until everything is ready, which goes against early testing. It can work for very small systems, but larger projects avoid it.

Incremental integration: The better idea is to integrate and test a few components at a time, so that a new failure most likely comes from the newly added piece or its interfaces. Incremental strategies differ in the order of adding components. To test a partly built system, we need temporary helpers: a stub stands in for a component that is called but not yet available, and returns simple, fixed answers; a driver is a piece of code that calls the component under test, standing in for a missing caller.

Top-down integration: Start from the top-level module (for example the main menu or controller) and add the modules it calls, level by level. Lower modules that are not ready are replaced by stubs. Advantages: the main control flow and user-visible behaviour are tested early, and an early skeleton can be demonstrated. Disadvantages: many stubs are needed, and low-level modules, where heavy computation often happens, are tested late. Top-down can go depth-first (follow one branch down fully) or breadth-first (complete one level at a time).

Bottom-up integration: Start with the lowest-level modules, which call nothing else, and test them using drivers. Then combine them into clusters and move upward, replacing drivers with real higher modules. Advantages: low-level utility and computation modules are tested thoroughly and early, and no stubs are needed. Disadvantages: drivers must be written, and the overall program does not exist as a working whole until the very end, so design-level problems in the top layers appear late.

Sandwich (hybrid) integration: Sandwich integration combines both, working top-down on the upper layers and bottom-up on the lower layers at the same time, meeting in a middle target layer. It suits large systems with many layers, though it is more complex to plan. In practice many teams also integrate by feature or by risk: they connect the components needed for the most important user flow first.

Worked integration order: Consider a structure where module A (the controller) calls B (orders) and C (payments); B calls D (inventory) and E (pricing); C calls F (gateway adapter). Top-down depth-first order: test A with stubs for B and C; replace the B stub with real B, using stubs for D and E; add D, then E; replace the C stub with real C, using a stub for F; finally add F. Bottom-up order: test D, E and F with drivers; then test B with real D and E using a driver for B's caller; test C with real F using a driver; finally test A with real B and C. In both orders, each step adds a small piece, so a failure points to a narrow area.

Continuous integration makes this routine: In modern teams, integration is not a once-a-month event. Every merged change triggers a build and an automated suite of unit and component integration tests, often within minutes. This catches interface breakage the day it happens. System integration with external partners still needs planned tests, often against sandboxes that payment gateways and SMS providers offer for testing.

Real-life example, a ride-sharing app: The fare module passes all its unit tests: given distance, time and surge factor, it computes the fare correctly. The map module passes its tests too. But in integration testing, the team finds the map module returns distance in metres while the fare module expects kilometres. A 5 km trip was being charged as 5,000 km. No unit test could catch this, because each unit was correct by its own contract; the defect was in the agreement between them. A single integration test with a known route revealed it.

Real-life example, an online exam portal: A university builds a portal where the question service, the timer service and the answer-saving service are separate. Top-down integration starts from the exam page with stubbed services returning fixed questions, so the UI flow can be tested early and shown to teachers. Then real services are added one by one. When the real answer-saving service is connected, testers notice that answers typed in the last 5 seconds are lost because the timer submits before the final save completes: a timing defect at an interface, found before a real exam rather than during one.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up stubs and drivers. A stub is called by the code under test (replaces something below it); a driver calls the code under test (replaces something above it). Top-down needs stubs, bottom-up needs drivers. Exams ask you to compare big bang with incremental integration, to list advantages and disadvantages of top-down and bottom-up, to give an integration order for a module chart, and to name typical defects at each level. Another trap: unit tests passing does not mean integration is fine; interface defects need integration tests.

Recap: Test levels organise testing by stage: unit, integration, system and acceptance, each with its own objectives, test basis and typical defects. The V-model pairs them with development stages, and Agile teams run all levels in short loops, shifting testing left. Unit tests check small pieces in isolation, quickly and in large numbers. Integration tests check interfaces between components and with external systems, ideally incrementally using top-down, bottom-up or sandwich order, with stubs and drivers filling the gaps. Next we climb to system and acceptance testing.
key_points: The four test levels are unit (component), integration, system and acceptance, each with its own objectives, test basis and defects.
The V-model pairs each development stage with a test level, so test design can start early.
Unit testing checks small pieces in isolation, mostly by developers, using frameworks and test doubles.
Integration testing targets interfaces: component integration inside a system, system integration with external systems.
Big bang integrates everything at once and makes failures hard to localise; incremental integration adds pieces gradually.
Top-down uses stubs and tests control flow early; bottom-up uses drivers and tests low-level modules early; sandwich mixes both.
A stub is called by the code under test; a driver calls the code under test.
lessons.tip: To remember stubs and drivers, picture a car: the driver sits on top and controls the car, so a driver replaces a missing caller above; a stub is a short stump below, so it replaces a missing module below.
lessons.task: Draw a module chart for a simple app you know (for example a library system: main menu, search, borrow, return, fine calculation, database access). Write a top-down and a bottom-up integration order, and list which stubs or drivers you would need at each step.

quiz.q: In top-down integration, what temporarily replaces lower-level modules that are not ready?
quiz.explain: Top-down testing calls modules below that may not exist yet, so stubs stand in for them.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of big bang integration?
options: When a failure occurs, it is hard to locate which interface caused it
It only works for object-oriented programs
quiz.explain: All components are joined at once, so a failure could come from any of many interfaces.

quiz.q: Which defect is integration testing especially good at finding?
options: A spelling mistake in a button label
One module sends distance in metres while another expects kilometres
A slow sorting algorithm inside one function
A missing comment in the code
quiz.explain: Unit mismatches between components are interface defects, the main target of integration testing.

quiz.q: Which statement about bottom-up integration is correct?
options: It needs stubs for all lower modules
It tests the user interface first
It is the same as big bang integration
It uses drivers and tests low-level modules early
quiz.explain: Bottom-up starts from the lowest modules and uses drivers to call them until real callers exist.

quiz.q: In the V-model, which development stage is paired with unit testing?
quiz.explain: Unit tests are designed from the detailed (module) design; architecture pairs with integration testing.

lessons.title: System Testing and Acceptance Testing
lessons.content:
Imagine a new flyover in your city. Engineers have tested every beam, every joint and every section. Before it opens, they still close the whole flyover and drive loaded trucks across it, check the drainage in rain, test the lights at night and measure how traffic flows on and off the ramps. Then the city authority inspects it against the contract and safety rules and only then signs the papers to open it to the public. The first big check is like system testing; the authority's inspection and sign-off is like acceptance testing.

System testing, what it is: System testing evaluates the complete, integrated system as a whole, checking that it meets its specified requirements, both functional and non-functional. Unlike unit and integration testing, which look at pieces and joins, system testing looks at end-to-end behaviour: a user registers, searches for a product, adds to cart, pays, receives an SMS, and the warehouse sees the order. It answers the question: does the whole system do what the specification says, under realistic conditions?

Test basis for system testing: System tests are designed from system and software requirement specifications, user stories with acceptance criteria, use cases, epics and features, risk analysis reports, models of system behaviour such as state diagrams, and user manuals. Because the basis is the specification rather than the code, most system testing uses black-box techniques, which lessons 7 to 10 cover in depth.

What system testing covers: Functional system tests check business processes, calculations, workflows, data handling, reports and user interactions. Non-functional system tests check performance and load, security, usability, reliability (how long it runs without failure and how it recovers), compatibility with browsers and devices, installability and maintainability-related aspects such as logging. Many organisations run these as separate test types inside the system level, sometimes with specialist testers.

Typical defects at system level: Incorrect calculations visible to users, wrong or unexpected functional behaviour, incorrect control and data flow across the whole system, failure to carry out end-to-end tasks, failure to work properly in the production-like environment, behaviour that differs from the user manual, and non-functional failures such as slow responses or crashes under load. A classic example: every module works, but the full checkout flow fails when the user goes back to change the delivery address, because the session loses the cart.

The test environment matters: System testing should run in an environment as close to production as possible: similar servers, operating systems, database versions, configuration, network setup and realistic data volumes. A system that works on a developer's laptop with 50 test records may fail in production with 5 million records and real network latency. Environment differences are one of the most common reasons defects escape to production. Teams often keep a staging environment that mirrors production specifically for system and acceptance testing.

Recovery and installation checks: Two system-level checks are easy to forget. Recovery testing deliberately causes failures, such as killing the application server, unplugging the database connection or filling the disk, and checks that the system recovers correctly: no lost transactions, clear error messages, automatic restart where promised. Installation testing checks that the system can be installed, upgraded and uninstalled on the supported platforms, that an upgrade keeps the user's existing data, and that a failed installation can be rolled back cleanly.

Traceability at system level: Because system tests come from requirements, each test case should be linked to the requirement it checks, and each requirement to its tests. This makes it easy to answer two questions managers always ask: which requirements have no tests yet, and which requirements are affected when a test fails? Lesson 15 shows the traceability matrix used for this.

Who does system testing: System testing is often done by independent testers, either a test team within the organisation or testers embedded in the delivery team but not the authors of the code. Independence helps because system testers think like users and read the specification fresh. In Agile teams, system-level regression suites are often automated and run on every release candidate, while testers explore new features manually.

End-to-end testing: End-to-end testing is a style of system testing (and sometimes system integration testing) that follows a real user journey across all layers and connected systems: mobile app, backend, database, payment gateway, notification service. It is valuable because it is closest to what users experience, but end-to-end tests are slow and fragile, so teams keep a small number of them for the most important journeys. The test pyramid lesson explains this trade-off.

Entry and exit criteria: Entry criteria define when a test level can start; exit criteria define when it is done. Example entry criteria for system testing: integration testing finished with no open critical defects, the build installed in the system test environment, test data ready, and test cases reviewed. Example exit criteria: at least 95 percent of planned test cases executed, 100 percent of high-priority cases passed, no open critical or high-severity defects, and the remaining known defects accepted by the product owner. In Agile, similar ideas appear as the Definition of Ready and the Definition of Done.

Acceptance testing, what it is: Acceptance testing checks whether the system is ready to be accepted and deployed, focusing on whether it meets user needs, business processes and contractual or regulatory requirements. Its main objective is not to find many defects (if many are found at this level, something earlier went wrong) but to build confidence and give stakeholders the information to decide: ship or not? Acceptance testing is closely tied to validation.

User acceptance testing (UAT): UAT is done by the intended users, or people representing them, in a realistic environment. Users perform real tasks: an accountant closes a month in the new accounting software, a pharmacist dispenses medicines in a pharmacy system. The test basis is business processes, user requirements, use cases and acceptance criteria. UAT finds gaps between what was specified and what users actually need, such as missing steps, confusing workflows or reports that do not match how the business works.

Operational acceptance testing (OAT): OAT is done by operations or system administration staff to check that the system can be run and supported. Typical checks: backup and restore, disaster recovery, installing, upgrading and uninstalling, user and permission management, maintenance tasks, data loading and migration from the old system, monitoring and alerting, and checks for security vulnerabilities and performance under expected load. A system users love is still not acceptable if nobody can restore it after a server crash.

Contractual and regulatory acceptance testing: Contractual acceptance testing checks the system against acceptance criteria written in a contract, common when a client pays a vendor to build custom software. The client verifies each agreed criterion before paying the final instalment. Regulatory acceptance testing checks compliance with laws and regulations, such as rules for banking, healthcare, data protection or accessibility. These tests are often witnessed or reviewed by the client or regulator.

Alpha and beta testing: These are used by companies that sell software to many customers, where you cannot test with every customer. Alpha testing is done at the developer's site, by potential users, customers or an independent test team, before the product goes outside. Beta testing is done by real users at their own locations, on their own devices and networks, before final release. Mobile app stores support this with beta tracks and tester groups. Beta testing reveals problems that appear only in diverse real environments: unusual phones, slow networks, different languages.

Writing acceptance criteria: Good acceptance criteria are clear, testable and agreed before development. A popular format is Given-When-Then. For a ride booking story: Given a rider with a saved card, When they confirm a ride and the driver accepts, Then the card is authorised for the estimated fare and the rider sees the driver's name, car number and arrival time. Each criterion becomes one or more acceptance tests. Lesson 18 shows how BDD tools can run such criteria automatically.

Factory and site acceptance: For systems with hardware or installation, such as a hospital's patient management system or a toll plaza payment system, acceptance is often split. Factory acceptance testing happens at the supplier's premises before shipping; site acceptance testing happens after installation at the customer's site, with real networks and devices. Many issues, like a barcode scanner model that differs from the one tested, only appear at the site.

Sign-off: At the end of acceptance testing, stakeholders formally accept the system, often by signing an acceptance document listing what was tested, results, and known defects with agreed workarounds or fix dates. Sign-off is a business decision informed by testing, not a purely technical one. A product with a few known minor defects can be accepted; a product with a defect that blocks a core business process usually cannot.

Real-life example, a hospital appointment system: A private hospital in Chattogram commissions an appointment and billing system. System testers verify that doctors' schedules, booking, cancellation, billing and SMS reminders all work end to end in a staging environment with a copy of the doctor list. In UAT, front-desk staff discover that the system does not let them book for a patient who has no mobile phone, which is common for elderly patients who come with a relative. The specification never mentioned it. In OAT, the IT team confirms that nightly backups can be restored within the agreed time. Only after these issues are resolved does the hospital sign off.

Real-life example, a mobile banking app update: A bank prepares a major update. System testing covers transfers, bill payments and statements on a test environment. Then a beta goes to a few thousand volunteer customers. Beta users on older, low-memory phones report that the app crashes when opening the statement screen with a year of transactions. The in-house test phones were all newer. The bank fixes the memory issue before the full rollout, avoiding a flood of crashes for millions of customers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Do not confuse system testing (does the system meet its specification, usually by testers) with acceptance testing (is it ready to accept, usually by users, customers or operators). Know the forms of acceptance testing: UAT, OAT, contractual, regulatory, alpha and beta, and especially the difference between alpha (developer's site) and beta (user's site). Exams also ask for entry and exit criteria examples, the test basis of each level, and why the system test environment should mirror production.

Recap: System testing checks the whole integrated system against functional and non-functional requirements in a production-like environment, often by independent testers using black-box techniques, guided by entry and exit criteria. Acceptance testing decides whether the system is ready to deploy: UAT by users, OAT by operations, contractual and regulatory checks against agreements and laws, and alpha and beta testing for market products. Clear, testable acceptance criteria and a formal sign-off complete the picture. Next we look at test types, which cut across all these levels.
key_points: System testing checks the complete integrated system against functional and non-functional requirements.
The system test environment should mirror production in configuration, data volume and network setup.
Entry criteria say when testing may start; exit criteria say when it is finished.
Acceptance testing builds confidence and supports the ship or no-ship decision, not mainly defect hunting.
UAT is done by users; OAT by operations staff (backup, restore, recovery, migration, monitoring).
Contractual and regulatory acceptance testing check agreements and laws.
Alpha testing happens at the developer's site; beta testing happens with real users at their own sites.
lessons.tip: For any test level question, quickly list four things: objective, test basis, typical defects, and who does it. Most exam answers about levels are built from exactly these four.
lessons.task: Pick a system you use (a university portal, a bus ticket website, a mobile wallet). Write three entry criteria and four exit criteria for its system testing, then write two acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then form for one feature.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the main purpose of acceptance testing?
options: To find as many defects as possible in individual functions
To test the interfaces between components
To check code coverage of the system
To build confidence and decide whether the system is ready to be accepted and deployed
quiz.explain: Acceptance testing focuses on readiness and user or business needs; many defects at this level signal earlier problems.

quiz.q: Checking that backups can be restored and that data migrates from the old system is part of:
quiz.explain: OAT checks that operations staff can run and support the system: backup, restore, recovery, migration and monitoring.

quiz.q: Where does beta testing take place?
options: At the developer's site with an independent test team
Only in the developer's CI pipeline
At real users' own locations, devices and networks
quiz.explain: Beta testing uses real users in their own environments; alpha testing happens at the developer's site.

quiz.q: Why should the system test environment be close to production?
options: Because many failures depend on configuration, data volume and network conditions
Because unit tests cannot run elsewhere
Because acceptance testing must happen first
Because stubs work only in production
quiz.explain: A system that works with small data on a laptop can fail with production-scale data and real networks.

quiz.q: Which of these is a reasonable exit criterion for system testing?
options: All unit tests have been written
The test plan has a nice cover page
No open critical or high-severity defects remain
quiz.explain: Exit criteria are measurable conditions, such as no open critical defects and a minimum percentage of tests executed.

lessons.title: Test Types: Functional, Non-Functional, Regression, Smoke and Sanity
lessons.content:
Think about a car's yearly fitness check. The inspector checks what the car does: do the brakes stop it, do the indicators blink, does the horn sound? He also checks how well it does things: how much smoke comes out, how loud the engine is, how quickly the brakes respond. If a mechanic replaced the brake pads yesterday, the inspector rechecks the brakes, and also glances at the wheels and the lights, because mechanics sometimes loosen something else by accident. These different questions are exactly what test types are about. Levels tell you when and at what scale you test; types tell you what you are testing for.

Levels versus types: In the last two lessons we met test levels: unit, integration, system and acceptance. A test type is a group of test activities aimed at testing specific characteristics of a system. The key insight is that types and levels are independent: almost any type can be performed at any level. You can do functional testing at unit level and at acceptance level; you can do performance testing on a single function or on the entire system. A common way to group types is into four: functional testing, non-functional testing, white-box (structural) testing, and change-related testing.

Functional testing: Functional testing checks what the system should do: the functions described in requirements, user stories, use cases or simply in the minds of users. Examples: a transfer moves the right amount between the right accounts, a search returns matching products, a report shows correct totals, a form rejects invalid phone numbers. Functional testing asks about functional completeness (are all required functions present?), functional correctness (do they give correct results?) and functional appropriateness (do they actually help users achieve their tasks?). Black-box techniques are the main tools.

Functional testing at different levels: At unit level, a functional test checks that calculateVat(1000) returns the right amount. At integration level, it checks that the order service correctly asks the inventory service to reserve stock. At system level, it checks the full journey of placing and paying for an order. At acceptance level, a shop owner checks that the daily sales report matches how they actually close the day. Same type, different scale.

Non-functional testing: Non-functional testing checks how well the system behaves: characteristics such as performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability from ISO/IEC 25010. Examples: the search responds within 2 seconds for 1,000 concurrent users, the app works on Android phones with 2 GB of RAM, a blind user can complete registration with a screen reader, the system recovers within 5 minutes after a server crash. The name sounds like "not important", but non-functional failures (slowness, crashes under load, security breaches) are often what users and news reports remember most.

Making non-functional requirements testable: A requirement like "the app must be fast" cannot be tested. Testers push for measurable versions: "95 percent of login requests complete within 1.5 seconds with 500 concurrent users on the production-like environment." Good non-functional requirements state a measure, a target value and the conditions. Later lessons cover performance, security, usability and accessibility testing in detail.

White-box testing as a type: White-box (structural) testing derives tests from the internal structure or implementation of the system. At unit level, structure means code: statements, branches, conditions and paths, which lessons 11 to 13 cover deeply. At integration level, structure can mean the call graph or the set of API endpoints: have we called every endpoint at least once? At system level, structure can be menu items, screens or business process steps: have we visited every screen? Coverage measures how much of that structure the tests have exercised.

Change-related testing: When software changes, either to fix a defect or to add or modify functionality, testing must confirm the change worked and check that nothing else broke. This group has two members, often confused with each other: confirmation testing and regression testing. Every modern team does both constantly, because software changes constantly.

Confirmation testing (re-testing): After a defect is fixed, confirmation testing re-runs the test cases that failed because of that defect, using the same steps and data, to confirm the defect is truly gone. Testers may also add a few new tests around the fix, since a fix for one input sometimes misses a similar input. For example, if transfers of exactly 25,000 Taka were rejected and the developer fixed the boundary, the tester re-runs the 25,000 test and also tries 24,999.99 and 25,000.01 if decimals are allowed.

Regression testing: A regression is when something that worked before stops working after a change. Regression testing re-runs tests on previously working areas to detect such unintended side effects. A change in the discount module might break the invoice printout; an upgrade of a library might break login; a database index change might slow down reports. Regression can come from code changes, configuration changes, environment changes (new operating system version, new browser) or data changes.

Why regression suites grow and get automated: Every release adds features, and each feature adds tests to the regression suite. A suite that started with 100 tests can have thousands after a few years. Running them manually before every release becomes impossible, so regression suites are the prime candidates for automation. Automated regression tests can run nightly or on every commit in CI, giving fast feedback. Because they repeat the same checks, they also remind us of principle 5: they guard against breakage but rarely find new kinds of defects.

Selecting regression tests: When there is no time to run everything, teams choose. Retest-all runs the full suite; it is the safest and the most expensive. Selective regression picks tests related to the changed areas and their dependencies, based on impact analysis. Prioritisation orders tests by risk, business importance, frequency of use or past failure history, so the most valuable ones run first. Worked example: a suite has 1,200 tests and the team can run 300 manually before tomorrow's release. They choose all 80 tests touching the changed payment module, 120 tests of high-risk flows like login and checkout, and 100 tests from areas that failed in the last three releases.

Smoke testing: Smoke testing is a broad, shallow set of tests that checks whether a new build is stable enough to be tested further. The name comes from hardware: switch on a new circuit and see if smoke comes out. Typical smoke checks: the application installs and starts, the login page loads, a user can log in, the main menu opens, a basic transaction completes. If smoke tests fail, the build is rejected immediately, saving the team from wasting hours testing a broken build. Smoke tests are often automated and run on every build; they are sometimes called build verification tests.

Sanity testing: Sanity testing is a narrow, focused check of specific functionality after a small change or bug fix, to decide whether it is reasonable to proceed with more detailed testing. If a developer fixed the rounding in the VAT calculation, a quick sanity check confirms VAT now looks right on a few invoices before the full regression run. A common way to remember: smoke is wide and shallow across the whole build; sanity is narrow and a bit deeper on one area. Be aware that different companies use these words slightly differently; in an interview, explain what you mean.

Other names you will hear: Job descriptions and test plans mention many more named types: compatibility testing (browsers, devices, operating systems), localisation testing (languages, date and currency formats), installation testing, recovery testing, end-to-end testing, exploratory testing and more. Most of them fit inside the four groups: compatibility and recovery are non-functional, end-to-end is usually functional at system level, and exploratory testing is an approach that can serve any type. When you meet a new name, ask which characteristic it targets and at which level it is applied.

Maintenance testing: Once software is in production, it keeps changing: bug fixes, enhancements, upgrades, migration to new platforms, and eventually retirement. Maintenance testing is testing done on these changes in an operational system. Triggers include modification (fixes, new features, emergency patches), migration (moving to a new server, database or cloud platform, including data conversion testing) and retirement (testing data archiving and the ability to restore archived data if it must be kept for years).

Impact analysis: Before changing a live system, impact analysis identifies the intended consequences and the possible side effects of the change, and which areas need regression testing. It uses traceability links, dependency diagrams and knowledge of the code. Impact analysis is hard when documentation is outdated, traceability is missing, tests are poorly maintained, or the people who built the system have left, which is common in older systems.

Putting types and levels together: Imagine a matrix with levels as rows and types as columns. At unit level: functional tests of a function, white-box statement and branch coverage, and maybe a micro-benchmark for performance. At integration level: functional tests of service calls, endpoint coverage, and timeout behaviour. At system level: end-to-end functional flows, load tests, security scans. At acceptance level: users checking business processes, operations checking backup and recovery. Regression and confirmation tests appear at every level whenever something changes.

Real-life example, a VAT rate change: The government changes the VAT rate for a category of goods, and an e-commerce company in Dhaka updates its tax configuration. A quick smoke test checks the new build starts and a basic order can be placed. A sanity check confirms the new rate on a few sample invoices. Confirmation testing re-runs the tests that verify tax calculation. Then regression testing covers invoices, refunds, discount combinations, reports for accountants and the mobile app, because tax touches many places. A regression found: refunds for orders placed before the change were being recalculated at the new rate. It was fixed before customers noticed.

Real-life example, migrating a university's results system: A university moves its results database from an old on-premise server to a cloud platform. Maintenance testing focuses on migration: testers compare record counts and checksums between old and new databases, spot-check hundreds of students' grades and CGPAs, confirm that Bangla names are stored correctly in the new character encoding, and run performance tests to check that publishing results day by day still works under heavy load.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The top confusion is re-testing versus regression: re-testing confirms a specific fix; regression checks that unchanged areas still work. Another is smoke versus sanity. Exams also ask whether a type can be done at a given level (almost always yes), to classify requirements as functional or non-functional ("must respond in 2 seconds" is non-functional), to list triggers of maintenance testing (modification, migration, retirement), and to explain why regression suites are good automation candidates.

Recap: Test types describe what we test for, and they cut across all levels. Functional testing checks what the system does; non-functional testing checks how well it does it; white-box testing measures coverage of structure; change-related testing includes confirmation testing of fixes and regression testing for side effects. Smoke tests check build stability broadly; sanity tests check a specific change narrowly. Maintenance testing handles modification, migration and retirement of live systems, guided by impact analysis. Next we look at testing without running code at all: static testing.
key_points: Test types describe what is tested for; test levels describe at what stage and scale. Any type can be done at any level.
Functional testing checks what the system does; non-functional testing checks how well (performance, usability, security, reliability and more).
White-box testing as a type measures coverage of structure: code at unit level, endpoints or menus at higher levels.
Confirmation testing re-runs failed tests after a fix; regression testing checks that unchanged areas still work.
Regression suites grow over time and are prime candidates for automation and prioritisation.
Smoke testing is broad and shallow to check build stability; sanity testing is narrow and focused on a specific change.
Maintenance testing is triggered by modification, migration and retirement, and depends on impact analysis.
lessons.tip: When a question mentions "after a fix", ask yourself: is it checking the fix itself (confirmation) or everything around it (regression)? That single distinction answers a surprising number of exam questions.
lessons.task: Take a recent update of an app on your phone (read its "What's new" notes). Write one smoke test, one sanity test, two confirmation tests and five regression tests you would run for that update, and mark each test as functional or non-functional.

quiz.q: A developer fixes a defect in the discount calculation. Which test activity re-runs the test that originally failed?
quiz.explain: Confirmation testing re-runs the failing test to confirm the fix; regression testing looks for side effects elsewhere.

quiz.q: Which requirement is non-functional?
options: 95 percent of searches must return results within 2 seconds under 1,000 concurrent users
The system must calculate VAT on each invoice line
Users must be able to reset their password by SMS
The report must list sales grouped by branch
quiz.explain: Response time under load is a performance efficiency characteristic, so it is non-functional.

quiz.q: A new build arrives. The team quickly checks that it installs, starts, allows login and opens the main screen before any detailed testing. This is:
quiz.explain: Smoke testing is a broad, shallow check that the build is stable enough to test further.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a typical trigger for maintenance testing?
options: Migrating the database to a new platform
Retiring the system and archiving its data
Writing the first version of the requirements
quiz.explain: Maintenance testing applies to operational systems: modification, migration and retirement.

quiz.q: Why are regression test suites good candidates for automation?
options: They do not need expected results
They are repeated often and grow with every release
quiz.explain: Regression tests are re-run after every change, so automating them saves time and gives fast feedback.

lessons.title: Static Testing: Reviews, Inspections and Static Analysis
lessons.content:
Before a wedding invitation card goes to the printing press, someone in the family reads the draft carefully. Is the bride's father's name spelled right? Is the date the 14th or the 15th? Does the venue address include the floor number? Finding the mistake on the draft costs a pen mark. Finding it after printing 500 cards costs money, time and embarrassment. Nobody "runs" the card to test it; they examine it. That is static testing: finding defects by examining work products without executing them.

Static versus dynamic testing: Dynamic testing runs the software and observes failures, then someone has to debug to find the defect behind each failure. Static testing examines the work product directly and finds defects themselves, without needing a failure first. Both have the same goal, better quality, and they complement each other. Some defects are easier to find statically (a requirement that contradicts another, a variable that is never initialised), others dynamically (a timing problem under load).

What can be statically tested: Almost any work product: requirement specifications, user stories and acceptance criteria, architecture and design documents, source code, database schemas, test plans, test cases and test scripts, user manuals, contracts, project plans, configuration files, and even web page content. Code can be examined by people (reviews) or by tools (static analysis). Documents written in natural language are mostly reviewed by people, though tools can check spelling, readability and some patterns.

Why static testing pays off: It finds defects early, often before any code exists, when they are cheapest to fix (principle 3). It catches defects that dynamic tests struggle with: ambiguous or missing requirements, design flaws, poor maintainability, coding standard violations, security weaknesses in code patterns, and deviations from the agreed interface. It also spreads knowledge: reviewers learn the system and the author learns from reviewers. Studies of inspections over several decades have repeatedly reported that a large share of defects can be removed before testing begins.

Typical defects found by reviews: In requirements: inconsistencies, ambiguities, contradictions, omissions, inaccuracies and redundancies. In design: inefficient structures, poor modularity, missing error handling. In code: variables with undefined values, unreachable code, duplicated code, excessive complexity, missing checks for null or empty input. In interfaces: mismatched parameters or units. In security: hard-coded passwords, unchecked input passed into queries. In test cases: wrong expected results, missing coverage, unclear steps.

A requirement review example: Consider this requirement: "The system shall respond quickly and users shall login with a valid password." A reviewer would ask: What does quickly mean, 1 second or 10? Is it measured under what load? What makes a password valid: length, characters, expiry? What happens after three wrong attempts? Is login by phone number, email or user ID? Five minutes of review turns one vague sentence into five clear, testable requirements, before a single line of code is written.

The review process: Most reviews, formal or not, follow similar activities. Planning: define scope, objectives, which documents, who takes part, time and entry criteria. Review initiation (kick-off): make sure everyone has the material and understands the goal and checklist. Individual review (preparation): each reviewer studies the work product alone and notes possible anomalies, questions and recommendations. Communication and analysis: the findings are discussed, often in a review meeting, and each one is classified (defect, question, improvement) with an owner and status. Fixing and reporting: the author fixes defects, updates are checked, and the results and metrics are reported. The international standard for work product reviews, ISO/IEC 20246, describes this kind of process.

Roles in a review: The author creates the work product and fixes the defects. Management decides what is reviewed, provides time and resources and monitors cost-effectiveness. The facilitator, often called the moderator, ensures the review meetings run effectively, mediates disagreements and creates a safe atmosphere. The review leader takes overall responsibility for the review: who participates, when and where. Reviewers, who may be subject experts, testers, developers or users, find anomalies. The scribe, or recorder, collects and documents the findings. In small reviews one person may hold several roles.

Informal review: The lightest form: no defined process and no formal documented output. A developer asks a teammate, "Can you take a look at this function?" Pair programming is a continuous informal review. The main goal is detecting anomalies quickly and cheaply. Informal reviews are very common in Agile teams and are effective when people are experienced.

Walkthrough: A walkthrough is led by the author, who walks participants through the work product, step by step, explaining the logic. Objectives include finding defects, improving the product, considering alternatives, and educating participants, for example teaching new team members a module. Preparation by reviewers is optional, the meeting can range from quite informal to fairly formal, and a scribe may record findings. A dry run, where participants trace sample inputs through the code by hand, is a classic walkthrough technique.

Technical review: A technical review is performed by technically qualified reviewers, ideally peers and experts, and led by a trained facilitator rather than the author. Its objectives are reaching consensus on technical decisions, detecting anomalies, evaluating quality and considering alternative solutions. Individual preparation before the meeting is expected. An architecture review before building a new payment system is a typical technical review.

Inspection: An inspection is the most formal review type. It follows a defined process with formal documented outputs, uses trained participants in clear roles, applies checklists and rules, has entry and exit criteria, and collects metrics such as defects found per page and time spent, so the process itself can be improved. The author cannot lead the inspection or act as the scribe. Its main objective is to find as many anomalies as possible, and its metrics feed process improvement, which links inspections to QA.

Fagan inspection: The classic inspection method was described by Michael Fagan at IBM in the 1970s.
