Its steps are planning (check entry criteria, choose participants, schedule), overview (the author explains the product to the group), preparation (each inspector studies the material alone, using checklists), inspection meeting (a reader paraphrases the product piece by piece while inspectors raise defects; the goal is finding, not fixing), rework (the author fixes the logged defects) and follow-up (the moderator verifies all fixes and decides whether a re-inspection is needed). Keeping meetings short and focused, typically not more than about two hours, keeps reviewers sharp.

Checklists: A checklist turns experience into questions. For code: Are all variables initialised before use? Are loop boundaries correct? Is every opened file or connection closed? Are all inputs validated? Are error codes checked? Is money stored in an appropriate type and not a floating-point type that causes rounding errors? For requirements: Is each requirement testable, unambiguous, consistent and traceable? Checklists should be short, specific and updated from defects found in real projects.

Modern code review: In most teams today, code review happens through pull requests (merge requests) on platforms such as GitHub or GitLab. A developer proposes a change, automated checks run, and one or two teammates comment on lines, request changes or approve. This is lighter than a Fagan inspection but keeps key ideas: a second pair of eyes, small reviewable chunks, and a record of decisions. Reviews work best when changes are small; a pull request with thousands of changed lines usually gets a shallow review.

Static analysis by tools: Static analysis tools examine source code (or compiled code) without running it. Compilers already do some: type errors, undeclared variables. Linters such as ESLint for JavaScript or Pylint for Python flag suspicious patterns and style violations. Broader platforms such as SonarQube report bugs, code smells, duplicated code, security hotspots and complexity. Static analysis can find unused variables, unreachable code, possible null dereferences, variables used before being assigned (a data-flow anomaly, covered in lesson 13), infinite loop patterns, and code that resembles known security vulnerabilities.

Limits of static analysis: Tools produce false positives (warnings that are not real problems) and false negatives (real problems they miss). A flood of low-value warnings makes developers ignore all warnings, so teams tune rule sets and fix or suppress warnings deliberately. Tools cannot judge whether the code meets the business requirement; for that you still need humans and dynamic tests. The best practice is to run static analysis automatically in the CI pipeline and block merges only on important rules.

Review metrics, a worked example: Inspections collect numbers so the process can be judged. Suppose four inspectors review a 20-page design document. Each spends 3 hours preparing and the meeting lasts 2 hours, so effort is 4 x 3 + 4 x 2 = 20 person-hours. They log 30 defects, of which 6 are major. That is 1.5 defects per page and 1.5 defects per person-hour. If later testing finds only 2 more design defects, the inspection caught 30 out of 32, about 94 percent. Numbers like these help decide whether inspections are worth their cost, and comparing them across projects shows when reviewers are rushing.

Success factors for reviews: Clear objectives for each review, the right review type for the situation, small chunks of material, enough time to prepare, trained participants, checklists, management support, and above all a culture where defects found in review are welcomed rather than used to judge people. If authors feel attacked, they stop submitting work for review. Metrics from reviews should improve the process, not rank developers.

Real-life example, a garments factory payroll system: A software firm building payroll for a garments factory holds a requirements walkthrough with the factory's HR and accounts staff. During the walkthrough, an accountant notices that the document calculates overtime on basic salary, while the factory's actual rule and labour regulations use a different base. No code existed yet. Fixing one paragraph prevented wrong overtime pay for thousands of workers, which would have caused disputes and possibly legal trouble.

Real-life example, static analysis catching a security hole: A university's course registration system is being updated. The CI pipeline runs a static analysis tool on every pull request. One new function builds a database query by joining strings with a student ID taken directly from the web form. The tool flags it as a possible SQL injection. The reviewer asks the developer to use a parameterised query. A dynamic test might have missed it if nobody tried a malicious input; the static check caught the pattern immediately.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Exams ask you to order or compare review types by formality: informal, walkthrough, technical review, inspection, with inspection the most formal and walkthrough led by the author. Know the roles and who cannot be the facilitator in an inspection (the author). Know the Fagan steps. Understand that static testing finds defects directly while dynamic testing finds failures. A common mistake is thinking static testing applies only to code; it applies to any work product.

Recap: Static testing examines work products without executing them, finding defects early and cheaply. Reviews range from informal reviews and author-led walkthroughs to technical reviews and formal inspections such as Fagan's, with defined roles, preparation, checklists and metrics. Modern teams use pull request reviews for code. Static analysis tools catch suspicious code patterns, standard violations and security risks automatically, but need tuning and human judgment. Next we start test design in earnest with equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis.
key_points: Static testing examines work products without running them and finds defects directly; dynamic testing finds failures.
Any work product can be statically tested: requirements, designs, code, test cases, manuals, contracts.
The review process: planning, initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, fixing and reporting.
Roles: author, management, facilitator (moderator), review leader, reviewers, scribe.
Review types by formality: informal, walkthrough (led by author), technical review, inspection (most formal, with metrics).
Fagan inspection steps: planning, overview, preparation, meeting, rework, follow-up.
Static analysis tools find suspicious code patterns, data-flow anomalies and security risks, but produce false positives.
lessons.tip: When preparing for a review, read the material once for understanding and a second time only with the checklist in hand. Two focused passes find far more than one long tired read.
lessons.task: Find a short notice, form or set of instructions from your university or an app's terms (half a page). Review it like an inspector: list every ambiguity, contradiction, missing piece of information and untestable statement you find, and rewrite two sentences so they become clear and testable.

quiz.q: Which review type is led by the author, who explains the work product step by step?
quiz.explain: In a walkthrough the author leads participants through the material; inspections are led by a trained facilitator.

quiz.q: Which statement about static testing is correct?
options: It can only be applied to source code
It requires running the software in a test environment
It finds failures, which must then be debugged
It can find defects in requirements before any code exists
quiz.explain: Static testing examines any work product, including requirements, and finds defects directly.

quiz.q: In a formal inspection, which role may the author NOT take?
options: Person who answers questions during the meeting
quiz.explain: In inspections the moderator (leader) must be someone other than the author, and the author should not be the scribe either.

quiz.q: Which step of a Fagan inspection is when each inspector studies the material alone with checklists?
quiz.explain: In preparation, inspectors individually study the product and note possible defects before the meeting.

quiz.q: A static analysis tool reports a warning that turns out not to be a real problem. This is called:
quiz.explain: A false positive is a reported problem that is not real; a false negative is a real problem the tool missed.

lessons.title: Equivalence Partitioning and Boundary Value Analysis in Depth
lessons.content:
A rice merchant does not taste every grain in a 50 kg sack. He pushes a probe into the sack at a few places and checks samples. But he is clever about where: he checks the top, the middle and especially the bottom, because that is where broken grains and dust collect. Equivalence partitioning is the "few samples" idea: inputs that behave the same need only one representative. Boundary value analysis is the "check the bottom of the sack" idea: problems gather at the edges. In Software Engineering you met both briefly with an age example; here we go further, with multiple inputs, formal counts and tricky non-numeric cases.

The problem these techniques solve: Exhaustive testing is impossible (principle 2), so we need a systematic way to choose a small set of inputs that is still likely to reveal defects. Black-box techniques give rules for this choice based only on the specification. Equivalence partitioning (EP) reduces the number of tests; boundary value analysis (BVA) puts them where defects are most likely. Together they are the most widely used test design techniques in the world.

Equivalence partitioning, the core idea: Divide the set of possible values of an input (or output, or internal value, or time) into partitions, also called equivalence classes, so that the system is expected to treat every value in a partition the same way. If one value in a partition reveals a defect, other values probably would too; if one value works, others probably work. Then pick at least one value from each partition. Partitions must not overlap, and together they should cover all possible values, including invalid ones.

Valid and invalid partitions: A valid partition contains values the system should accept and process normally. An invalid partition contains values the system should reject or handle as errors. Both matter. A common rule: combine several valid partitions in one test case when convenient, but test each invalid partition in a separate test case. If you send an invalid amount and an invalid phone number in the same test, the first error message may hide whether the second was handled at all; this is called defect masking.

Worked example, a recharge screen: Suppose a mobile recharge screen accepts amounts from 20 to 1,000 Taka in whole Taka. Partitions for amount: invalid below (less than 20), valid (20 to 1,000), invalid above (more than 1,000). Further invalid partitions: non-numeric text ("abc"), empty input, decimal values (25.50) if paisa is not allowed, and negative numbers (which are part of "below 20" but are worth a separate thought because they may be parsed differently). Representatives: 5, 300, 1,500, "abc", empty, 25.50. Six tests cover every kind of behaviour described.

Partitions from rules inside the valid range: Specifications often split the valid range further. Suppose recharges of 20 to 99 Taka get no bonus, 100 to 499 Taka get 5 percent bonus talk time, and 500 to 1,000 Taka get 10 percent. Now there are three valid partitions, because the system behaves differently in each. Representatives: 50, 300 and 700. Always ask: where does the specification say the behaviour changes? Each change creates a new partition.

Partitions for a Bangladeshi phone number: Suppose the same screen takes an 11-digit mobile number starting with 01 followed by a valid operator digit (3 to 9). Valid partition: 11 digits with a valid prefix such as 017 or 019. Invalid partitions: wrong prefix (012), 10 digits, 12 digits, letters inside the number, empty, and a number written with the country code (+880) if the specification does not allow it. Notice that partitions here are about format, length and content, not numeric size.

Multiple inputs, weak versus strong: When there are several inputs, how do we combine partitions? Weak equivalence class testing assumes inputs are independent and uses as few tests as possible, so that every partition of every input is covered at least once. The number of tests equals the largest number of partitions of any single input. Strong equivalence class testing assumes interactions matter and tests every combination of partitions, the Cartesian product. Adding "robust" means invalid partitions are included too.

Worked example, weak versus strong: Take amount with three valid partitions (no bonus, 5 percent, 10 percent) and connection type with two valid partitions (prepaid, postpaid). Weak normal testing needs max(3, 2) = 3 tests: (50, prepaid), (300, postpaid), (700, prepaid). Every partition appears at least once. Strong normal testing needs 3 x 2 = 6 tests, every combination. Strong testing finds defects caused by interactions, such as a bonus that is wrongly applied to postpaid customers, but grows quickly as inputs are added. Choosing between them is a risk decision.

EP coverage: Coverage for EP is the number of partitions exercised by at least one test, divided by the total number of identified partitions, as a percentage. In the recharge example with 3 valid and 6 invalid partitions for amount, testing 50, 300, 700, 5 and 1,500 covers 5 of 9 partitions, about 56 percent. Adding "abc", empty, 25.50 and -10 reaches 100 percent. Coverage tells you whether each identified behaviour has been tried; it cannot tell you whether you identified all the partitions.

Boundary value analysis, the core idea: BVA applies to partitions whose values are ordered, such as numbers, dates, lengths or sizes. The boundary values are the minimum and maximum values of each partition. Developers often get edges wrong: writing less-than instead of less-than-or-equal, starting a loop at 1 instead of 0, or forgetting the last day of the month. So BVA tests values on and next to boundaries, where defects concentrate.

Two-value and three-value BVA: In two-value BVA, for each boundary you test the boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition. For 20 to 1,000: 19 and 20 at the lower end, 1,000 and 1,001 at the upper end, four tests. In three-value BVA, you test the boundary and both its neighbours: 19, 20, 21 and 999, 1,000, 1,001, six tests. Three-value BVA is more thorough. For example, if the developer wrote amount == 20 as a special case instead of amount >= 20, the value 21 would expose it, while 19 and 20 alone might not.

Boundaries of internal partitions: With the bonus rules, there are boundaries between valid partitions too: 99 and 100, 499 and 500. Using two-value BVA on all edges gives 19, 20, 99, 100, 499, 500, 1,000, 1,001: eight values, each testing that the behaviour switches at exactly the right point. A defect like if (amount > 100) give 5 percent bonus fails at 100, which is precisely the kind of mistake BVA is designed to catch.

The textbook counts for several variables: Classic textbooks, notably Jorgensen's, describe BVA for functions of n independent variables. Normal BVA keeps all variables at a nominal (middle) value except one, which takes min, min+, max- and max; with one all-nominal test this gives 4n + 1 tests. Robust BVA adds min- and max+ (just outside), giving 6n + 1. Worst-case BVA drops the single-fault assumption and takes the Cartesian product of the five values (min, min+, nominal, max-, max) for each variable: 5 to the power n tests. Robust worst-case uses seven values per variable: 7 to the power n.

Worked counts for two variables: Let amount range over 20 to 1,000 (min 20, min+ 21, nominal 510, max- 999, max 1,000) and recharges per day range over 1 to 5 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, nominal 3). Normal BVA: 4 x 2 + 1 = 9 tests, for example (20, 3), (21, 3), (999, 3), (1,000, 3), (510, 1), (510, 2), (510, 4), (510, 5) and (510, 3). Robust BVA: 6 x 2 + 1 = 13, adding (19, 3), (1,001, 3), (510, 0) and (510, 6). Worst-case: 5 x 5 = 25. Robust worst-case: 7 x 7 = 49. With 5 variables, worst-case would already be 3,125 tests, which shows why the single-fault assumption is so useful.

Non-numeric boundaries: Boundaries hide everywhere. String length: if a name must be 2 to 50 characters, test 1, 2, 50 and 51. Collections: an empty cart, one item, the maximum allowed, and one more. Dates and times: an offer valid until 31 December at 11:59 pm, the 28th, 29th and 1st around February in leap and non-leap years, midnight. Money with decimals: if paisa is allowed, the neighbours of 20.00 are 19.99 and 20.01, because the smallest step is 0.01. Always determine the smallest meaningful increment before choosing neighbours.

When EP and BVA are not enough: Both techniques assume that values within a partition are processed the same way and that inputs are largely independent. When outputs depend on combinations of conditions, decision tables (next lesson) work better. When behaviour depends on history, state transition testing is needed. When the specification itself is wrong about where the boundary is, only reviews and validation catch it. Also, EP and BVA say nothing about which code was executed; white-box coverage measures that.

Real-life example, a university admission form: An admission portal accepts SSC and HSC GPA from 1.00 to 5.00 with two decimal places, and requires a combined GPA of at least 7.00 for one department. EP gives partitions for each GPA: invalid below 1.00, valid 1.00 to 5.00, invalid above 5.00, plus non-numeric and too many decimals. BVA tests 0.99, 1.00, 5.00 and 5.01 for each, and for the combined rule 6.99 and 7.00. During testing, 7.00 was rejected because the code compared floating-point sums like 3.50 + 3.50 in a way that introduced rounding error. Changing to exact decimal arithmetic fixed it, and a deserving applicant would no longer be turned away.

Real-life example, an e-commerce cart limit: A Dhaka online shop limits each order to 10 units of the same discounted product during a flash sale. Testers try 0, 1, 10 and 11 units. With 11 the site correctly shows an error, but they also try increasing the quantity from 10 to 11 using the plus button in the cart rather than typing, and the limit is bypassed because the button path skipped the validation. The boundary was right, but one input path missed it, a reminder to apply boundaries to every way a value can enter the system.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include testing only valid partitions, combining several invalid inputs in one test, forgetting partitions inside the valid range, and choosing neighbours with the wrong step size for decimals. Exam questions typically give a specification and ask for partitions, representative values, two-value or three-value boundary values, the minimum number of tests for 100 percent EP coverage, or the 4n + 1 and 5 to the power n counts. Read carefully whether the range is inclusive and what the smallest increment is.

Recap: Equivalence partitioning groups inputs and outputs into classes the system should treat alike, valid and invalid, and tests one value per class, keeping invalid partitions in separate tests. With several inputs, weak testing covers each partition once while strong testing covers all combinations. Boundary value analysis tests at and around the edges of ordered partitions, in two-value or three-value form; textbook counts for n variables are 4n + 1, 6n + 1, 5 to the power n and 7 to the power n. Next we handle combinations of conditions with decision tables.
key_points: Equivalence partitioning divides values into classes treated alike and tests at least one value from each, valid and invalid.
Test each invalid partition separately to avoid defect masking.
Every place the specification changes behaviour creates a new partition, including inside the valid range.
Weak equivalence class testing needs as many tests as the largest number of partitions; strong testing uses all combinations.
Two-value BVA tests each boundary and its outside neighbour; three-value BVA also tests the inside neighbour.
For n variables: normal BVA 4n+1, robust 6n+1, worst-case 5^n, robust worst-case 7^n tests.
Boundaries also exist for string lengths, collection sizes, dates, times and decimal money values.
lessons.tip: Before choosing boundary neighbours, always write down the smallest step of the value (1 Taka, 0.01 Taka, 1 character, 1 day). Half of the BVA mistakes in exams come from using the wrong step.
lessons.task: A bus ticket website allows booking 1 to 6 seats per order, for journeys 1 to 30 days ahead, and gives a 10 percent discount for 4 or more seats. List all equivalence partitions for both inputs, write two-value boundary values for each, and compute the number of tests for normal BVA and worst-case BVA.

quiz.q: A field accepts whole numbers from 20 to 1,000. Which set is three-value boundary value analysis?
quiz.explain: Three-value BVA tests each boundary and the values just below and just above it.

quiz.q: Why should each invalid partition be tested in a separate test case?
options: Invalid inputs are always rejected anyway
One error may mask whether another invalid input was handled
It reduces the total number of tests
Tools cannot run tests with more than one invalid value
quiz.explain: If two invalid values are combined, the first error message can hide a missing check for the second.

quiz.q: Amount has 3 valid partitions and connection type has 2. How many tests does weak normal equivalence class testing need at minimum?
quiz.explain: Weak testing covers every partition at least once, so it needs the largest partition count: max(3, 2) = 3. Strong testing needs 6.

quiz.q: How many test cases does normal boundary value analysis need for a function of 3 independent variables?
quiz.explain: Normal BVA needs 4n + 1 = 4 x 3 + 1 = 13 tests; worst-case would be 5^3 = 125.

quiz.q: Money values allow paisa (two decimal places). Using two-value BVA, what are the values at the lower boundary of a range starting at 20.00?
quiz.explain: The smallest step is 0.01, so the outside neighbour of 20.00 is 19.99.

lessons.title: Decision Tables and Cause-Effect Graphing
lessons.content:
Think about the rules your family uses to decide who goes to the bazar. If it is Friday and Abbu is home, Abbu goes. If it is not Friday but you have no class, you go. If it is raining, nobody goes and the order goes online, unless the fridge is empty, in which case someone goes anyway. Try saying all of that clearly in one sentence and you will get tangled. Write it as a small table of conditions and actions and suddenly every case is visible, including the strange ones nobody thought about. That is the power of a decision table.

Why we need decision tables: Equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis treat inputs mostly one at a time. But much business logic depends on combinations: a loan depends on age and income and credit history together; a delivery fee depends on location and order value and membership. Testing each condition separately can miss defects that only appear in a particular combination. Decision tables capture combinations systematically and give a test for each meaningful one.

Structure of a decision table: The table has four parts. Conditions are listed in the upper rows, actions in the lower rows. Each column is a rule: one combination of condition values together with the actions that should happen. Condition entries are usually T and F (true or false, or Y and N); action entries are usually X (do it) or blank (do not). Each rule normally becomes one test case: set up inputs to match the conditions, and check that exactly the marked actions happen.

How many rules: With n conditions that are each true or false, the full table has 2 to the power n rules, because each condition doubles the combinations. Two conditions give 4 rules, three give 8, four give 16, ten give 1,024. This growth is why decision tables are best for focused pieces of logic, and why we try to simplify them.

A worked example, a bank's personal loan: The rules are: an applicant who has defaulted on a previous loan is rejected. Otherwise, an applicant whose age is not between 21 and 60 is rejected. Otherwise, if monthly income is at least 30,000 Taka the loan is approved, and if income is lower the application goes to manual review by an officer. Conditions: C1 age is 21 to 60, C2 income is at least 30,000, C3 has a previous default. Actions: A1 approve, A2 reject, A3 send to manual review. With three conditions the full table has 8 rules.

Filling the full table: List all 8 combinations of (C1, C2, C3). Whenever C3 is true (four combinations), the action is reject. When C3 is false and C1 is false (two combinations, C2 true or false), the action is reject. When C3 is false, C1 is true and C2 is true, approve. When C3 is false, C1 is true and C2 is false, manual review. Writing all eight out by hand is a great exercise because it forces you to check every combination against the specification, and it often reveals questions the specification did not answer.

Collapsing with don't-care entries: Notice that when C3 is true, the values of C1 and C2 do not matter: all four columns have the same action. We can merge them into one rule with a dash, meaning "don't care", for C1 and C2. Similarly, when C3 is false and C1 is false, C2 does not matter. The collapsed table has 4 rules: R1 (C1 -, C2 -, C3 T) reject; R2 (C1 F, C2 -, C3 F) reject; R3 (C1 T, C2 T, C3 F) approve; R4 (C1 T, C2 F, C3 F) manual review. Check: R1 covers 4 original columns, R2 covers 2, R3 and R4 cover 1 each, 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 8, so nothing was lost.

Turning rules into test cases: For each rule, choose concrete data. R1: age 35, income 50,000, previous default yes, expect reject. R2: age 19, income 50,000, no default, expect reject. R3: age 35, income 45,000, no default, expect approve. R4: age 35, income 20,000, no default, expect manual review. Now combine with BVA for the numeric conditions: add ages 20, 21, 60, 61 and incomes 29,999 and 30,000 in rules where those conditions matter. Decision tables decide which combinations; BVA decides exact values.

When to collapse and when not to: Collapsing reduces tests, but it assumes the implementation really ignores the don't-care conditions. If a programmer accidentally checked income before default, a defaulter with high income might be approved. A test of R1 with low income would never notice. For high-risk logic, testers sometimes test the full expanded table, or at least choose don't-care values that are most likely to expose a wrong order of checks, here a defaulter with high income and a valid age.

Impossible and infeasible combinations: Some combinations cannot happen. If the conditions are "age is under 18" and "age is over 60", both cannot be true at once. Such columns are marked infeasible and removed. Removing them is fine, but the tester should confirm with the specification that they are truly impossible, not just unlikely. Sometimes "impossible" combinations happen through bad data imported from another system.

Extended-entry decision tables: Conditions do not have to be true or false. In an extended-entry table a condition can take several values. Suppose a courier charges by zone (inside Dhaka, Dhaka suburbs, outside Dhaka) and by parcel weight (up to 1 kg, more than 1 kg). The table has 3 x 2 = 6 rules, each with its own fee. In general, the number of rules is the product of the number of values of each condition. Extended entries keep the table compact and readable when conditions are naturally multi-valued.

Decision table coverage: Coverage is the number of rules (columns) exercised by at least one test divided by the total number of feasible rules, as a percentage. In the collapsed loan table, testing R1, R3 and R4 gives 3 of 4 rules, 75 percent; adding R2 gives 100 percent. Some standards and teams define coverage against the full expanded table instead; state which one you are using.

Benefits beyond testing: Building a decision table is also a powerful static test of the requirements. When you fill in every column, you quickly find combinations the specification never mentions (what happens to a 65-year-old with no default and high income? The specification says reject, but did the business really intend that?) and contradictions (two rules that give different actions for the same combination). These questions go back to the business analyst before any code is written.

Cause-effect graphing, the idea: Cause-effect graphing, described in Glenford Myers' classic book on software testing, is a more formal way to reach a decision table when logic is complex. Causes are input conditions (each true or false); effects are outputs or system actions. The tester draws a graph that connects causes to effects using Boolean operators: identity, NOT, AND and OR, sometimes with intermediate nodes for sub-expressions.

Constraints in cause-effect graphs: Real causes are not always independent, so the notation includes constraints. Exclusive (E): at most one of the causes can be true. Inclusive (I): at least one must be true. One and only one (O): exactly one must be true. Requires (R): if one cause is true, another must be true too. A masking constraint (M) can link effects: one effect being true forces another to be false. These constraints remove impossible combinations before the decision table is produced.

From graph to table: Once the graph is complete, it is converted into a limited-entry decision table: for each effect, the tester traces backwards to find combinations of causes that make it true or false, respecting constraints. Each resulting column becomes a test case. The method is systematic and catches logic that is easy to get wrong in prose, but drawing graphs for large systems is laborious, so in practice many testers go straight to decision tables and use cause-effect thinking informally.

A tiny cause-effect example: A file-update command works like this: if the first character is A or B and the second character is a digit, the file is updated. If the first character is wrong, message X is shown. If the second character is not a digit, message Y is shown. Causes: C1 first character is A, C2 first character is B, C3 second character is a digit. Effects: E1 update, E2 message X, E3 message Y. Graph: an intermediate node for C1 OR C2; E1 = (C1 OR C2) AND C3; E2 = NOT (C1 OR C2); E3 = NOT C3. C1 and C2 have an exclusive constraint, because one character cannot be both A and B.

Real-life example, a university tuition waiver: A private university gives 50 percent waiver for CGPA at least 3.90, 25 percent for 3.75 to 3.89, an extra 10 percent for siblings studying at the same time, and no waiver if the student has a disciplinary record. A tester builds an extended-entry decision table: CGPA band (three values), sibling (yes or no), disciplinary record (yes or no), giving 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 combinations before collapsing. While filling it, she asks: does a student with CGPA 3.70 and a sibling get 10 percent, or nothing? The rules were silent. The registrar's office decided 10 percent, the specification was updated, and the test cases were written accordingly.

Real-life example, an e-commerce free delivery rule: A shop gives free delivery inside Dhaka for orders of 1,000 Taka or more, free delivery anywhere for premium members, and charges normally otherwise. A decision table with conditions (inside Dhaka, order at least 1,000, premium member) has 8 rules. Testing all 8 reveals that a premium member outside Dhaka with an order under 1,000 is charged, because the code checked location first and exited. Equivalence partitioning on each condition separately had passed; only the combination exposed the defect.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes are forgetting combinations, collapsing columns whose actions differ, assuming don't-care means "never matters" in the code, and not combining decision tables with BVA for numeric conditions. Exams ask you to build a table from a paragraph, count rules (2 to the power n, or a product for extended entries), collapse it, compute decision table coverage, derive test cases, and sometimes draw a simple cause-effect graph with AND, OR, NOT and the E, I, O, R constraints.

Recap: Decision tables list conditions and actions, with each column a rule that becomes a test case. Full tables have 2 to the power n rules for n binary conditions, or the product of values for extended entries. Don't-care entries collapse equivalent columns, but risky logic may deserve the full table. Coverage counts exercised rules. Cause-effect graphing formalises the path from causes to effects with Boolean operators and constraints before producing the table. Next we test behaviour that depends on history: state transition and use-case testing.
key_points: Decision tables test combinations of conditions: conditions and actions in rows, each column a rule and a test case.
n binary conditions give 2^n rules; extended-entry tables have the product of each condition's number of values.
Don't-care entries collapse columns with the same action, but risky logic may need the full table.
Remove infeasible combinations only after confirming they truly cannot happen.
Decision table coverage is exercised rules divided by total feasible rules.
Combine decision tables (which combinations) with BVA (exact numeric values).
Cause-effect graphing links causes to effects with AND, OR, NOT and constraints E, I, O, R and M before building the table.
lessons.tip: Whenever a requirement contains the words "if", "unless", "except" or "only when" more than twice, stop reading and draw a decision table. The gaps in the requirement will jump out at you.
lessons.task: Your mobile operator offers: a data pack of 10 GB for 7 days at a discount if you are a prepaid user and have recharged at least 300 Taka in the last 30 days; postpaid users always get the discount; nobody gets it while their account is suspended. Build the full decision table, collapse it, and write one test case with concrete data for each collapsed rule.

quiz.q: A decision table has 4 independent true-or-false conditions. How many rules does the full table have?
quiz.explain: Each binary condition doubles the combinations: 2^4 = 16 rules.

quiz.q: An extended-entry decision table has a condition with 3 values, another with 2 values and a third with 2 values. How many rules are in the full table?
quiz.explain: The number of rules is the product of the values: 3 x 2 x 2 = 12.

quiz.q: What does a dash (don't care) mean in a collapsed decision table rule?
options: The value of that condition does not change the action for that rule
quiz.explain: A dash means any value of that condition leads to the same action, so several columns were merged.

quiz.q: A collapsed table has 5 feasible rules and the tests exercise 4 of them. What is the decision table coverage?
quiz.explain: Coverage = exercised rules / feasible rules = 4 / 5 = 80 percent.

quiz.q: In cause-effect graphing, what does the exclusive (E) constraint mean?
options: At most one of the linked causes can be true at the same time
At least one cause must be true
One effect forces another to be false
If one cause is true, another must also be true
quiz.explain: E means the causes cannot be true together; I means at least one, O exactly one, R requires, M masks effects.

lessons.title: State Transition Testing and Use-Case Testing
lessons.content:
Think about a traffic light at a busy Dhaka intersection. Pressing the pedestrian button does different things depending on what the light is doing right now. If the light is green for cars, the button starts a countdown. If it is already red for cars, the button does nothing new. The same event, a button press, leads to different results depending on the current state. Many systems behave like this: ATMs, login screens, online orders, ride bookings. To test them we need a technique that models states and the events that move between them.

What a state machine is: A state machine describes a system that can be in one of a finite number of states at any time. A state is a condition the system remains in until something happens, such as "Idle", "Waiting for PIN" or "Order shipped". An event is something that happens, such as a button press, a message arriving or a timer expiring. A transition is a change from one state to another caused by an event. An action is what the system does during the transition, such as showing a message or sending an SMS. A guard is a condition that must be true for the transition to happen, written in square brackets, for example [balance at least amount].

Why the order of inputs matters: Equivalence partitioning and decision tables treat inputs as if the order and history did not matter. But typing a wrong PIN for the third time should behave very differently from typing it for the first time. The input is identical; the history is different. State transition testing captures this by treating the history as a state. It is widely used for embedded software, protocols, user interfaces with modes and workflows such as orders and approvals.

A worked model, an ATM PIN check: States: S1 Idle, S2 waiting for PIN (first try), S3 second try, S4 third try, S5 access granted, S6 card retained. Events: insert card, valid PIN, invalid PIN. Transitions: S1 to S2 on insert card; S2 to S5 on valid PIN; S2 to S3 on invalid PIN; S3 to S5 on valid PIN; S3 to S4 on invalid PIN; S4 to S5 on valid PIN; S4 to S6 on invalid PIN, with the action "retain card and show message". That is 7 valid transitions in total.

The state diagram: Draw each state as a rounded box or circle and each transition as an arrow labelled with "event [guard] / action". The diagram makes the flow easy to see and discuss with developers and business people. Often just drawing the diagram reveals specification gaps: what happens if the customer presses Cancel while waiting for the PIN? What if there is no input for 30 seconds? Neither event is in our model yet, and both are real.

The state table: A state table lists every state as a row and every event as a column, and each cell shows the resulting state (and action) or marks the combination as invalid. With 6 states and 3 events, the table has 6 x 3 = 18 cells. Only 7 contain valid transitions; the other 11 are combinations where the event should have no effect or should be rejected, such as "valid PIN" while Idle or "insert card" while access is already granted. The state table is valuable precisely because it forces you to think about all those empty cells.

Valid transition coverage (0-switch): The most common coverage goal is that every valid transition is exercised at least once, often called 0-switch coverage or all-transitions coverage. For the ATM model, four test sequences do it: insert, valid (S1 to S2 to S5); insert, invalid, valid (S1 to S2 to S3 to S5); insert, invalid, invalid, valid (to S4 then S5); insert, invalid, invalid, invalid (ending in S6). Together these exercise all 7 transitions. Four is also the minimum here, because each sequence ends in a final state and there are four different transitions leading into final states.

Weaker and stronger coverage: All-states coverage only requires visiting each state at least once; it is weaker, since you can visit every state without taking every transition. 1-switch coverage requires every valid pair of consecutive transitions, which finds defects that depend on the previous step. In our model, the number of pairs at each state is incoming transitions times outgoing transitions: S2, S3 and S4 each have 1 incoming and 2 outgoing, so there are 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 pairs. In general, N-switch coverage tests sequences of N + 1 consecutive transitions, and the number of tests grows quickly.

Invalid transition testing: Valid-transition tests check that the system does the right thing. Invalid transition tests check that the system refuses to do wrong things. From the state table, each invalid cell suggests a test: in S6 (card retained), try "valid PIN" and check that access is not granted; in S1, send "valid PIN" without a card and check that it is ignored. Testers usually test each invalid transition in a separate test, similar to invalid partitions. Many security defects are really invalid transitions that the system wrongly accepts, such as reaching the payment success page without paying.

Guards and actions in tests: When guards exist, each transition with a guard needs tests where the guard is true and where it is false, ideally combined with boundary values. For a withdrawal transition guarded by [amount at most balance and amount at most daily limit], test amounts at the balance boundary and at the daily limit boundary. Actions also need checking: the transition to S6 must not only change state but also retain the card and show the right message.

Where state models come from: Sometimes the specification already contains state diagrams, for example in embedded systems or telecom protocols. More often the tester builds the model from requirements and user stories, with help from developers. Order workflows are a classic source: an order might be Created, Paid, Packed, Shipped, Delivered, Returned, Cancelled. Asking "from which states can an order be cancelled?" often produces surprising answers and surprising defects.

Use-case testing, what it is: A use case describes how an actor (a user or another system) interacts with the system to achieve a goal. It has a name, actors, preconditions, a main success scenario (the normal step-by-step flow), alternative flows (other valid ways to reach the goal), exception flows (what happens when things go wrong), and postconditions. Use-case testing derives test cases from these flows, so tests mirror real usage.

A worked use case, withdraw cash: Actor: account holder. Precondition: the customer is authenticated at the ATM. Main success scenario: 1 customer selects Withdraw; 2 the system shows amount options; 3 customer selects 2,000 Taka; 4 the system checks balance and daily limit; 5 the system dispenses cash; 6 the system prints a receipt and updates the balance. Alternative flow 3a: customer enters a custom amount instead of choosing an option. Alternative flow 6a: customer chooses no receipt. Exception 4a: insufficient balance, the system shows a message and returns to the menu. Exception 4b: daily limit exceeded. Exception 5a: cash dispenser empty, transaction cancelled and nothing debited. Exception 5b: network timeout after debit but before dispensing, the system must reverse the debit.

Turning flows into tests: The basic test follows the main success scenario. Each alternative and exception flow becomes at least one more test: custom amount, no receipt, insufficient balance, limit exceeded, dispenser empty, timeout. That is 7 tests for this use case. Use-case coverage is the number of flows tested divided by the total number of flows: if only the main flow and three exceptions are tested, coverage is 4 out of 7, about 57 percent. Inside each flow, EP and BVA choose exact amounts, for example a custom amount exactly equal to the remaining daily limit.

Why use-case tests find important defects: They follow real user goals across several screens and components, so they catch integration problems and missing steps. Exception flows are where many serious defects hide, because developers spend most attention on the happy path. The network timeout case above, where money could be debited but not dispensed, is exactly the kind of defect that causes customer complaints, angry social media posts and regulatory trouble. Use cases also make good acceptance tests because business people understand them.

Hidden events, timeouts and resets: Beginners model only the events a user triggers. Real systems also react to time and to the environment: a session expires after 5 minutes of inactivity, an OTP becomes invalid after 2 minutes, a network connection drops, the phone receives a call in the middle of a payment, the app is sent to the background. Each of these is an event and deserves arrows in the diagram. Also ask how the machine returns to its starting state: in the ATM model, nothing leads from S5 or S6 back to Idle, but a real ATM must reset after ejecting or retaining the card. Adding such a reset transition changes the coverage count and adds new sequences worth testing, such as a second customer inserting a card right after the first one's card was retained.

Combining with other techniques: State transition testing decides the sequences; other techniques decide the data inside them. The PIN values themselves can be partitioned (correct, wrong, too short, letters), and amounts in a withdrawal state can use BVA. Likewise, when one transition depends on several conditions, a small decision table can describe its guard. Good testers mix techniques freely instead of treating each one as a separate exam chapter.

Real-life example, an online order lifecycle: A Dhaka e-commerce company models orders with states Created, Paid, Packed, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled and Refunded. The state table shows that cancellation should be possible from Created and Paid only. Testers try invalid transitions and find that the customer app still shows the Cancel button after the order is Packed, and pressing it cancels the order while the warehouse ships it anyway. The customer gets both a refund and the parcel. An invalid transition test caught a defect that cost real money in production for a competitor the year before.

Real-life example, a ride-sharing trip: States: Searching, Driver assigned, Driver arrived, On trip, Completed, Cancelled. A tester checks 1-switch sequences and finds a defect only in the pair "Driver arrived, then rider cancels": the cancellation fee is charged twice when the driver also marks no-show within the same second. Single transitions all worked; only a specific sequence exposed the race between the two events.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Typical mistakes are confusing states with events, forgetting invalid transitions, and assuming all-states coverage is as strong as all-transitions coverage. Exams often give a state diagram or a description and ask you to draw the state table, count valid and invalid transitions, write test sequences for 0-switch coverage, or compute the minimum number of tests. For use cases, they ask you to identify main, alternative and exception flows and derive test cases.

Recap: State transition testing models systems whose behaviour depends on history using states, events, transitions, guards and actions, shown as diagrams and tables. Coverage levels include all states, all valid transitions (0-switch), and N-switch sequences, plus separate tests for invalid transitions. Use-case testing turns main, alternative and exception flows into tests that mirror real goals, with EP and BVA choosing the data. Next we tackle combinations of many parameters and the testing that relies on experience.
key_points: State transition testing models behaviour that depends on history: states, events, transitions, guards and actions.
State diagrams show the flow; state tables list every state-event pair and expose invalid combinations.
0-switch (all-transitions) coverage exercises every valid transition; all-states coverage is weaker.
1-switch coverage tests pairs of consecutive transitions; count them as incoming times outgoing at each state.
Invalid transitions should be tested separately to check the system refuses them.
Use-case testing derives tests from the main success scenario, alternative flows and exception flows.
Use-case coverage is flows tested divided by total flows; EP and BVA choose data inside each flow.
lessons.tip: When you model states, name them with adjectives or "waiting for" phrases (Locked, Paid, Waiting for PIN) and name events with verbs (insert card, pay, cancel). Mixing the two is the most common reason student diagrams go wrong.
lessons.task: Draw a state diagram for the bKash-style "send money" flow on your phone or a similar app: from entering a number, through amount, reference, PIN and confirmation, including what happens on a wrong PIN and on cancel. Build its state table, count valid and invalid transitions, and write enough test sequences for 0-switch coverage.

quiz.q: In a state model, what is a guard?
options: An event that starts the system
A condition that must be true for a transition to happen
A state that cannot be left
An action shown on the screen
quiz.explain: A guard, written in square brackets, must be true for the transition to fire, for example [amount at most balance].

quiz.q: A state table has 5 states and 4 events, and 8 cells contain valid transitions. How many invalid state-event combinations are there?
quiz.explain: Total cells are 5 x 4 = 20; 20 - 8 = 12 invalid combinations.

quiz.q: Which coverage is stronger than all-states coverage but weaker than 1-switch coverage?
quiz.explain: Visiting all states is weakest, covering all transitions is stronger, and pairs of transitions (1-switch) is stronger still.

quiz.q: In use-case testing, where do many serious defects tend to hide?
options: In exception and alternative flows that developers pay less attention to
Only in the main success scenario
quiz.explain: Developers focus on the happy path; error and alternative flows are often less tested and contain serious defects.

quiz.q: A use case has a main flow, 2 alternative flows and 3 exception flows. Tests cover the main flow and 2 exceptions. What is the use-case flow coverage?
quiz.explain: There are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 flows and 3 are tested, so coverage is 3 / 6 = 50 percent.

lessons.title: Combinatorial (Pairwise) Testing and Experience-Based Testing
lessons.content:
Imagine a tea stall that offers tea with or without sugar, with or without milk, and in a small or large cup. To taste every possible order you would need 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cups. Now add five types of tea leaves, three sweeteners, hot or iced, and four cup sizes, and the number explodes into hundreds. A smart tea master does not taste every combination. She makes sure that every pair of choices, such as milk with iced, or large cup with no sugar, has been tried at least once, because most problems come from one choice or from two choices clashing. That is the core idea of pairwise testing. In the second half of this lesson we look at the opposite style of test design: techniques that rely on the tester's skill and experience rather than formal models.

The combinatorial explosion: Modern software runs with many configuration parameters: browser, operating system, screen size, language, network type, payment method, user role, feature flags. If a checkout page has 4 parameters with 3 values each, testing all combinations needs 3 to the power 4 = 81 tests. With 10 parameters of 3 values each, it needs 59,049. With a few more, it becomes impossible. Yet defects caused by parameter interactions are real: a payment method that fails only on one browser with one language.

What research says about interactions: Studies by researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) looked at failures in many real systems and found that most failures were triggered by a single parameter value or by the interaction of two parameters, and almost all by interactions of a small number of parameters, no more than about six. This means that covering all pairs of values catches a large share of interaction defects at a tiny fraction of the cost of covering everything. It is not a guarantee, but it is an excellent trade-off.

Three levels of combination coverage: All-combinations coverage tests every combination of every value of every parameter: complete but usually impossible. Each-choice coverage requires that every value of every parameter appears in at least one test; the minimum number of tests equals the largest number of values of any single parameter. Pairwise coverage (also called all-pairs or 2-wise) requires that every possible pair of values for every pair of parameters appears in at least one test. Higher strengths, such as 3-wise, cover every triple of values.

Pairwise worked example, three on-off settings: Suppose an app has three settings: dark mode (on or off), notifications (on or off) and offline mode (on or off). All combinations need 8 tests. Pairwise needs only 4: (off, off, off), (off, on, on), (on, off, on), (on, on, off). Check any two settings, for example dark mode and notifications: the four tests give off-off, off-on, on-off and on-on, all four pairs. The same holds for dark mode with offline, and notifications with offline. Four tests instead of eight cover every pair.

Pairwise worked example, a checkout page: Four parameters with three values each: network (WiFi, 4G, 3G), payment (card, mobile wallet, cash on delivery), delivery area (Dhaka city, other city, rural) and customer type (new, regular, premium). All combinations: 81. A pairwise set needs only 9 tests: WiFi, card, Dhaka, new; WiFi, wallet, other city, regular; WiFi, cash, rural, premium; 4G, card, other city, premium; 4G, wallet, rural, new; 4G, cash, Dhaka, regular; 3G, card, rural, regular; 3G, wallet, Dhaka, premium; 3G, cash, other city, new. Pick any two parameters and you will find all 9 value pairs exactly once. That is 9 tests instead of 81.

Building a pairwise set by hand: For small problems you can do it on paper. Start with the two parameters that have the most values and write all their pairs, one per row; that gives the minimum number of rows you will need. Then fill the remaining columns one by one, choosing for each row a value that creates pairs not yet covered, and keep a checklist of the pairs still missing. If some pair cannot fit into existing rows, add a new row for it, using any values for the other columns. The result may not be the smallest possible set, but it will be valid, and checking it pair by pair is an excellent way to understand what pairwise coverage really means.

Orthogonal arrays: The 9-test set above is an orthogonal array, a mathematical structure where, for every pair of columns, every pair of values appears the same number of times. Orthogonal arrays have been used in experiment design for a long time, and testers borrowed them. They are elegant, but they only exist for certain numbers of parameters and values. In practice, testers use tools that generate small covering arrays for any mix of parameters.

Tools and constraints: Microsoft's PICT (Pairwise Independent Combinatorial Testing) is a well-known free command-line tool: you list parameters and values in a text file and it generates a compact pairwise (or higher-strength) set. Similar tools exist in many languages and test management systems. Real parameters often have constraints, for example Safari only runs on Apple devices, or cash on delivery is unavailable for rural areas. Good tools let you write such constraints so that impossible combinations are not generated.

When pairwise is a good choice and when it is not: Pairwise fits configuration testing (browsers, devices, settings), form fields that mostly act independently, and API parameters. It is less suitable when you know specific combinations matter (use decision tables), when the order of actions matters (use state transitions), or when the system is safety-critical and needs stronger coverage. Also remember that pairwise chooses combinations, not values: the values themselves should come from EP and BVA.

Classification tree method: Another systematic approach for combinations is the classification tree method. The tester draws a tree: the top is the test object, branches are classifications (aspects such as payment method or customer type), and leaves are classes (the partitions). Test cases are then drawn as rows below the tree by picking one leaf from each classification. Tools supporting this method can also generate pairwise combinations. The tree is a nice visual way to explain coverage to stakeholders.

Experience-based testing, the other side: Formal techniques rely on models of the specification. Experience-based techniques rely on the tester's knowledge of similar systems, of typical developer mistakes, of the business domain and of past failures. They are especially useful when specifications are poor, time is short, or as a complement to formal techniques that might miss what the model did not include. Their weakness is that results depend heavily on the tester's skill and are harder to measure.

Error guessing: In error guessing the tester anticipates mistakes developers are likely to make and designs tests to expose them. A methodical form is a fault attack: list possible defects, failures and their symptoms, then design tests for each. Typical guesses: empty input, very long input, zero, negative numbers, special characters such as apostrophes in names (O'Brien) or Bangla text, leading and trailing spaces, duplicate submissions by double-clicking, pressing the back button after payment, two users editing the same record, and dates like 29 February or 31 April.

Checklist-based testing: The tester uses a list of items to check, built from experience, standards or past defects: "every form has a meaningful error message for each invalid field", "every page works with the font size set to large", "all money values show two decimal places". Checklists give consistency between testers and over time, and can cover non-functional aspects like usability and accessibility. They should be updated as new kinds of defects are discovered, otherwise they suffer from the pesticide paradox.

Exploratory testing: In exploratory testing, test design, execution and learning happen at the same time. The tester does not follow a script; she explores the software, observes, forms hypotheses about where it might break, and immediately designs the next test based on what she learned. It is not random clicking: good exploratory testing is purposeful, focused and documented. It is excellent for finding unexpected defects, for learning a new product quickly, and for testing when specifications are thin.

Session-based test management: To make exploratory testing manageable, sessions are time-boxed, often 60 to 120 minutes, and guided by a charter: a short mission statement. A popular template is "Explore (target) with (resources) to discover (information)", for example "Explore the refund flow with orders in different states to discover incorrect refund amounts". During the session the tester takes notes: what was tested, defects and questions found, and ideas for future sessions. A short debrief with the test lead afterwards turns the session into reportable information.

Making experience-based testing accountable: Managers sometimes distrust experience-based testing because it seems invisible. The fix is good records: the charter, the time spent, the areas covered, the defects found and the open questions. Over several sessions, these notes show which areas have been explored deeply and which barely touched. Many teams combine approaches: formal techniques build a regression baseline, and exploratory sessions hunt for the defects the models could not imagine. Studies and industry experience both suggest that the mix finds more than either style alone.

Real-life example, a mobile app compatibility matrix: A Bangladeshi edtech app supports Android versions spread across many phones, two languages (Bangla and English), light and dark themes, and three network types. All combinations of a realistic set of values run into the hundreds. The team uses a pairwise tool with constraints and gets about 20 configurations, then runs their main smoke suite on each through a cloud device service. One pair fails: Bangla language with dark theme on a particular older Android version, where Bangla text in buttons becomes invisible because of a hard-coded colour. Testing each parameter alone would not have revealed it.

Real-life example, exploratory session before Eid sales: Before an Eid sale, a tester at an online shop runs a 90-minute session with the charter "Explore the cart and voucher system with multiple vouchers and quantity changes to discover pricing errors". Following her nose, she applies a voucher, removes an item to drop below the voucher's minimum, and finds that the discount is not removed. Then she tries the same in the mobile app and finds a second path. No scripted test covered this order of actions; the defect would have cost thousands of Taka per day during the sale.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include thinking pairwise guarantees finding all interaction defects, ignoring constraints between parameters, and treating exploratory testing as unplanned clicking. Exams ask you to compute the number of all-combination tests (product of values), the minimum for each-choice coverage (largest number of values), to build a small pairwise set, to explain why pairwise works, and to describe error guessing, checklist-based testing, exploratory testing, charters and session-based test management.

Recap: Combinatorial testing tames the explosion of configuration combinations. All-combinations is usually impossible; each-choice covers every value once; pairwise covers every pair of values and catches most interaction defects at a fraction of the cost, using orthogonal arrays or tools like PICT, with constraints for impossible combinations. Experience-based techniques complement formal ones: error guessing and fault attacks, checklist-based testing, and exploratory testing organised into chartered, time-boxed sessions. Next we open the box and start white-box testing with statement and branch coverage.
key_points: All-combinations testing needs the product of all value counts and quickly becomes impossible.
Each-choice coverage needs at least as many tests as the parameter with the most values.
Pairwise coverage ensures every pair of values of every two parameters appears in some test.
Studies found most failures involve one or two interacting parameters, which is why pairwise is effective.
3 binary parameters need 8 tests for all combinations but only 4 for pairwise; 4 parameters with 3 values need 81 versus 9.
Tools such as PICT generate pairwise sets and handle constraints between parameters.
Experience-based techniques: error guessing (fault attacks), checklist-based testing, and exploratory testing with charters and time-boxed sessions.
lessons.tip: When you write a charter, finish the sentence "to discover..." with something specific. "Explore the app to find bugs" is not a charter; "explore voucher stacking to discover wrong totals" is.
lessons.task: Pick a website you use and list four parameters (for example browser, device, language, logged-in or guest) with 2 or 3 values each. Count all combinations, then build a pairwise set by hand and check that every pair appears. Finally write two exploratory charters for the same site.

quiz.q: A form has 3 parameters with 4, 3 and 2 values. How many tests does all-combinations coverage need?
quiz.explain: All combinations is the product of the value counts: 4 x 3 x 2 = 24.

quiz.q: For the same parameters (4, 3 and 2 values), what is the minimum number of tests for each-choice coverage?
quiz.explain: Each value must appear at least once, so you need as many tests as the parameter with the most values: 4.

quiz.q: Why is pairwise testing effective?
options: Most failures are triggered by one parameter or an interaction of two
It removes the need for boundary values
It only works for safety-critical software
quiz.explain: Research found most interaction failures involve one or two parameters, so covering all pairs finds many defects cheaply.

quiz.q: Which statement about exploratory testing is correct?
options: It means clicking randomly without any goal
It cannot find defects that scripted tests miss
It requires detailed test scripts written in advance
Test design, execution and learning happen at the same time, often guided by a charter
quiz.explain: Exploratory testing is simultaneous learning, design and execution, organised with charters and time-boxed sessions.

quiz.q: A tester lists likely developer mistakes (empty input, double submission, apostrophes in names) and designs tests for each. This is:
quiz.explain: Error guessing anticipates likely mistakes; a methodical list of possible faults is called a fault attack.

lessons.title: White-Box Testing I: Statement and Branch Coverage
lessons.content:
Imagine you are checking whether a security guard really patrols every corridor of a big office building at night. You cannot follow him around, but you can put a small sticker reader at every door and every junction. In the morning you look at which readers were touched. If the corridor behind the canteen shows zero touches, you know it was never patrolled, no matter how confident the guard sounds. White-box coverage works the same way. We instrument the code, run the tests, and see which statements and which decisions were exercised. Areas never touched are areas where defects can hide untested.

What white-box testing is: White-box testing, also called structural or glass-box testing, designs and evaluates tests based on the internal structure of the software, most often its source code. Black-box techniques ask "did we test what the specification says?"; white-box techniques ask "did our tests exercise what the code actually contains?". Both views are needed. Black-box tests can miss code that implements behaviour nobody specified; white-box tests can miss behaviour that was specified but never implemented, because missing code has no structure to cover.

The control flow graph, a quick recap: In Software Engineering you drew control flow graphs (CFGs). Each node is a statement or a basic block (a straight sequence of statements with one entry and one exit), and each edge is a possible transfer of control. A decision node, such as an if, a while condition or a switch, has more than one outgoing edge. Coverage criteria are defined on this graph: visit every node (statement coverage), take every edge out of every decision (branch coverage), and so on.

Statement coverage defined: Statement coverage is the percentage of executable statements that have been executed by a test suite: statement coverage = (executed statements / total executable statements) x 100. Comments, blank lines and declarations without executable code are not counted. Reaching 100 percent means every executable statement ran at least once. Some books and tools talk about line coverage, which is similar but counts lines rather than statements.

A worked function: Consider this delivery fee function, written as numbered pseudo-code. Line 1: function fee(amount, isMember). Line 2: fee = 60. Line 3: if amount > 1000. Line 4: fee = 0. Line 5: if isMember. Line 6: fee = fee / 2. Line 7: return fee. The executable statements are lines 2 to 7: six statements. The function charges 60 Taka, makes delivery free for orders above 1,000 Taka, and halves the fee for members.

Statement coverage worked: Test T1 uses amount 1,500 and isMember true. It executes lines 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7: all six statements, so statement coverage is 6 / 6 = 100 percent with a single test. Test T2 alone, amount 500 and isMember false, executes lines 2, 3, 5 and 7, skipping lines 4 and 6: statement coverage is 4 / 6, about 67 percent. Notice how easily 100 percent statement coverage was reached with just one test.

Branch (decision) coverage defined: Branch coverage is the percentage of branch outcomes exercised: for every decision, both the true and the false outcome (or every case of a switch) must be taken. Branch coverage = (exercised branch outcomes / total branch outcomes) x 100. Our function has two decisions (lines 3 and 5), each with two outcomes, so there are 4 branch outcomes in total. Some standards distinguish decision coverage (outcomes of decisions) from branch coverage (edges in the control flow graph), but for ordinary if statements the numbers are the same.

Branch coverage worked: T1 (1,500, true) takes line 3 true and line 5 true: 2 of 4 outcomes, 50 percent branch coverage, even though statement coverage was 100 percent. Adding T2 (500, false) takes line 3 false and line 5 false, giving all 4 outcomes: 100 percent branch coverage with two tests. This is the key lesson: 100 percent statement coverage does not imply 100 percent branch coverage, because an if without an else has a false outcome that executes no statement of its own.

Why the false branch matters: Imagine a version of the function where line 2 was accidentally deleted, so fee is only set inside the if on line 4. With T1 the code still works, because line 4 sets fee to 0 before it is used. With T2, fee is used on line 7 without ever being set, giving an error or a garbage value depending on the language. Statement coverage with T1 alone would report 100 percent and say nothing; branch coverage would force T2 and expose the defect. Many real defects live in "what happens when the condition is false".

Finding the minimum number of tests: For independent if statements in sequence, one test can take the true outcome of all of them and another the false outcome of all of them, so two tests give 100 percent branch coverage no matter how many ifs there are, as long as the inputs can be chosen freely. Nested ifs are different: if a second if sits inside the true branch of the first, you need one test for the outer false outcome and two tests inside it (inner true and inner false), so three tests. For statement coverage, count how many separate paths are needed to reach every statement; with if-else pairs, both sides contain statements, so at least two tests are needed even for statement coverage.

The subsumption relationship: A criterion A subsumes criterion B if every test suite that achieves 100 percent of A also achieves 100 percent of B. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage: if every outcome of every decision is taken, every statement on those paths is executed (assuming there is no unreachable code). The opposite is not true, as our example shows. This hierarchy continues upwards in the next lessons: condition coverage, MC/DC, multiple condition coverage and path coverage.

Loops and branch coverage: A while loop's condition is a decision with two outcomes: enter the loop body, or skip or exit it. Consider: total = 0; i = 0; while i < n: total = total + price[i]; i = i + 1. A test with n = 3 enters the loop (true) and finally exits it (false), so both outcomes are covered. A test with n = 0 takes only the false outcome. Branch coverage is satisfied by n = 3 alone, yet the n = 0 case (an empty cart) is a classic source of defects. Coverage measures are a minimum, not a guarantee; lesson 13 adds loop testing rules.

Switch statements and exceptions: For a switch with four cases and a default, branch coverage requires each case and the default to be executed: five outcomes. Exception handling also creates branches: a try block can complete normally or jump into a catch block. To cover the catch, you must make the error happen, often by using a test double that throws (lesson 19). Unexecuted catch blocks are one of the most common gaps in real coverage reports, and they are exactly the code that runs on the worst day.

Other structural measures: Statements and branches are not the only things to count. Function (method) coverage asks whether every function was called at least once; it is coarse but useful for spotting whole features that no test touches. Call coverage asks whether every call site was executed. At integration level, teams track whether every API endpoint or every message type was exercised. All of these follow the same pattern: list the structural items, run the tests, count which were hit.

How coverage is measured: Coverage tools instrument the code, adding invisible counters at statements and branches, then run the tests and report which counters were hit. Well-known tools include JaCoCo for Java, coverage.py for Python, Istanbul (nyc) for JavaScript and gcov for C and C++. Reports usually colour lines green (executed), red (never executed) and yellow (partly covered decision, only one outcome taken). Most CI pipelines can publish these reports on every pull request.

Reading a coverage report: Do not just read the overall percentage. Look at the red and yellow lines and ask: which behaviour is this, and why is it untested? Often the answer reveals a missing test case: an error path, an unusual input, a configuration branch. Sometimes it reveals dead code that nobody needs any more, which can be deleted. Sometimes it is code that is very hard to reach, which may hint at a design that needs refactoring.

What coverage does not tell you: Coverage tells you code was executed, not that it was checked. A test that calls fee(1500, true) and asserts nothing still counts towards coverage. Coverage also says nothing about missing code: if the specification says students get free delivery and nobody implemented it, there is no line to be red. And it says nothing about data: the same line can work for most values and fail for one boundary. That is why white-box and black-box techniques are used together.

Coverage targets: Many teams set a minimum target for unit test coverage, for example 80 percent of lines or branches, and fail the build if new code drops below it. Targets help keep testing habits alive, but if the number becomes the goal, people write tests that execute code without meaningful assertions just to raise the percentage. A healthier approach is to require high coverage on critical modules (payments, pricing, security) and to review uncovered code rather than chase 100 percent everywhere.

Real-life example, a loan EMI calculator: A fintech team in Dhaka has 95 percent statement coverage on its EMI (monthly instalment) calculator, and everyone is proud. A tester opens the branch report and sees a yellow line: if interestRate == 0, the code uses a special formula, because the normal EMI formula divides by the rate. The true outcome was never tested. Testing an interest-free instalment plan, which the company had just started offering for smartphones, revealed that the special formula used the wrong number of months. Branch coverage pointed straight at the gap.

Real-life example, an error path in a payment service: An online ticketing company's payment service had a catch block for gateway timeouts that was always red in the coverage report. The team added a test using a stub gateway that times out. The test showed that on timeout, the code marked the ticket as paid before confirming payment status. In production, during heavy demand for holiday train tickets, this would have issued tickets without payment. One previously uncovered branch, one serious defect.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Typical mistakes: believing 100 percent statement coverage means the code is well tested, forgetting the false outcome of an if without else, counting non-executable lines, and treating coverage as proof of correctness. Exams usually give a short function and ask you to count statements and branch outcomes, compute coverage for given tests, find the minimum tests for 100 percent statement and for 100 percent branch coverage, and explain why branch coverage subsumes statement coverage.

Recap: White-box testing measures how much of the code's structure tests exercise. Statement coverage counts executed statements; branch coverage counts taken outcomes of decisions, including the silent false outcome of an if. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, not the other way around. Coverage tools colour code to show gaps, but coverage shows execution, not correctness, and cannot see missing code. Next we look inside decisions themselves: condition coverage and MC/DC.
key_points: White-box testing designs and measures tests from the code's internal structure.
Statement coverage = executed statements / total executable statements x 100.
Branch coverage = exercised decision outcomes / total outcomes x 100, including the false outcome of an if without else.
100 percent statement coverage does not imply 100 percent branch coverage; branch coverage subsumes statement coverage.
Loops, switch cases and exception handlers all create branches that need tests.
Coverage tools (JaCoCo, coverage.py, Istanbul, gcov) colour executed, missed and partly covered lines.
Coverage shows code was executed, not that it was checked, and cannot reveal missing code.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see an if without an else, draw the invisible else arrow on paper. Most branch-coverage exam mistakes come from forgetting that invisible path.
lessons.task: Write a small function of your own (for example a cinema ticket price with discounts for children and for weekdays) with two if statements. Number the statements, draw the control flow graph, and find the minimum number of tests for 100 percent statement coverage and for 100 percent branch coverage. If you can, run it with a coverage tool such as coverage.py.

quiz.q: A function has 10 executable statements and a test suite executes 8 of them. What is the statement coverage?
quiz.explain: Statement coverage = 8 / 10 x 100 = 80 percent.

quiz.q: A function contains two independent if statements without else. What is the minimum number of tests for 100 percent branch coverage?
quiz.explain: One test can take both true outcomes and another both false outcomes, so 2 tests cover all 4 outcomes.

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: 100 percent statement coverage always gives 100 percent branch coverage
100 percent branch coverage implies 100 percent statement coverage, but not the other way round
Branch coverage and statement coverage are identical
quiz.explain: Taking every decision outcome executes every reachable statement, but executing every statement can skip false outcomes.

quiz.q: In a coverage report, what does a yellow (partly covered) decision usually mean?
options: The line contains a syntax error
Only one outcome of the decision was taken by the tests
The test failed on that line
quiz.explain: Partly covered decisions have at least one outcome (for example the false branch) that no test exercised.

quiz.q: Which problem can coverage measurement NOT reveal?
options: A catch block that never runs
A requirement that was never implemented in the code
An if statement whose false outcome is untested
A loop whose body never executes
quiz.explain: Missing code has no lines to measure, so coverage cannot reveal an unimplemented requirement.

lessons.title: White-Box Testing II: Condition Coverage and MC/DC
lessons.content:
Think about the rule at a university exam hall door: you may enter if you have your admit card AND (your ID card OR a letter from the department). The guard checks the whole rule and lets people in or not. Now imagine the guard has a habit: he only really checks the admit card and waves everyone through regardless of the ID or letter. If every student you send happens to have all three documents, you would never notice his habit. To catch it, you must send cases where one document alone decides the result. That is exactly what modified condition/decision coverage, MC/DC, is built for.
