Decisions and conditions: In the last lesson, branch coverage treated each decision as one unit with two outcomes. But a decision is often made of several conditions joined by Boolean operators. In if (hasAdmit and (hasId or hasLetter)), the decision is the whole expression, and the conditions are the atomic Boolean parts: hasAdmit, hasId and hasLetter. A condition cannot be broken down further. Branch coverage can be achieved without ever testing how individual conditions behave, so defects inside complex decisions can hide.

Our running example: Let A = has admit card, B = has ID card, C = has department letter, and the decision D = A and (B or C). With three conditions there are 2 to the power 3 = 8 combinations. Number them: 1 (T,T,T) gives D true; 2 (T,T,F) true; 3 (T,F,T) true; 4 (T,F,F) false; 5 (F,T,T) false; 6 (F,T,F) false; 7 (F,F,T) false; 8 (F,F,F) false. Keep this table in front of you; every coverage level in this lesson is about choosing rows from it.

Decision coverage, revisited: Decision coverage needs D to be true at least once and false at least once. Rows 1 and 8 achieve it. But rows 1 and 8 never test B or C on their own: if the programmer had written D = A and B, rows 1 and 8 would still give the same results (true and false). The defect, ignoring C, slips through.

Condition coverage: Condition coverage requires each condition to take both true and false at least once. Rows 4 (T,F,F) and 5 (F,T,T) achieve it: A is true then false, B false then true, C false then true. But look at D: row 4 gives false and row 5 gives false. The decision never became true! So condition coverage does not guarantee decision coverage. This surprising result is a favourite exam question, and it is why condition coverage alone is rarely used.

Condition/decision coverage: The obvious fix is to require both: every condition takes both values and the decision takes both outcomes. Rows 1 (T,T,T) and 8 (F,F,F) satisfy condition/decision coverage: each condition is true in row 1 and false in row 8, and D is true then false. Yet, as we saw, these two rows still cannot show whether B and C really matter. Condition/decision coverage is better on paper but still weak at detecting conditions that are wrongly ignored or misplaced.

Multiple condition coverage: The strongest condition-level criterion is multiple condition coverage, also called combinatorial condition coverage: test all 2 to the power n combinations of condition values in each decision. For our example that is all 8 rows. It is thorough, but it explodes: a decision with 6 conditions needs 64 tests, and with 10 conditions it needs 1,024. Also, with short-circuit evaluation many combinations are impossible to distinguish, as we will see below. In practice it is used only for small, critical decisions.

MC/DC, the idea: Modified condition/decision coverage sits between condition/decision coverage and multiple condition coverage. It requires: every decision takes all outcomes, every condition takes all values, and each condition is shown to independently affect the decision's outcome. Independently affecting means: there is a pair of tests where only that condition changes (others stay the same), and the decision's outcome changes. Such a pair is called an independence pair. MC/DC proves every condition actually matters, with far fewer tests than all combinations.

Finding independence pairs for A: Look for two rows that differ only in A and give different results. Rows 1 and 5 differ only in A (T,T,T versus F,T,T) and give true versus false: an independence pair. Rows 2 and 6 also work, and so do rows 3 and 7. Rows 4 and 8 differ only in A but both give false, so they do not show A's effect. So A has three possible pairs: (1,5), (2,6), (3,7).

Finding pairs for B and C: For B, compare rows differing only in B. Rows 2 (T,T,F) and 4 (T,F,F) give true versus false: a pair. Rows 1 and 3 both give true, rows 5 and 7 both false, rows 6 and 8 both false: none of those work. So B has exactly one pair, (2,4). For C, rows 3 (T,F,T) and 4 (T,F,F) give true versus false: the pair (3,4). The others fail. This shows why B and C are hard to test: B only matters when A is true and C is false, and C only matters when A is true and B is false.

Choosing a minimal MC/DC set: We must include rows 2 and 4 (for B) and rows 3 and 4 (for C). That gives rows 2, 3 and 4. For A, we need a pair that reuses as many of these rows as possible: (2,6) adds only row 6, and (3,7) adds only row 7. So a minimal MC/DC set is rows 2, 3, 4 and 6: (T,T,F), (T,F,T), (T,F,F) and (F,T,F). Four tests, compared with eight for multiple condition coverage. Check: D is true in rows 2 and 3 and false in 4 and 6, and every condition takes both values. All requirements met.

Two warm-up patterns worth memorising: For a plain and of two conditions, D = A and B, the MC/DC set is (T,T), (F,T) and (T,F): starting from the all-true row, flip each condition once and watch the result fall to false. For a plain or, D = A or B, the set is (F,F), (T,F) and (F,T): starting from the all-false row, flip each condition once and watch the result rise to true. The same trick extends to longer chains: for and-chains start from all true, for or-chains start from all false, and flip one condition at a time. Mixed expressions like ours need the truth table, but these patterns let you check your answer quickly.

The n plus 1 rule: For a decision with n independent conditions, MC/DC usually needs at least n + 1 tests, and often exactly n + 1 for simple expressions like ours (3 conditions, 4 tests). In the worst case it needs up to 2n. Compare the growth: with 10 conditions, MC/DC needs around 11 tests while multiple condition coverage needs 1,024. That linear growth is what makes MC/DC practical for large safety-critical programs.

The ladder of criteria at a glance: From weakest to strongest for a single decision: statement coverage, then decision (branch) coverage, then condition/decision coverage, then MC/DC, then multiple condition coverage. Plain condition coverage sits off to the side, because it does not even guarantee decision coverage. Path coverage, in the next lesson, measures something different again, sequences of decisions through the whole function, and can grow far faster than any of these. Knowing this ladder helps you justify a choice: a payroll rounding rule might need MC/DC, while a logging toggle needs only branch coverage.

Short-circuit evaluation: Most languages evaluate and and or lazily: in A and (B or C), if A is false, B and C are not evaluated at all, because the answer is already false. So rows 5, 6, 7 and 8 all behave identically in the machine. This has two effects. Multiple condition coverage is partly meaningless, since you cannot observe differences among those rows. And for MC/DC, some standards accept a "masking" variant where a condition's independence is shown even if other conditions change, as long as those other conditions are masked (cannot affect the result). The "unique-cause" form we used above, where only one condition changes, is the stricter version.

Where MC/DC is required: MC/DC was popularised by aviation. The airborne software guidance DO-178C, used by aviation authorities to certify aircraft software, requires MC/DC for the most critical level (Level A, where a failure could be catastrophic), decision coverage for Level B, and statement coverage for Level C. Other safety domains, such as automotive software under ISO 26262, also recommend MC/DC for their highest-integrity code. For a typical web app it is usually more than needed, but the thinking behind it, "prove each condition matters", is valuable everywhere.

Practical tips: Keep decisions simple: a decision with eight conditions is hard to read, hard to test and probably hides a defect. Extract complex conditions into well-named functions, such as isEligible(applicant). Use coverage tools that support condition or MC/DC reporting where available. And remember that MC/DC tests the structure of the decision as written: if the requirement itself is wrong, MC/DC faithfully tests the wrong logic.

Real-life example, an e-commerce cash-on-delivery rule: The rule says cash on delivery is allowed if the order is under 10,000 Taka AND (the area is inside Dhaka OR the customer has more than 5 successful past orders). The developer wrote it correctly, but in a later refactor someone changed the inner "or" to "and". Branch coverage tests (one order accepted, one rejected) kept passing. An MC/DC suite, which included a row where the area is outside Dhaka but past orders are 6, failed immediately, because that customer was now wrongly refused. The independence pair for "past orders" caught the change.

Real-life example, a metro rail gate: Imagine software for a metro rail entry gate opens if (card is valid AND balance is at least minimum fare AND NOT card is blacklisted) OR staff override is pressed. That is four conditions. Multiple condition coverage would need 16 combinations. A tester derives an MC/DC set of 5 tests, each pair showing one condition flipping the gate's decision. One pair exposes that the blacklist check was ignored when balance was exactly at the minimum fare, because of a misplaced bracket. For a public transport system handling many thousands of passengers a day, that is a defect worth finding.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include confusing conditions with decisions, assuming condition coverage implies decision coverage, picking independence pairs where more than one condition changes, and forgetting that the decision outcome must change within the pair. Exams ask you to build the truth table, find independence pairs, give a minimal MC/DC set, compare test counts (2 to the power n versus n + 1), and order criteria by strength: statement, then decision, then condition/decision, then MC/DC, then multiple condition.

Recap: Decisions contain conditions, and branch coverage can miss defects inside them. Condition coverage tests each condition both ways but may never flip the decision; condition/decision coverage requires both but can still miss ignored conditions. Multiple condition coverage tests all 2 to the power n combinations and explodes. MC/DC requires each condition to independently change the outcome, using independence pairs, typically with n + 1 tests, and is mandated for the most critical avionics software. Next we finish white-box testing with paths, loops, data flow and mutation.
key_points: A decision is a whole Boolean expression; conditions are its atomic parts.
Condition coverage does not imply decision coverage: each condition can flip while the decision stays the same.
Condition/decision coverage requires both, but can still miss conditions that are wrongly ignored.
Multiple condition coverage tests all 2^n combinations and becomes impractical quickly.
MC/DC requires each condition to independently change the decision, shown by an independence pair.
For A and (B or C), a minimal MC/DC set has 4 tests, n + 1, versus 8 for multiple condition coverage.
DO-178C requires MC/DC for Level A, decision coverage for Level B and statement coverage for Level C.
lessons.tip: For MC/DC, write the full truth table first, then for each condition circle the pairs of rows that differ only in that condition and give different outcomes. Choosing the final set from circled pairs is then just a puzzle of reusing rows.
lessons.task: Take the decision D = (A or B) and C. Write its full truth table, find all independence pairs for A, B and C, and choose a minimal MC/DC test set. Check that your set has n + 1 = 4 tests and that every condition and the decision take both values.

quiz.q: For D = A and (B or C), the tests (T,F,F) and (F,T,T) are run. Which coverage do they achieve?
options: Condition coverage but not decision coverage
quiz.explain: Every condition is true once and false once, but D is false in both tests, so decision coverage is not achieved.

quiz.q: What does MC/DC require in addition to condition/decision coverage?
options: Each condition shown to independently affect the decision's outcome
Every loop executed zero, one and many times
quiz.explain: MC/DC adds independence: for each condition, a pair of tests where only it changes and the outcome changes.

quiz.q: A decision has 5 independent conditions. Roughly how many tests do multiple condition coverage and MC/DC need?
quiz.explain: Multiple condition coverage needs 2^5 = 32; MC/DC typically needs about n + 1 = 6.

quiz.q: Which DO-178C software level requires MC/DC?
quiz.explain: Level A, the most critical, requires MC/DC; Level B requires decision coverage and Level C statement coverage.

quiz.q: Why does short-circuit evaluation matter for condition coverage?
options: When the first operand already decides the result, later conditions are not evaluated
It makes every condition evaluated twice
It removes the need for decision coverage
It only happens in assembly language
quiz.explain: In A and (B or C), a false A means B and C are never evaluated, so some combinations cannot be distinguished.

lessons.title: White-Box Testing III: Paths, Loops, Data Flow and Mutation
lessons.content:
Imagine a delivery rider in Old Dhaka who must get from Chawkbazar to Sadarghat. There are many lanes, and at every junction he can turn left or right. Checking that each lane was used once (like branch coverage) is one thing; checking every possible complete route is another, and the number of routes explodes with every junction. A smart dispatcher instead picks a small set of routes that together use every lane and every key junction, and pays extra attention to the roundabout where riders go around and around. That is the spirit of this lesson: path testing, basis paths, loop testing, data-flow testing, and finally mutation testing, which tests the tests themselves.

Path coverage: A path is a complete sequence of statements from the entry of a function to its exit. Path coverage requires every possible path to be executed at least once. It is the strongest of the control-flow criteria, because it covers every combination of decision outcomes along the way. It subsumes branch coverage: if you have taken every path, you have taken every branch.

Why path coverage explodes: Each independent if statement in sequence doubles the number of paths. The delivery fee function from lesson 11 had 2 ifs and therefore 2 x 2 = 4 paths. A function with 10 sequential ifs has 2 to the power 10 = 1,024 paths. A loop makes things worse: a loop that can run 0 to 20 times, with an if inside, has a separate path for every number of iterations and every pattern of true and false outcomes inside. For real programs, full path coverage is usually impossible, and some paths are infeasible (no input can make them happen).

Cyclomatic complexity, a quick recap: In Software Engineering you met McCabe's cyclomatic complexity, V(G), with three equivalent formulas: V(G) = E - N + 2P (edges minus nodes plus twice the number of connected components), V(G) = number of binary decisions + 1, and V(G) = number of regions in the planar control flow graph. It measures the number of linearly independent paths through a function. Higher values mean more complex code that is harder to understand and test; many teams flag functions above about 10 for review or refactoring.

Basis path testing: Instead of all paths, basis path testing executes a basis set: V(G) linearly independent paths, where each new path introduces at least one edge not used by previous paths. For the fee function, V(G) = 2 decisions + 1 = 3. A basis set is: P1 amount 500, not member (both decisions false); P2 amount 1,500, not member (first true, second false); P3 amount 500, member (first false, second true). Three tests instead of four total paths, and they guarantee branch coverage. The fourth path (both true) is a combination of the others in the mathematical sense, but it may still hide a defect, which is why basis path testing is a practical compromise, not a complete answer.

Infeasible paths: Some paths in the graph cannot happen in reality. If one if checks x > 10 and a later if, with x unchanged, checks x < 5, the path where both are true is infeasible. Testers must recognise infeasible paths rather than wasting time trying to force them. A large number of infeasible paths is also a smell: it often means the code is more complicated than the logic it implements.

Loop testing, why loops need special care: Loops are where off-by-one errors, empty-collection crashes, infinite loops and performance problems live. Branch coverage only asks that the loop condition be true once and false once, which a single run with a few iterations satisfies. Loop testing, a set of rules popularised by Boris Beizer, adds specific iteration counts.

Simple loops: For a simple loop that can run at most n times, test: skipping the loop entirely (0 iterations), exactly one pass, two passes, a typical number m of passes where m is less than n, and n - 1, n and n + 1 passes (the last one checks that the loop correctly refuses to go beyond its maximum). For a cart that can hold at most 20 items, test carts with 0, 1, 2, about 10, 19, 20 and an attempt at 21 items. You will notice this is just boundary value analysis applied to the number of iterations.

Nested, concatenated and unstructured loops: For nested loops, testing every combination of iteration counts explodes, so start with the innermost loop: hold outer loops at their minimum values and apply the simple-loop tests to the inner one, then move outward one loop at a time, keeping inner loops at typical values. Concatenated loops (one after another) can be tested as independent simple loops if they do not share data; if the second loop uses the first loop's results, treat them like nested loops. Unstructured loops, with jumps into the middle, should be redesigned rather than tested heroically.

Data-flow testing, the idea: Control-flow criteria follow the shape of the code. Data-flow testing follows the life of each variable: where it gets a value and where that value is used. Many defects are about data rather than control: using a variable before it is set, overwriting a value before anyone reads it, or using the wrong one of several assignments. Data-flow testing chooses paths that connect each definition to its uses.

Definitions and uses: A definition (def) of a variable is any statement that gives it a value, such as an assignment or reading input. A use is any statement that reads its value. Uses are split into computation uses (c-use), where the value is used to compute something or output it, and predicate uses (p-use), where it appears in a condition that decides a branch. A def-clear path for a variable is a path from a definition to a use with no other definition of that variable in between. A def-use pair (du-pair) is a definition and a use connected by at least one def-clear path.

A worked data-flow example: Consider: line 1 total = 0; line 2 discount = 0; line 3 for each item in cart: total = total + item.price; line 4 if total > 1000; line 5 discount = total x 0.1; line 6 pay = total - discount; line 7 print pay. For discount, there are two defs (lines 2 and 5) and one c-use (line 6). Pair (2, 6) needs a path where line 5 is skipped, so total must be 1,000 or less. Pair (5, 6) needs total above 1,000. For total, defs are at lines 1 and 3; uses include the p-use at line 4 and c-uses at lines 3, 5 and 6. A test with an empty cart exercises the pair from line 1 directly to line 4, a case easily forgotten.

Data-flow coverage criteria: All-defs coverage requires that for every definition, at least one def-clear path to some use is executed. All-c-uses and all-p-uses require reaching every computation use or every predicate use respectively. All-uses coverage requires, for every definition, a def-clear path to every use it can reach. All-du-paths, the strongest common criterion, requires every def-clear path (without loops repeating) for every du-pair. Research by Rapps and Weyuker defined this family and its subsumption order; all-uses subsumes branch coverage for typical programs.

Data-flow anomalies: Static analysis tools look for suspicious patterns in the life of a variable. A ur anomaly is a use of a variable that was never defined on some path (reading garbage or causing an error). A dd anomaly is a definition followed by another definition with no use in between, suggesting the first was pointless or the second was meant for another variable. A dk anomaly is a definition followed by the variable being killed (going out of scope) without ever being used. These do not always mean defects, but they often point to them, and compilers and linters warn about several of them.

Mutation testing, testing the tests: Coverage tells you code was executed, not that your tests would notice if it were wrong. Mutation testing measures that directly. A tool creates many small modified versions of the program, called mutants, each with one deliberate change: replacing greater-than with greater-than-or-equal, plus with minus, true with false, deleting a statement, or changing a constant. Then it runs your test suite against each mutant. If at least one test fails, the mutant is killed: your tests detected the change. If all tests pass, the mutant survived: your tests are blind to that change.

Mutation score worked: Suppose a tool generates 50 mutants of a pricing module. Analysis shows 5 are equivalent mutants: changes that do not alter behaviour at all, for example changing i < n to i != n in a loop where i always increases by 1 from 0. Of the remaining 45, the tests kill 36. Mutation score = killed / (total - equivalent) x 100 = 36 / 45 x 100 = 80 percent. The 9 survivors are a precise to-do list: each shows a change your tests could not see, often a missing boundary test or an assertion that checks too little.

Mutation tools and cost: Popular tools include PIT (pitest) for Java, Stryker for JavaScript, TypeScript and .NET, and mutmut for Python. Mutation testing is expensive, because the suite runs once per mutant; tools reduce cost by running only tests that cover the mutated line and by testing only changed code in pull requests. Identifying equivalent mutants still needs human judgement. Even so, running mutation testing on the most critical modules is one of the best ways to find weak tests.

Real-life example, a loop defect in an SMS sender: A school notice system sends SMS to guardians in batches of 100. Branch coverage was complete. Loop testing with exactly 100, 101 and 200 guardians revealed that when the list size was an exact multiple of 100, the last batch was sent twice, because the loop used less-than-or-equal on the batch index. Guardians of 100 students received duplicate notices and the school paid twice for those messages. The n and n + 1 loop tests found what coverage did not.

Real-life example, mutation testing on a VAT module: A team proud of 92 percent branch coverage on its VAT calculation ran PIT for the first time. Several mutants survived, including one that changed rounding from "round half up" to "round down". No test checked an amount where the rounding direction mattered, such as a value ending in exactly half a paisa. Adding three targeted tests killed the mutants. Months later, a library upgrade changed the default rounding mode, and those tests failed immediately instead of letting incorrect invoices reach customers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include thinking path coverage is practical for real programs, confusing basis paths with all paths, forgetting the 0-iteration and n + 1 loop tests, mixing up c-use and p-use, and ignoring equivalent mutants when computing the mutation score. Exams ask you to compute V(G) and list basis paths, write loop tests for a given maximum, identify defs, uses and du-pairs in a code fragment, name data-flow anomalies, and calculate a mutation score.

Recap: Path coverage is the strongest control-flow criterion but explodes and includes infeasible paths, so basis path testing uses V(G) independent paths as a practical compromise. Loop testing adds iteration counts: 0, 1, 2, typical, n - 1, n and n + 1, starting from the innermost loop for nested loops. Data-flow testing follows definitions and uses, with criteria from all-defs up to all-du-paths and anomalies like ur, dd and dk. Mutation testing judges the test suite itself by the share of non-equivalent mutants it kills. Next we step back from code to management: the test process, planning and strategy.
key_points: Path coverage executes every entry-to-exit path; it subsumes branch coverage but explodes and includes infeasible paths.
Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E - N + 2P = decisions + 1 gives the number of basis paths to test.
Loop tests for a maximum n: 0, 1, 2, typical m, n - 1, n and n + 1 iterations; start nested loops from the innermost.
Data-flow testing links definitions to uses: c-use in computations, p-use in predicates, along def-clear paths.
Criteria grow from all-defs to all-uses to all-du-paths; anomalies include ur, dd and dk.
Mutation testing creates mutants; a mutant is killed if some test fails.
Mutation score = killed / (total - equivalent) x 100.
lessons.tip: For every loop you test, ask two quick questions: what happens with zero items, and what happens with one more than the maximum? Those two tests catch more loop defects than any other pair.
lessons.task: Write a short function that loops over a list of marks (maximum 50 students), sums them, and flags the class if the average is below 40. Mark every def, c-use and p-use, list the du-pairs for each variable, compute V(G), and write the loop tests. Then invent five mutants by hand and check which of your tests would kill each one.

quiz.q: A function has 4 binary decisions. What is its cyclomatic complexity?
quiz.explain: V(G) = number of binary decisions + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5.

quiz.q: Using loop testing rules, which set of iteration counts should be tested for a loop with a maximum of 10?
quiz.explain: Simple-loop rules: skip, once, twice, typical, n - 1, n and n + 1.

quiz.q: In data-flow testing, what is a p-use?
options: A use of the variable to compute an output
A use of the variable in a condition that decides a branch
A variable that is never used
quiz.explain: A predicate use (p-use) appears in a decision; a computation use (c-use) appears in a calculation or output.

quiz.q: A tool creates 60 mutants, 10 are equivalent and the tests kill 40. What is the mutation score?
quiz.explain: Mutation score = 40 / (60 - 10) x 100 = 40 / 50 = 80 percent.

quiz.q: A variable is assigned a value and then assigned again before the first value is ever read. Which anomaly is this?
quiz.explain: A dd anomaly is two definitions with no use in between, suggesting the first was pointless or the wrong variable was used.

lessons.title: The Test Process, Test Planning and Test Strategy
lessons.content:
Think about organising a big family wedding. Somebody has to decide the budget, the guest list, which caterer to hire, who handles decorations, what happens if it rains, and how you will know everything is ready on the day. During the preparations, someone keeps checking progress and changes plans when the caterer cancels. After the event, someone settles the bills and notes what to do differently next time. Testing a software product is a similar project inside the project: it needs a process, a plan, a strategy, estimates, monitoring and a proper close.

Why testing needs a process: Without a process, testing becomes whatever people have time for at the end, usually some clicking around the day before release. A defined test process makes testing repeatable, visible and manageable: people know what to do and when, managers can see progress, and the organisation can improve over time. The process should be tailored to the context: a small startup and a bank use the same ideas at very different levels of formality.

The test process activities: A widely used model groups test work into seven activities. Test planning defines objectives and the approach. Test monitoring and control compares progress against the plan and takes action. Test analysis decides what to test by identifying test conditions from the test basis. Test design decides how to test by turning conditions into test cases using techniques. Test implementation prepares everything needed: test procedures, suites, data and environments. Test execution runs the tests and logs results and defects. Test completion closes the work, writes the summary report and captures lessons. These activities overlap and repeat, especially in Agile, rather than running strictly one after another.

Test analysis in more detail: In analysis, testers study the test basis (requirements, user stories, designs, risk analysis) and identify test conditions: things that could be tested, such as "transfer limit enforcement" or "refund for cancelled orders". Analysis also evaluates the test basis itself, finding ambiguities and missing information, which makes it a powerful static test. A useful question during analysis is "what could go wrong here, and how would we know?"

Test design and implementation: In design, test conditions become test cases using the techniques from lessons 7 to 13, and testers decide what test data and environments are needed. In implementation, they assemble test cases into test procedures and suites, prepare and load test data, set up environments and tools, write automation scripts, and check that everything is ready, often with a smoke test of the environment. Many delays in real projects come from environments and data, not from test design.

Test execution: Execution runs the tests, manually or automatically, compares actual results with expected results, logs outcomes (passed, failed, blocked, not run), reports defects for failures, performs confirmation testing after fixes and runs regression tests. Good execution logs record which build, which environment and which data were used, so failures can be reproduced and progress can be trusted.

Test monitoring and control: Monitoring gathers information about progress and quality: how many tests have run and passed, how many defects are open by severity, what coverage has been reached, how much effort has been spent. Control is acting on that information: re-prioritising tests when time is short, adding testers to a risky area, changing entry criteria when builds are unstable, or warning stakeholders that a release date is at risk. Monitoring without control is just watching a problem grow.

Test completion: When a release ships, a project ends or a test level finishes, completion activities include checking that all defects are closed or deferred with agreement, writing a test summary (completion) report, archiving testware (test cases, data, scripts, environments) for future reuse, handing over to maintenance or operations teams, and holding a retrospective to capture lessons. Teams that skip completion repeat the same mistakes in the next project.

The test plan: A test plan describes the objectives, resources and processes for a test project or level. Classic content, originally described in the IEEE 829 standard and now in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3, includes: scope (test items, features to be tested and not to be tested), objectives, assumptions and constraints, the test approach (levels, types, techniques, independence, automation), entry and exit criteria, suspension and resumption criteria (when to pause testing, for example if smoke tests fail, and when to restart), test deliverables, environment needs, roles and responsibilities, staffing and training, schedule, risks and contingencies, and approvals.

Features not to be tested: Explicitly listing what will not be tested is one of the most valuable parts of a plan. If the plan says "the old reporting module is out of scope because it is unchanged and will be retired next quarter", everyone knows the decision and its reason, and nobody is surprised later. Silent gaps are dangerous; written, agreed gaps are management decisions.

Test strategy approaches: A test strategy describes the general approach to testing, often at organisation or programme level, while the plan applies it to one project. Common strategy types are: analytical (based on analysis of a factor, most often risk, as in risk-based testing), model-based (tests from models such as state machines or usage profiles), methodical (systematic use of checklists, quality characteristics or failure taxonomies), process-compliant or standard-compliant (following an external standard or regulation), directed or consultative (guided by advice from stakeholders or experts), regression-averse (heavy reuse and automation of existing tests to avoid breaking what works), and reactive (responding to the system as it is delivered, typically through exploratory testing). Real strategies usually blend several.

Agile testing quadrants: In Agile teams, Brian Marick's testing quadrants help plan a balanced mix. Quadrant 1 is technology-facing tests that support the team, such as unit and component tests, mostly automated. Quadrant 2 is business-facing tests that support the team, such as functional and story tests and examples, automated or manual. Quadrant 3 is business-facing tests that critique the product, such as exploratory testing, usability testing and user acceptance testing, mostly manual. Quadrant 4 is technology-facing tests that critique the product, such as performance and security testing, usually tool-based. A plan with nothing in one quadrant has a blind spot.

Entry, exit and suspension criteria: Entry criteria protect testers from wasting time on unready builds: requirements reviewed, build installed, smoke tests passed, test data ready. Exit criteria define done: planned coverage reached, a minimum share of tests executed and passed, no open critical defects, residual risk accepted. Suspension criteria say when to stop temporarily: for example, if more than 30 percent of smoke tests fail or the environment is down. In practice exit criteria are often bent under deadline pressure; when that happens, the test report should state clearly which criteria were not met and what risk remains.

Estimation, why it is hard: Test effort depends on product size and complexity, quality of the test basis, quality of the code (more defects mean more retesting), the stability of environments, team skills, the degree of automation and the required rigour. Estimates are predictions, not promises, and should be revised as information arrives. Two families of techniques are common: metrics-based (using data from past projects) and expert-based (using the judgement of experienced people).

Metrics-based estimation worked: Suppose your company's past project needed 600 person-days of development and 240 person-days of testing, a test-to-development ratio of 40 percent. A new, similar project is estimated at 450 person-days of development. Using the same ratio, test effort is about 450 x 0.40 = 180 person-days. Ratios only work when projects are genuinely similar in type, technology and team; otherwise adjust them or combine with expert judgement.

Expert-based estimation: Wideband Delphi asks several experts to estimate independently, discuss the differences, and estimate again until estimates converge. Planning Poker, used in Scrum, is a lightweight form: each team member shows a card with their estimate at the same time, outliers explain their reasoning, and the team re-votes. Both reduce the risk of one loud person anchoring everyone else.

Three-point estimation worked: For each task, estimate an optimistic value a, a most likely value m and a pessimistic value b. The common PERT formula gives the expected value E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 and a standard deviation SD = (b - a) / 6. For system testing of a payments release, suppose a = 6 days, m = 9 days and b = 18 days. Then E = (6 + 36 + 18) / 6 = 60 / 6 = 10 days, and SD = (18 - 6) / 6 = 2 days. You might report "about 10 days, likely between 8 and 12". The long pessimistic tail pulled the estimate above the most likely value, which is realistic for testing, where unstable builds and late fixes often cause delays.

Real-life example, planning UAT for a district hospital system: A team rolling out a patient registration system to district hospitals writes a test plan with clear scope (registration, billing and SMS reminders; not the pharmacy module, which is unchanged), entry criteria (system testing passed with no critical defects, trained users available), and suspension criteria (stop if the regional network is down). The estimate uses three-point values per hospital because network conditions differ. When one district's network keeps failing, monitoring shows UAT falling behind, and control moves that district to the end of the schedule and brings in a mobile data backup. The release date holds.

Real-life example, a reactive strategy for a hackathon product: A small Dhaka startup has two weeks to launch a minimum viable product for a competition. A heavy formal plan would waste their time. They choose a reactive and analytical blend: a one-page plan listing the three most important user journeys and the top risks, short exploratory sessions after each build, and automated unit tests only for payment calculations. The plan is light but conscious: they know what they are not testing and accept the risk for this launch.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes are writing a plan once and never updating it, confusing test strategy (general approach) with test plan (applied to a project), omitting features not to be tested, and treating estimates as fixed promises. Exams ask you to list the test process activities and their outputs, name parts of a test plan, match scenarios to strategy types, apply the three-point formula, and distinguish entry, exit and suspension criteria.

Recap: The test process covers planning, monitoring and control, analysis, design, implementation, execution and completion, tailored to the context. The test plan states scope, objectives, approach, criteria, resources, schedule and risks, including what will not be tested. Strategies may be analytical, model-based, methodical, process-compliant, directed, regression-averse or reactive, and Agile quadrants help balance them. Estimates come from metrics and expert judgement, with the three-point formula E = (a + 4m + b) / 6. Next we zoom into the building blocks of all this: test cases, suites and test data.
key_points: Test process activities: planning, monitoring and control, analysis, design, implementation, execution and completion.
Analysis decides what to test (test conditions); design decides how (test cases); implementation prepares procedures, data and environments.
A test plan covers scope, objectives, approach, entry, exit and suspension criteria, deliverables, environment, roles, schedule and risks.
Explicitly listing features not to be tested turns silent gaps into agreed decisions.
Strategy types include analytical (risk-based), model-based, methodical, process-compliant, directed, regression-averse and reactive.
Agile testing quadrants balance technology-facing and business-facing tests that support the team or critique the product.
Three-point estimation: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 and SD = (b - a) / 6.
lessons.tip: In any test plan you write, fill in "features not to be tested" first. It forces the hardest conversation early, and examiners and managers both notice when it is missing.
lessons.task: Write a one-page test plan for testing your university's online course registration during the next enrolment week: scope, out-of-scope items, three entry criteria, three exit criteria, one suspension criterion, three risks, and a three-point estimate for system testing with your own a, m and b values.

quiz.q: Which test process activity identifies test conditions, deciding what to test?
quiz.explain: Analysis identifies test conditions from the test basis; design then turns them into test cases.

quiz.q: Using three-point estimation with a = 4, m = 6 and b = 14 days, what is the expected effort?
A strategy that relies on exploratory testing in response to the delivered system is called:
quiz.explain: A reactive strategy reacts to the system as delivered, typically through exploratory testing.

quiz.q: What do suspension criteria in a test plan describe?
options: The features that will not be tested
The format of the test summary report
When testing should be paused, for example when smoke tests fail, and when it can resume
quiz.explain: Suspension and resumption criteria define when to stop testing temporarily and the conditions to restart.

quiz.q: In the Agile testing quadrants, where do performance and security tests belong?
options: Quadrant 1, technology-facing tests that support the team
Quadrant 4, technology-facing tests that critique the product
Quadrant 2, business-facing tests that support the team
Quadrant 3, business-facing tests that critique the product
quiz.explain: Performance and security testing are technology-facing and critique the product, usually with tools.

lessons.title: Test Cases, Test Suites, Test Data and the Test Oracle
lessons.content:
A good recipe for khichuri does not say "cook some rice and dal until it tastes nice". It lists the ingredients and their amounts, the steps in order, and what the result should look like: soft, slightly mushy, yellow from turmeric. Anyone following it should get the same result, and if the result is wrong, you can tell which step went wrong. A test case is a recipe for checking one thing about the software. Write it vaguely and two testers will do different things and reach different conclusions; write it well and anyone can run it, repeat it and trust it.

The vocabulary ladder: Several related words describe test work at different levels of detail. A test condition is something that can be tested, identified during analysis, such as "money transfer respects the daily limit". A test scenario is a story-level description of a situation to test, often covering a user journey, such as "a customer sends money several times in one day until the limit is reached". A test case is a set of preconditions, inputs, actions, expected results and postconditions designed to check one condition or a small group of them. A test procedure is a sequence of test cases in execution order with any setup and wrap-up steps. A test script is usually an automated test procedure. A test suite is a set of test cases or procedures grouped for execution, such as "smoke suite" or "payments regression suite".

Anatomy of a test case: A typical test case contains: a unique ID (for example TC-PAY-017); a short title stating the purpose; links to the requirement, user story or risk it covers; preconditions (what must be true before starting, such as "user is logged in with balance of 30,000 Taka"); test data; steps, each a clear action; expected results for each step or at the end; postconditions (the expected state afterwards, such as "balance is 5,000 Taka and one transaction is logged"); priority; and the environment or configuration if relevant. During execution, the actual result, status, build number, date and tester are recorded.

A worked test case: ID TC-SEND-021. Title: transfer exactly at the daily limit is accepted. Covers: requirement REQ-SEND-04 (daily limit 25,000 Taka). Preconditions: user registered and verified; no transfers today; balance 30,000 Taka. Data: receiver 01712345678 (a test account), amount 25,000. Steps: 1 open Send Money; 2 enter receiver; 3 enter amount 25,000; 4 enter PIN; 5 confirm. Expected: confirmation screen shows success; receiver balance increases by 25,000; sender balance is 5,000 minus any fee defined in the fee table; an SMS is sent to both. Postcondition: today's sent total equals 25,000; a further transfer of 1 Taka is rejected (covered by TC-SEND-022).

High-level and low-level test cases: A high-level (logical) test case describes what to test without exact values, for example "send money exactly at the daily limit". A low-level (concrete) test case has exact data and steps, like TC-SEND-021. High-level cases are faster to write, adapt well when details change, and leave room for experienced testers to vary data. Low-level cases are better for less experienced testers, for regulated environments needing exact evidence, and for automation. Many teams write high-level cases early and make them concrete when the system stabilises.

Qualities of a good test case: Each test case should have one clear objective, so a failure points to one problem. It should have a precise expected result: "works correctly" is not an expected result. It should be independent where possible, not relying on another test having run first, so tests can run in any order or in parallel. It should be repeatable, giving the same result each time on the same build. It should be traceable to the basis it tests. And it should be maintainable: avoid hard-coding details that change often, such as screen positions, when the purpose does not depend on them.

Common test case smells: Vague steps ("check the page"), missing expected results, many unrelated checks in one case, dependence on data that may disappear, hidden preconditions that only the author knows, and copy-paste duplicates that differ only slightly. Another smell is expected results copied from the actual system output: if the system was wrong when the test was written, the test now enshrines the defect.

Organising test suites: Suites group tests for a purpose. By scope: a smoke suite (minutes), a sanity suite for a feature, a full regression suite (hours). By feature: login, payments, reports. By level: unit, API, UI. By priority: critical paths first. Good organisation lets a team run the right subset at the right time: smoke on every build, payments regression on every payments change, full regression nightly or before release. Test management tools such as TestRail, Zephyr or Xray (a Jira add-on) store test cases, suites and execution history.

The traceability matrix: A requirements traceability matrix (RTM) is a table linking requirements to test cases (and often to defects and results). Rows are requirements; columns or cells list the tests that cover each. It answers key questions: which requirements have no tests (coverage gaps)? If a requirement changes, which tests must be updated (impact analysis)? If a test fails, which requirements are at risk? Forward traceability goes from requirements to tests; backward traceability goes from tests back to requirements, revealing tests that check nothing anybody asked for.

Traceability worked: A release has 20 requirements. The RTM shows that 18 have at least one test case and 2 (an export feature and an audit log) have none. Requirements coverage is 18 / 20 = 90 percent. Of the 18 covered, tests for 15 have passed, 2 have failed and 1 is blocked. A useful report line: "90 percent of requirements are covered by tests; 75 percent (15 of 20) are verified as passing; 2 requirements have no tests and are at unknown risk." That one sentence tells a product owner far more than "we ran 412 test cases".

Test data, why it is hard: Tests need data: customers, accounts, products, orders, balances, historical transactions. Data must be in the right state (a customer who is blocked, an order that is half-refunded), at the right boundaries (balance exactly at the limit), in the right volume (millions of rows for performance tests), and consistent across systems. Bad test data is a top cause of blocked tests and false failures.

Sources of test data: Production copies are realistic but dangerous: they contain personal data such as names, phone numbers, national ID numbers and transaction histories, and using them in test environments can breach privacy laws and company policy. Masking (or anonymisation) replaces sensitive fields with realistic fake values while keeping formats and relationships, for example replacing every real phone number with a valid-looking fake one consistently across tables. Synthetic data is generated from scratch by scripts or tools to match rules and distributions; it is safe and can be designed to include boundaries and rare cases. Subsetting copies a small consistent slice of production to save space.

Privacy and test data: Many countries have data protection laws, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and regulators and banks in many countries also set their own rules. A safe default for students and companies alike: never use real personal data in test environments unless it is properly masked and you have explicit permission. Test accounts on payment gateways and telecom sandboxes exist precisely so that testers do not need real customers' money or numbers.

Test environments: Most organisations have several environments: development (for developers), test or QA (for testers, often unstable), staging or pre-production (a close mirror of production, for system, acceptance and performance testing), and production. Each needs the right build, configuration, data and connected services. Environment problems, such as an expired certificate in staging or a third-party sandbox being down, are a major source of delays. Infrastructure-as-code and containers help create consistent environments on demand.

The test oracle problem: To decide whether a test passed, you need to know the expected result. The source of that knowledge is called a test oracle. Specifications are the obvious oracle, but they are often incomplete or vague. Other oracles include: a previous version of the system (if it was correct, the new one should give the same answer, which is the basis of regression testing), a comparable product or a parallel calculation in a spreadsheet, a domain expert, and heuristic oracles that check plausibility rather than exact values (a total can never be negative; a list sorted ascending must never decrease). The difficulty of obtaining reliable expected results is known as the oracle problem.

Metamorphic testing: When the exact expected output is unknown, you can sometimes check relations between outputs. For a search function, adding a filter should never return more results than without the filter. For a route planner, the distance from A to B should equal the distance from B to A on two-way roads. For a currency converter, converting 100 Taka to dollars and back should give about 100 Taka, minus known fees. These metamorphic relations let you test complex systems such as machine learning models, scientific calculations and search engines where exact answers are hard to know.

Real-life example, a payroll test suite: A payroll company in Dhaka keeps an RTM linking every salary rule (overtime, festival bonus, tax deduction, provident fund) to concrete test cases with synthetic employees: one paid exactly at a tax threshold, one joining mid-month, one with zero overtime. When the government changes the tax-free income limit, impact analysis through the RTM shows exactly which 37 test cases need new expected values. Without traceability, testers would have rerun everything and still missed some.

Real-life example, masked data catches a real defect: A bank's testers use masked production data for system testing. Because masking preserved realistic patterns, the data included customers whose names contained a dot and a hyphen, and a few whose addresses exceeded 200 characters. The new statement printing feature crashed for those accounts. Synthetic data written by the team had only simple names and short addresses. Realistic but safe data found a defect that clean, invented data had hidden.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include vague expected results, chaining test cases so one failure blocks ten others, testing with real personal data, and writing expected results by copying actual output. Exams ask you to define test condition, scenario, case, procedure and suite and put them in order of detail, write a complete test case from a requirement, build a small traceability matrix and compute requirements coverage, compare production, masked and synthetic data, and explain the oracle problem with examples.

Recap: Test conditions say what to test, scenarios describe situations, test cases give preconditions, data, steps and expected results, procedures order them, and suites group them for execution. Good cases have one objective, precise expected results, independence, repeatability and traceability. A traceability matrix links requirements and tests for coverage and impact analysis. Test data should be realistic yet safe: masked or synthetic, never raw personal data. Oracles, from specifications to metamorphic relations, tell us what correct looks like. Next we follow what happens when a test fails: the defect lifecycle and bug reports.
key_points: Test condition (what), scenario (situation), test case (inputs, steps, expected results), procedure (order) and suite (group) differ in level of detail.
A good test case has an ID, purpose, traceability, preconditions, data, steps, precise expected results and postconditions.
Good test cases have one objective and are independent, repeatable, traceable and maintainable.
A traceability matrix links requirements to tests; requirements coverage = requirements with tests / total requirements.
Test data can be production copies (risky), masked, synthetic or subsetted; never use unmasked personal data.
Environments include development, test, staging and production, and staging should mirror production.
A test oracle tells you the expected result; metamorphic relations help when exact answers are unknown.
lessons.tip: Read each expected result you write and ask: could two different testers disagree on whether this passed? If yes, rewrite it with a number, a message text or a specific state.
lessons.task: Pick one feature of an app you use (for example changing your password). Write five complete test cases in the format of this lesson, including one boundary case and one negative case, then build a small traceability matrix linking them to three requirements you write yourself.

quiz.q: Which item is the least detailed: test case, test condition, test procedure or test script?
quiz.explain: A test condition is just something to be tested; cases, procedures and scripts add progressively more detail.

quiz.q: A release has 25 requirements and 20 have at least one test. What is the requirements coverage?
quiz.explain: Requirements coverage = 20 / 25 = 80 percent.

quiz.q: Which is the safest source of test data containing customer phone numbers?
options: Real numbers of team members' relatives
Masked or synthetic data with realistic but fake numbers
quiz.explain: Masked or synthetic data keeps realistic formats without exposing real people's personal data.

quiz.q: Checking that adding a filter never increases the number of search results is an example of:
options: A metamorphic relation used as an oracle
quiz.explain: Metamorphic testing checks relations between outputs when the exact expected result is unknown.

quiz.q: Why should test cases be independent of each other where possible?
options: So that one failure does not block others and tests can run in any order or in parallel
So that they can share a single expected result
So that they do not need preconditions
So that traceability is not needed
quiz.explain: Independent tests isolate failures, can run in parallel, and do not cascade when one breaks.

lessons.title: The Defect Lifecycle and Writing Good Bug Reports
lessons.content:
Imagine calling an electrician because "the light is not working". He arrives and asks: which light, since when, does the switch click, is the bulb new, does the fan in the same room work? If you had told him "the bedroom ceiling light stopped working yesterday after a storm; the fan on the same switchboard works; I tried a new bulb", he could have brought the right tools and fixed it in ten minutes. A bug report is your message to the developer-electrician. The clearer it is, the faster the defect is fixed. And once reported, every defect goes on a journey through states until it is finally closed: the defect lifecycle.

Why defect management matters: Testing produces information, and defects are its most important output. If defects are reported vaguely, lost, duplicated, argued about endlessly or silently ignored, testing effort is wasted. Defect management is the process of recording, classifying, investigating, prioritising, fixing, verifying and closing defects, and learning from them. It also produces data for metrics and process improvement, which later lessons use.

What gets reported: Testers report anomalies: any condition that deviates from expectation based on requirements, designs, standards or user expectations. Not every anomaly is a defect. It might be a test error (wrong expected result, wrong data), an environment problem, a misunderstanding of the requirement, or an intended change nobody told the testers about. That is why reports are investigated before being accepted as defects, and why politely worded, factual reports matter.

The defect lifecycle: Exact state names vary by tool and company, but a typical lifecycle looks like this. New: the tester has logged the report. Assigned: a lead or triage group has accepted it and assigned it to a developer. Open or In progress: the developer is investigating and fixing. Fixed or Resolved: the developer has changed the code and the fix is in a build. Retest or Ready for test: the tester is checking the fix. Verified: the confirmation test passed. Closed: the defect is finished. Reopened: the confirmation test failed or the defect came back, so it goes back to the developer.

Other exits from the lifecycle: Not every report follows the happy path. Rejected (or Not a bug, Works as designed): after investigation, the behaviour is correct or the report was a test error. Duplicate: the same defect was already reported; the new report is linked to the original. Deferred (or Postponed): it is a real defect, but the fix is planned for a later release, usually because it is low risk and time is short. Cannot reproduce: the developer cannot make the failure happen; the tester should add information, logs or exact steps. Each of these states needs a reason recorded, so decisions are visible later.

A worked lifecycle: A tester logs BUG-412 "Refund amount doubled when order cancelled twice" as New. In the daily triage, the lead assigns it to the payments developer: Assigned. The developer reproduces it, finds a missing check, fixes it: Fixed in build 3.4.1. The tester re-runs the steps on build 3.4.1, the refund is correct: Verified. She also runs related regression tests on refunds, which pass, and the defect is Closed. A week later the same symptom appears through the mobile app; the defect is Reopened with new steps, and the cycle continues.

Severity versus priority: These two fields are the most confused in defect management. Severity describes the impact of the defect on the system or user: how bad is it when it happens? Priority describes the urgency of fixing it: how soon must it be fixed, considering business needs, release plans and risk? Severity is usually suggested by the tester; priority is usually decided by the product owner or triage group. Common scales are severity (critical or blocker, major, minor, trivial) and priority (P1 urgent to P4 low).

Severity and priority examples: The bank's name misspelled on the login page of a banking app: low severity (nothing functional breaks) but high priority (embarrassing, seen by every customer, fix today). The app crashes when generating a yearly tax certificate in a rarely used admin screen that is needed only in July: high severity but, in November, lower priority. Wrong interest calculated on all savings accounts: high severity and high priority. A slightly misaligned icon in an old settings page: low severity and low priority. Keeping the two separate lets teams make sensible trade-offs.

Anatomy of a good bug report: A good report contains: a unique ID (assigned by the tool); a clear summary title; the environment (app version or build, operating system, browser or device, test environment, account used); preconditions; numbered steps to reproduce; expected result; actual result; reproducibility (always, sometimes, once, for example "4 out of 5 attempts"); severity and suggested priority; attachments such as screenshots, screen recordings, log excerpts or network traces; references to the requirement or test case; and the reporter and date.

Writing the title: The title is what people read in lists, emails and meetings, so it must stand alone. A useful pattern is: where it happens, what happens, under which condition. Weak: "Payment bug". Better: "Checkout: card payment shows success but order stays Unpaid when network drops after OTP". A good title makes duplicates easy to spot and helps the triage group judge severity at a glance.

Steps, expected and actual: Steps should be minimal and exact: someone new should be able to follow them without asking questions. Start from a known state, give exact data, and remove steps that are not needed to reproduce. The expected result should cite the source when possible ("per REQ-REF-07 the refund equals the amount paid, 1,250 Taka"). The actual result should describe what happened, factually, without guessing the cause or using emotional words. If you have a theory about the cause, add it separately as a note.

Isolating the defect: Before reporting, good testers spend a few minutes narrowing it down. Does it happen in another browser? With another account? With a smaller amount? Only after logout and login? This isolation makes reports far more useful and often turns "the app sometimes crashes" into "the app crashes when a product name contains an emoji". However, testers should not spend hours debugging; that is the developer's job. The goal is a reproducible, well-described failure.

Tone and collaboration: Bug reports are read by people who worked hard on the code. Write about the product, not the person: "Refund doubles when..." not "Developer forgot to check...". Avoid capital letters, sarcasm and words like "terrible". Be open to the answer "works as designed": sometimes the requirement is the real problem, and then the conversation moves to the product owner. A respectful reporting culture makes developers want to read testers' reports first.

Triage: In most teams, new defects are reviewed regularly, daily during intense testing, by a triage group or defect review board: often a test lead, a development lead and the product owner. They confirm the defect is valid, check for duplicates, set priority, assign an owner and decide on a target release. Triage keeps the defect backlog under control and ensures the most important problems are fixed first.

Keeping the backlog healthy: A defect backlog with hundreds of old, unprioritised items is almost as bad as no tracking at all, because nobody can see what matters. Healthy teams regularly close reports that are no longer relevant (the feature was removed), merge duplicates, re-check deferred defects before each release, and watch the age of open critical defects. A simple rule such as "no critical defect may stay open longer than two days without an owner and a plan" keeps attention where it belongs.

Defect tracking tools: Defects are tracked in tools such as Jira, Azure DevOps, Bugzilla, Redmine or GitHub Issues. These tools enforce the lifecycle (which transitions are allowed), keep history and comments, link defects to code changes and test cases, and produce reports such as open defects by severity or average time to fix. A shared tool is essential: defects tracked in personal spreadsheets or chat messages get lost.

Root cause analysis: Fixing a defect removes one problem; finding its root cause can prevent many. The 5 Whys technique asks "why?" repeatedly. Why was the refund doubled? Because the cancel API was called twice. Why? Because the button was not disabled after the first tap. Why? Because the UI guideline does not mention double-submission. Why? Because nobody reviewed guidelines against past incidents. Root cause: missing process for updating guidelines after incidents. The fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram organises possible causes into categories such as people, process, tools, environment, requirements and code, so the team does not jump to the first explanation.

Classifying defects for learning: Teams also record attributes such as the phase where the defect was introduced (requirements, design, code), the phase where it was found, the type (logic, interface, data, UI) and the module. Over time, patterns appear: if many defects are introduced in requirements but found only in system testing, requirement reviews need strengthening. IBM's Orthogonal Defect Classification is one well-known scheme for this kind of analysis.

Real-life example, a ride-sharing fare defect: A tester finds that some riders are charged the night surcharge for trips starting at 9:58 pm. She isolates it: it happens only when the trip ends after 10 pm, and only on Android. Her report title: "Android: night surcharge applied to whole trip when trip starts before 10 pm and ends after". She attaches two receipts, the expected fare from the fare rules document, and app logs. The triage group sets high priority because thousands of riders travel at that hour. The fix is verified the next day; the report was so precise that the developer needed no follow-up questions.

Real-life example, severity versus priority during a festival sale: Two days before a big sale, a tester finds two defects. One: the order history page crashes for customers with more than 500 orders, a high-severity defect affecting a few dozen wholesale customers. Two: the sale banner shows the wrong end date, a low-severity cosmetic issue seen by everyone. The product owner sets the banner as P1 (fix today) and the crash as P2 (fix this week, with a workaround of exporting history by email). Both decisions were reasonable once severity and priority were kept separate.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include vague titles, missing steps or environment, mixing several defects in one report, emotional language, confusing severity with priority, and closing defects without confirmation testing. Exams ask you to draw or describe the lifecycle with states and transitions, give examples of high severity with low priority and vice versa, list the contents of a good defect report, criticise a badly written report, and explain root cause analysis with 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram.

Recap: Defects move through a lifecycle: New, Assigned, Open, Fixed, Retest, Verified and Closed, with exits such as Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, Deferred and Cannot reproduce. Severity measures impact; priority measures urgency, and they are set separately. Good bug reports have a clear title, environment, minimal exact steps, expected and actual results, reproducibility and evidence, written factually and politely. Triage controls the backlog, tools enforce the workflow, and root cause analysis turns defects into process improvement. Next we use risk to decide where to test hardest.
key_points: A typical lifecycle: New, Assigned, Open, Fixed, Retest, Verified, Closed, with Reopened if the confirmation test fails.
Other outcomes: Rejected (not a bug), Duplicate, Deferred and Cannot reproduce, each with a recorded reason.
Severity is the impact of a defect; priority is the urgency of fixing it, decided with business input.
A good report has a clear title, environment, preconditions, minimal exact steps, expected and actual results, reproducibility and attachments.
Isolate the failure briefly before reporting, but leave debugging to developers.
Triage groups confirm, prioritise and assign defects; tools like Jira enforce the workflow.
Root cause analysis with 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram prevents families of similar defects.
lessons.tip: Before you press submit, read your bug report as if you were a new developer who has never seen the app. If you would need to ask even one question to reproduce it, add that answer to the report.
lessons.task: Find a real minor problem in an app or website you use (a typo, a layout issue, a confusing message). Write a complete bug report for it using the anatomy in this lesson, assign severity and priority with a one-line reason for each, and then do a 5 Whys analysis guessing how it might have happened.

quiz.q: A confirmation test fails after a developer marks a defect as fixed. What state does the defect usually move to?
quiz.explain: If the fix does not work, the defect is reopened and goes back to the developer.

quiz.q: The company name is misspelled on the home page that every customer sees. How would this usually be classified?
quiz.explain: Nothing functional breaks (low severity), but it is highly visible and embarrassing, so it should be fixed quickly (high priority).

quiz.q: Which title is the best for a bug report?
options: Checkout: card payment shows success but order stays Unpaid when network drops after OTP
quiz.explain: A good title says where, what and under which condition, so it stands alone in lists and meetings.

quiz.q: Who usually decides the priority of a defect?
options: Only the tester who found it
The product owner or a triage group, considering business needs
The customer who reported a different problem
quiz.explain: Testers suggest severity; priority reflects business urgency and is typically set during triage with the product owner.

quiz.q: Which technique repeatedly asks why a problem happened to find its root cause?
quiz.explain: The 5 Whys technique digs from the symptom down to a process-level root cause by repeatedly asking why.

lessons.title: Risk-Based Testing
lessons.content:
Before Eid, millions of people travel home from Dhaka. A family packing for the journey cannot check everything equally. They check the tickets and the phone charger many times, because forgetting them would ruin the trip, and they barely think about the third pair of socks. They also pay attention to things that are likely to go wrong: the bus that is often late, the ferry crossing that gets crowded. That instinct, spend effort where the chance of trouble and the damage of trouble are greatest, is exactly what risk-based testing turns into a method.

Why testing needs risk: Exhaustive testing is impossible, time is always limited, and some failures matter much more than others. A typo on the "About us" page and a wrong balance in a wallet are both defects, but no sensible team treats them the same. Risk-based testing uses an analysis of risks to decide what to test, how deeply, in what order, and when testing is enough. It is the most widely used analytical test strategy.

What a risk is: A risk is a factor that could result in a future negative consequence. It has two dimensions: likelihood (also called probability), how likely the problem is to occur, and impact (also called harm or consequence), how bad it would be if it did. The level of risk combines them, often as risk level = likelihood x impact. A very likely but trivial problem and a very unlikely but catastrophic problem can both deserve attention, for different reasons.

Product risks and project risks: Product risks (also called quality risks) are about the product failing to satisfy users or stakeholders: wrong calculations, poor performance, security holes, bad usability, data loss. Project risks are about the project itself: late delivery of builds, staff leaving, test environments not ready, a vendor's API sandbox being unavailable, unclear requirements, budget cuts. Testing mainly reduces product risks; project risks are managed by the project manager, though testers must report those that threaten testing, such as an environment that is never ready.

What drives likelihood: Technical factors make defects more likely: complex logic, new or unfamiliar technology, many interfaces, recent large changes, code with a history of defects (defect clustering), time pressure, inexperienced or distributed teams, and weak requirements. Developers and architects are good sources for likelihood: they know which parts of the code scare them.

What drives impact: Business factors make failures more harmful: how often a feature is used, how many users it affects, financial loss, legal and regulatory consequences, safety, damage to reputation, and whether a workaround exists. Product owners, business analysts, customer support and operations staff are good sources for impact: they know which complaints hurt most.

Risk identification: Risks are identified in workshops, brainstorming, interviews with stakeholders, checklists of quality characteristics (ISO/IEC 25010 is a good prompt), reviews of past incidents and defect data, and retrospectives. The output is a risk register: a list of risks, each described clearly, for example "delivery fee may be wrong for orders combining multiple vendors", not just "delivery fee".

Risk analysis worked: A food delivery app team rates six product risks on a 1 to 5 scale for likelihood (L) and impact (I). Delivery fee calculation, recently rewritten and complex: L 4, I 4, score 16. Payment processing: L 3, I 5, score 15. Login with OTP: L 2, I 5, score 10. Restaurant search: L 4, I 2, score 8. Order history page: L 3, I 2, score 6. Profile picture upload: L 2, I 1, score 2. Sorted by score: delivery fee 16, payment 15, login 10, search 8, history 6, profile picture 2.

From scores to test depth: The team defines bands. High (15 and above): thorough testing with several black-box techniques, white-box coverage targets on the code, independent review, extensive automated regression and exploratory sessions. Medium (8 to 14): systematic black-box tests of main flows and boundaries plus regression. Low (7 and below): smoke checks and light exploratory testing. So the delivery fee and payment get the most effort, login and search medium, and order history and profile picture light testing. Everyone can see why, and the decisions can be discussed.

From scores to test order: Risk also sets the order. High-risk areas are tested first, so if time runs out, what remains untested is the least risky. This is a crucial difference from testing in the order of the menu or the order features were built. When a release date is fixed and testing is squeezed, risk-based ordering means the team still delivered the most valuable information.

Qualitative and quantitative analysis: The 1 to 5 scales above are qualitative: judgement turned into numbers for comparison. Quantitative analysis uses real probabilities and costs when they are available. Risk exposure = probability x loss. If there is a 10 percent chance that a pricing defect causes 50 lakh Taka in refunds, the exposure is 0.10 x 50,00,000 = 5 lakh Taka. That figure helps decide whether spending 2 lakh on extra testing is worth it. Most teams use qualitative analysis, because reliable probabilities are rare.

Risk mitigation through testing: For each significant product risk, the team chooses responses: which test levels and types address it, which techniques, how much coverage, which reviews, which testers (more experienced people on higher risks), and whether to add monitoring in production. Testing is not the only mitigation: risks can also be reduced by design changes, by adding validation, by feature flags that let a risky feature be turned off quickly, or by training support staff.

How much testing is enough: Risk also answers the eternal question of when to stop. Instead of "when the time runs out" or "when all test cases have run", exit criteria can be stated in risk terms: every high risk has tests designed with at least two techniques and all of them pass; every medium risk has its main flows and boundaries tested; no open defect is linked to a high risk. When these are met, the remaining uncertainty is in low-risk areas, and stopping is a defensible business decision rather than a guess.

Risk in Agile teams: In Scrum, risk analysis does not need a separate phase. During backlog refinement, the team adds a quick risk rating to each story, often just high, medium or low, and uses it to decide how many acceptance criteria to write, whether to pair a tester with the developer, and how much automation the story deserves. At sprint review, the team checks whether any new risks appeared, such as a new third-party dependency. Small, frequent risk conversations keep the analysis alive instead of letting it rot in a document.

Risk monitoring and residual risk: Risks change during a project. A module that keeps failing tests becomes more likely to fail; a feature that the business cancels loses its impact. The risk register should be updated as testing progresses. When testing finishes, residual risk is the risk that remains: areas not tested deeply, known defects not fixed, and the general uncertainty that testing can never remove (principle 1). Good test reports state residual risk clearly so that stakeholders accept it knowingly.

Reporting in risk terms: Managers do not decide releases from "we ran 812 tests". They decide from statements like: "all high risks have been tested and pass; two medium risks (search ranking and order history) have open minor defects with workarounds; low risks received smoke testing only." Risk-based reporting connects testing to business decisions, which is what makes testers trusted advisers rather than bug counters.

FMEA, a related technique: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis comes from engineering and is used for safety-critical and high-reliability systems. For each possible failure mode, the team rates severity (S), occurrence (O) and detection (D, how hard it is to detect before it reaches the user), typically on 1 to 10 scales, and computes a risk priority number RPN = S x O x D. A failure mode with severity 8, occurrence 3 and detection 5 has RPN 120. Higher RPNs get attention first. The detection factor is a useful idea for testers: a failure that would be silent is more dangerous than one that is obvious.

Pitfalls of risk-based testing: Risk scores are judgements and can be biased: a loud stakeholder can inflate a pet feature's impact, and teams tend to underestimate risks in areas they built themselves. Use several viewpoints, compare with past defect data, and revisit scores. Another pitfall is ignoring low-risk areas completely; low risk is not zero risk, so give them at least smoke tests. Finally, do not let risk analysis become a heavy document nobody reads: a one-page risk table that the team updates every sprint is better than a beautiful report written once.

Real-life example, a mobile wallet release: A wallet company plans a release with a redesigned home screen, a new utility bill payment for electricity and gas, and a change to cash-out fee rules. The risk workshop rates the fee change highest (affects every cash-out, involves money, logic rewritten), bill payment high (new integration with external billers), and the home screen medium (visible but mostly layout). Testing plans follow: decision tables and BVA for every fee rule, contract tests and sandbox system integration tests with each biller, and exploratory and compatibility testing on popular low-end phones for the home screen. A defect in the fee for amounts exactly at a slab boundary is found on day two, because that area was tested first.
