Real-life example, a project risk that blocked testing: A government service portal depends on a national identity verification service. The test plan's risk register lists "verification sandbox unavailable" as a project risk with high likelihood. The mitigation is prepared early: a stub service that mimics the verification responses, including failures and timeouts. When the real sandbox goes down for a week, testing continues against the stub, and only a small set of end-to-end tests waits for the real service. Without risk planning, the whole test schedule would have slipped.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include confusing product and project risks, using only impact or only likelihood, treating risk scores as precise facts, and failing to update the risk register. Exams ask you to classify risks as product or project, compute risk levels from a matrix and order test priorities, explain how risk affects test depth, order and exit criteria, compute risk exposure or an FMEA RPN, and define residual risk.

Recap: Risk-based testing directs effort to where failures are most likely and most harmful. Risk level combines likelihood (driven by technical factors) and impact (driven by business factors). Product risks are what testing reduces; project risks threaten the project and testing itself. A risk matrix ranks areas, which then guides depth, order and exit decisions, and residual risk is reported clearly at the end. FMEA adds detection to the picture. Next we move from management to code again, with unit testing frameworks, TDD and BDD.
key_points: Risk level combines likelihood and impact, often as likelihood x impact.
Product (quality) risks concern the product failing; project risks concern schedule, staff, environments and vendors.
Technical factors drive likelihood; business factors drive impact.
Risk scores decide test depth (techniques, coverage, reviewers) and test order (highest risk first).
Risk exposure = probability x loss; FMEA uses RPN = severity x occurrence x detection.
Residual risk is what remains after testing and must be reported clearly.
Update the risk register as testing reveals new information, and never ignore low-risk areas completely.
lessons.tip: When you join any project, ask two people two questions: ask a developer "which part of the code worries you most?" and a business person "which failure would hurt us most?" Their answers are your first risk analysis.
lessons.task: List eight features of an online shopping app. Rate each for likelihood and impact on a 1 to 5 scale with one-line reasons, compute scores, sort them, and define high, medium and low bands with the testing you would do in each band. Finally, write two project risks and a mitigation for each.

quiz.q: Which of these is a project risk rather than a product risk?
options: The payment calculation might be wrong
The test environment may not be ready on time
The app might be slow under load
Personal data might leak through the API
quiz.explain: An unready test environment threatens the project schedule; the others are risks of the product failing.

quiz.q: A feature has likelihood 4 and impact 5 on 1 to 5 scales. What is its risk level using likelihood x impact?
quiz.explain: Risk level = 4 x 5 = 20.

quiz.q: How does risk-based testing usually affect the order of testing?
options: Features are tested in menu order
Low-risk areas are tested first to warm up
The newest code is always tested last
High-risk areas are tested first, so whatever is left untested is lower risk
quiz.explain: Testing the highest risks first ensures the most important information is obtained even if time runs short.

quiz.q: An FMEA rates a failure mode with severity 7, occurrence 4 and detection 5. What is the RPN?
What is residual risk?
options: The risk of the test team leaving
A risk that has been fully removed by testing
The cost of the test tools
The risk that remains after testing, which stakeholders must accept knowingly
quiz.explain: Testing reduces but never removes all risk; what remains must be reported so decisions are informed.

lessons.title: Unit Testing Frameworks, TDD and BDD
lessons.content:
A good cook tastes the dal while cooking, not only when the guests arrive. A pinch of salt, taste, a little more water, taste again. Each small check takes seconds, and problems are fixed when they are tiny. Unit testing frameworks give programmers the same habit: tiny automatic checks that run in seconds after every change. Test-driven development goes further and writes the taste test before adding the salt. Behaviour-driven development makes the "how should it taste" conversation happen with the whole family, in plain language, before anyone starts cooking.

Why frameworks exist: You could test a function by writing a small main program that prints results and reading them by eye. That works for one function on one day. It does not scale to thousands of functions changed by many people every day. A unit testing framework provides a standard way to write tests, an automatic runner that finds and runs them, assertions that compare actual and expected results, setup and cleanup helpers, and clear reports of what passed and failed. Most importantly, it makes tests repeatable and fast enough to run on every change.

The xUnit family: Kent Beck wrote SUnit for Smalltalk, and then, with Erich Gamma, JUnit for Java. Its design inspired a whole family called xUnit: NUnit and xUnit.net for .NET, unittest in Python's standard library, and many others. Other popular frameworks follow similar ideas with their own style: pytest for Python, Jest and Mocha for JavaScript, and the test package used in Dart and Flutter. Learn the shared concepts once and you can pick up any of them quickly.

Core concepts: A test case is usually a function or method, often named starting with test or marked with an annotation such as @Test. Assertions check expectations, for example assertEquals(expected, actual) in JUnit or a plain assert actual == expected in pytest; when an assertion fails, the test fails with a message showing both values. A fixture is the known state a test needs: objects, data, a temporary file. Setup code creates fixtures before each test and teardown code cleans up afterwards. The test runner discovers tests, runs them, and reports results to the console and to CI tools.

Arrange, Act, Assert: A widely used structure keeps each test readable. Arrange prepares the objects and data. Act calls the one behaviour being tested. Assert checks the outcome. For example, for a shopping cart: arrange a cart with two items of 150 Taka and one of 200 Taka; act by calling cart.total(); assert that the result is 500. A test that arranges, acts, asserts, acts again and asserts again is usually two tests squeezed into one, and when it fails, it is harder to tell why.

Naming and parameterised tests: Test names should say what behaviour is expected, such as total_is_zero_for_empty_cart or transfer_rejected_when_amount_exceeds_daily_limit. When a test fails in CI, its name alone should tell the team what broke. Parameterised (data-driven) tests run the same test logic with a table of inputs and expected outputs, which is perfect for equivalence partitions and boundary values: one test function, a list such as (19, rejected), (20, accepted), (1000, accepted), (1001, rejected).

The FIRST properties: Good unit tests are Fast (milliseconds, so thousands can run in a minute), Independent or Isolated (no test depends on another or on shared state), Repeatable (same result every time, in any environment, without network or clock surprises), Self-validating (pass or fail automatically, no human reading logs), and Timely (written at the right time, ideally just before or with the code). Tests that break these properties, especially slow or flaky tests, slowly destroy a team's trust in the whole suite.

Where tests live in a project: Most projects keep tests in a separate folder that mirrors the source folders, for example src/pricing/fee.py and tests/pricing/test_fee.py, so it is obvious which tests cover which code. Tests are versioned in Git together with the code, reviewed in the same pull requests, and run by the same build command. Treat test code as real code: give it clear names, remove duplication with helper functions, and delete tests that no longer describe wanted behaviour.

Unit test smells: Some warning signs suggest a test needs rework. A test with no assertions only proves that code did not crash. A test with many unrelated assertions hides which behaviour failed. A test that sleeps for a few seconds to wait for something is slow and flaky. A test that reads the current date or calls the internet will one day fail for reasons unrelated to the code. And a test that must be updated every time the implementation changes, even when behaviour does not, is checking how the code works rather than what it does.

Test-driven development, the cycle: TDD, popularised by Kent Beck, reverses the usual order. In tiny cycles: Red, write a small test for the next bit of behaviour and watch it fail (proving the test can fail); Green, write the simplest code that makes it pass; Refactor, clean up the code and tests while keeping everything green. Then repeat. Each cycle takes minutes. The design grows step by step, guided by tests that describe the behaviour.

TDD worked example, leap years: The rule: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, except years divisible by 100, which are not, except years divisible by 400, which are. Cycle 1, red: assert isLeap(2024) == true fails because isLeap does not exist. Green: write isLeap(year) returning year % 4 == 0. Cycle 2, red: add assert isLeap(2023) == false; it already passes, which is fine, it documents behaviour. Cycle 3, red: assert isLeap(1900) == false fails, because 1900 is divisible by 4. Green: return year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0. Cycle 4, red: assert isLeap(2000) == true fails. Green: return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0. Refactor: rename variables or extract helpers if needed; all four tests stay green.

What the example teaches: Each new test targeted a rule that the current code did not yet handle, and each fix was the smallest step. The tests 1900 and 2000 are exactly the tricky boundary cases that developers often forget; TDD forced them to be thought about. At the end you have both working code and a precise, executable description of the rule. If someone later "simplifies" the function to year % 4 == 0, two tests fail instantly.

Benefits and limits of TDD: Benefits include high unit test coverage as a side effect, simpler and more modular designs (code that is easy to test is usually loosely coupled), fewer regressions, and confidence to refactor. Limits: it takes practice; it is harder for user interfaces and code tightly bound to external systems; tests can lock in a poor design if refactoring is skipped; and TDD verifies that code does what the developer intended, not that the intention matches the user's needs. It complements, not replaces, other testing.

Behaviour-driven development: BDD, introduced by Dan North, grew out of TDD. It shifts the focus from "tests" to "behaviour" and encourages developers, testers and business people to describe expected behaviour together using concrete examples in a shared language. The conversation is the most valuable part: discussing examples exposes misunderstandings before code is written. The examples can then be automated as acceptance tests.

Gherkin syntax: BDD scenarios are often written in Gherkin, a structured plain-language format. A Feature describes a capability. Each Scenario has steps: Given (the context), When (the action), Then (the expected outcome), with And and But for extra steps. Example: Feature: Cash out. Scenario: Cash out within the daily limit. Given a customer with balance 10,000 Taka and no cash out today, When the customer cashes out 5,000 Taka at an agent, Then the balance becomes 5,000 Taka minus the cash-out fee, And the customer receives an SMS confirmation. A Scenario Outline with an Examples table runs the same scenario for several rows of data, ideal for boundaries.

Running BDD scenarios: Tools such as Cucumber (for Java, JavaScript, Ruby and others) and behave (for Python) read Gherkin files and match each step to a step definition: a small piece of code that performs the step, for example calling the API to cash out. When the scenario runs, Given steps set up data, When steps act, and Then steps assert. The result is living documentation: a readable specification that is executed on every build and therefore cannot silently go out of date.

ATDD and the three amigos: Acceptance test-driven development (ATDD) is closely related. Before a story is developed, the "three amigos", a business representative, a developer and a tester, meet to agree on acceptance criteria and write acceptance tests, often as Gherkin scenarios or examples tables. Development is done when those acceptance tests pass. This practice, also called specification by example, catches ambiguities at the cheapest possible moment and gives testers a central role from the start.

Real-life example, TDD for a fare calculator: A Dhaka bus ticketing startup builds a fare function: base fare plus per-kilometre rate, with a student discount and a minimum fare. The developer uses TDD. Tests arrive in order: minimum fare for a 1 km ride, normal fare for 10 km, student discount, discount never pushing fare below minimum. The fourth test failed at first, revealing that the discount was applied after the minimum check. Fixed in minutes, before any tester saw the feature. Six months later, a fare policy change broke two tests, and the team updated them deliberately rather than accidentally shipping wrong fares.

Real-life example, BDD for an e-commerce return policy: A product owner, a developer and a tester discuss "customers can return products within 7 days". Writing examples, the tester asks: 7 days from order or from delivery? Including the delivery day? What about products bought on a flash sale? The examples become Gherkin scenarios, including "Given an order delivered on 1 March, When the customer requests a return on 8 March, Then the return is accepted" and "on 9 March, rejected". The ambiguities were settled in a 30-minute meeting instead of in angry customer calls.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include testing many behaviours in one test, depending on test execution order, skipping the refactor step in TDD, writing Gherkin that describes clicks and screens instead of behaviour ("When I click the blue button" instead of "When the customer confirms the order"), and believing TDD removes the need for other testing. Exams ask you to explain red-green-refactor with an example, list FIRST properties, describe Arrange-Act-Assert, write a Gherkin scenario, and compare TDD, BDD and ATDD.

Recap: Unit testing frameworks from the xUnit family and its relatives provide test cases, assertions, fixtures, setup and teardown, and runners that make tests fast and repeatable. Good tests follow Arrange-Act-Assert and the FIRST properties. TDD writes a failing test first, then the simplest passing code, then refactors, in tiny cycles. BDD and ATDD bring business, development and testing together around concrete examples written in Given-When-Then and automated with tools like Cucumber. Next we learn how to isolate units from their dependencies with test doubles.
key_points: Unit testing frameworks provide tests, assertions, fixtures, setup and teardown, and an automatic runner.
JUnit started the xUnit family; pytest, NUnit, Jest and others follow similar ideas.
Arrange-Act-Assert keeps each test focused on one behaviour; parameterised tests suit partitions and boundaries.
FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.
TDD cycle: red (failing test), green (simplest passing code), refactor (clean up while staying green).
BDD describes behaviour with examples in Gherkin: Given, When, Then; tools like Cucumber and behave run them.
ATDD has business, development and testing (the three amigos) agree acceptance tests before development.
lessons.tip: When practising TDD, always watch each new test fail before writing code. A test you have never seen fail might be testing nothing at all.
lessons.task: Using any language you know (Python with pytest is easy to start), follow TDD to build a function that decides an exam grade from marks (80 and above A+, 70 to 79 A, and so on down to F below 40). Write one failing test at a time, make it pass, and refactor. Then write the same rules as a Gherkin Scenario Outline with an Examples table.

quiz.q: In the TDD cycle, what happens in the green step?
options: The design is improved while tests stay passing
The simplest code is written to make the failing test pass
A new failing test is written
quiz.explain: Red writes a failing test, green makes it pass with the simplest code, and refactor cleans up.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the FIRST properties of good unit tests?
options: Thorough documentation in a separate file
quiz.explain: FIRST stands for Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating and Timely.

quiz.q: In Gherkin, which keyword describes the context before the action?
quiz.explain: Given sets up the context, When describes the action, and Then states the expected outcome.

quiz.q: Why should a test written in TDD be seen failing before the code is written?
options: To prove the test can actually detect the missing behaviour
Because frameworks require at least one failure
To increase the number of failed tests in reports
quiz.explain: Seeing it fail shows the test really checks something; a test that never fails may be testing nothing.

quiz.q: In ATDD, who are the "three amigos"?
options: A business representative, a developer and a tester
The project manager, the client and the CEO
quiz.explain: The three amigos bring business, development and testing perspectives together to agree acceptance tests before development.

lessons.title: Test Doubles: Dummies, Stubs, Spies, Mocks and Fakes
lessons.content:
When a film needs a dangerous scene, the hero does not jump from the building; a stunt double does. The double looks enough like the hero for that one shot and keeps the real actor safe. When we test a piece of code that sends money through a payment gateway, sends SMS, or reads the current time, we do not want real money to move, real phones to buzz, or the result to depend on what time it is. So we replace those dependencies with stand-ins for the test. These stand-ins are called test doubles, and knowing which kind to use is a core skill of modern testing.

Why isolate a unit: A unit test should check one unit's logic, quickly and reliably. Real dependencies get in the way. A real payment gateway is slow, costs money, needs credentials, and may be down. A real database needs setup and cleanup. Real time changes every second. Real networks fail randomly. Most importantly, if the test fails, you want to know the problem is in your unit, not in a dependency. Test doubles let you control what dependencies return and observe what your unit asks of them.

Dependency injection makes doubles possible: To swap a real dependency for a double, the unit must not create the dependency itself. If OrderService contains the line gateway = new RealPaymentGateway(), the test cannot replace it. With dependency injection, the gateway is passed in, for example through the constructor: new OrderService(gateway, smsSender, clock). In production you pass real objects; in tests you pass doubles. Code that is hard to test is often code that creates its own dependencies, which is one reason TDD tends to improve design.

The five kinds of test doubles: Gerard Meszaros, in his book xUnit Test Patterns, gave names that are now standard. Dummy: an object passed only to fill a parameter, never actually used. Stub: provides canned answers to calls made during the test. Spy: a stub that also records how it was called, so the test can check afterwards. Mock: an object pre-programmed with expectations about the calls it should receive, which verifies those expectations. Fake: a working but simplified implementation, unsuitable for production, such as an in-memory database. In everyday speech many people call all of these "mocks", but the differences matter when choosing.

The running example: An OrderService has a method placeOrder(order). It asks a PaymentGateway to charge the customer; if the charge succeeds, it marks the order Paid, saves it through an OrderRepository, and asks an SmsSender to text the customer; if the charge is declined, it marks the order PaymentFailed; if the gateway times out, it marks the order Pending and schedules a retry. It also accepts a Logger for diagnostic messages. We will use a different kind of double for each dependency.

Dummy in action: Our tests do not care about logging. The constructor still requires a Logger, so we pass a dummy: an object that satisfies the type but whose methods do nothing. If the test accidentally depends on the dummy, that is a sign the test is checking the wrong thing. Dummies keep tests short and focused.

Stubs in action: To test the three payment outcomes, we create a stub gateway for each test. Test 1: the stub returns "approved", and we assert the order status is Paid. Test 2: the stub returns "declined", and we assert PaymentFailed. Test 3: the stub throws a timeout error, and we assert Pending and that a retry was scheduled. Without stubs, producing a real timeout or a real decline on demand would be almost impossible. Stubs are how we reach error branches and exception handlers that white-box coverage showed were never executed.

Spies and mocks in action: We also want to check that the customer gets exactly one SMS with the right number and text after a successful payment, and no SMS after a decline. With a spy SmsSender, the test runs placeOrder and then asks the spy: how many messages were sent, to which number, with what text? With a mock, the test sets the expectation before acting (send must be called once with this number) and the mock verifies it, failing the test if the call is missing or different. Libraries such as Mockito for Java, unittest.mock for Python and Jest's mock functions for JavaScript make both styles easy.

Fakes in action: For the OrderRepository we could stub each call, but a fake is often simpler: an in-memory repository that stores orders in a dictionary. It behaves like a real repository for the purposes of the test: save an order, load it back, list orders. Fakes are great when many tests need realistic behaviour from a dependency, and they run in microseconds. Their risk is drifting from the real thing, so teams often test the fake and the real implementation against the same contract tests.

State verification versus behaviour verification: Martin Fowler's well-known essay "Mocks Aren't Stubs" describes two styles. State verification checks the result after acting: the order status is Paid, the repository contains the order. Behaviour verification checks the interactions: the gateway was asked to charge 1,250 Taka, the SMS sender was called once. Stubs and fakes support state verification; mocks are built for behaviour verification. Both are useful. Prefer state verification when the outcome is observable; use behaviour verification for side effects like sending messages or calling external services, where the interaction is the outcome.

Choosing a double quickly: Ask what the test needs from the dependency. If it needs nothing, use a dummy. If it needs the dependency to return certain values, use a stub. If it needs to check what the unit sent out, use a spy or a mock. If many tests need realistic, stateful behaviour, write a fake once and reuse it. If the dependency is simple, fast and deterministic, such as a Money value object or a date formatter, use the real thing and skip doubles altogether.

The danger of over-mocking: When every collaborator is mocked and every call is verified, tests become a mirror of the implementation. Rename an internal method or reorder two harmless calls, and dozens of tests fail although the behaviour is unchanged. Such tests make refactoring painful and give false alarms. Guidelines: verify only interactions that matter to the outcome; prefer fakes or real objects for simple, fast, deterministic collaborators such as value objects; and remember that a test full of mocks can pass while the real integration is broken, which is why integration and contract tests are still needed.

Don't mock what you don't own: A common guideline says not to mock third-party types directly, such as a payment SDK's classes. If you mock them, your test encodes your assumptions about how the library behaves, and those assumptions may be wrong or may change. Instead, wrap the third-party library in your own small adapter interface (PaymentGateway), double your interface in unit tests, and test the adapter itself against the real library or its sandbox in a few integration tests.

Doubles for time, randomness and environment: Some of the most useful doubles replace hidden dependencies. A clock double lets you test "an OTP expires after 2 minutes" instantly, by setting the fake clock forward, instead of sleeping for 2 minutes. A random number generator with a fixed seed makes a "random" lottery or shuffle repeatable. An environment or configuration double lets you test behaviour for different settings without changing the machine. Any code that calls the current time or a random function directly is hard to test until those are injected.

Service virtualisation: At integration and system level, teams sometimes double whole services. Tools such as WireMock can run a fake HTTP server that returns configured responses, including delays and errors, standing in for a partner API whose sandbox is unreliable. This is the same idea as a stub, scaled up. It lets testing continue when the real service is unavailable, as in the identity verification example in the risk lesson, but it must be complemented by tests against the real service before release.

Flaky tests: A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code. Common causes are real time and dates, randomness, shared state between tests, dependence on test order, asynchronous code checked too early, network calls and slow external services. Flaky tests are poisonous: people start ignoring red builds, and real failures slip through. Test doubles fix many causes: inject a fake clock, seed randomness, use fakes instead of shared databases, stub the network. For the rest, use proper waiting (wait until a condition is true, not a fixed sleep) and isolate test data.

Test isolation: Each test should create what it needs and clean up afterwards, leaving no trace for the next test. Shared mutable fixtures, such as one database row used by several tests, create hidden dependencies. Frameworks support isolation through fresh fixtures per test, transactions rolled back after each test, and random unique identifiers for created data. Isolated tests can run in parallel, which keeps large suites fast.

Real-life example, a bKash-style payment integration: A Dhaka e-commerce team integrates a mobile wallet payment. Unit tests use a stub wallet adapter to cover approved, declined, insufficient balance, timeout and duplicate-callback cases; a spy checks that exactly one confirmation SMS is sent; a fake repository stores orders in memory. A small set of integration tests run nightly against the wallet provider's sandbox, testing the real adapter. One night the sandbox changes a response field name. The unit tests stay green (correctly, since the business logic is unchanged), and the adapter integration test fails, pointing straight at the real problem.

Real-life example, fixing a flaky OTP test: A bank's test suite had an OTP test that failed about once a week: it created an OTP, waited 119 seconds using real time, and checked it was still valid. On a busy CI machine the wait sometimes ran a little long and the OTP expired. The team injected a clock interface into the OTP service, used a fake clock in the test, and set it to exactly 119 and then 121 seconds. The test now runs in milliseconds, checks both boundaries, and has never flaked again.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include calling every double a mock, mocking everything including simple value objects, verifying irrelevant calls, mocking third-party classes directly, and trusting unit tests with doubles as proof that integration works. Exams ask you to define dummy, stub, spy, mock and fake and match them to scenarios, explain state versus behaviour verification, explain why dependency injection helps testing, describe causes and cures of flaky tests, and discuss the risks of over-mocking.

Recap: Test doubles replace real dependencies so units can be tested quickly, reliably and in isolation, made possible by dependency injection. Dummies fill parameters, stubs give canned answers, spies record calls, mocks verify expected interactions, and fakes provide lightweight working implementations. Prefer state verification where possible, use behaviour verification for important side effects, avoid over-mocking, wrap what you do not own, and double hidden dependencies like time and randomness to kill flakiness. Next we look at the big picture of automation: the test pyramid and UI automation.
key_points: Test doubles replace real dependencies so a unit can be tested fast, reliably and in isolation.
Dependency injection (passing dependencies in) makes it possible to substitute doubles.
Dummy fills a parameter; stub returns canned answers; spy records calls; mock verifies expected calls; fake is a simplified working implementation.
State verification checks results; behaviour verification checks interactions, mainly with mocks.
Over-mocking ties tests to implementation details and causes false failures during refactoring.
Wrap third-party libraries in your own adapters and double the adapter, not the library.
Flaky tests come from time, randomness, shared state, order dependence, async timing and networks; doubles and isolation fix most of them.
lessons.tip: Before reaching for a mock, ask: can I check the result instead of the conversation? If the outcome is visible in state, a stub or fake plus a state assertion usually gives a sturdier test.
lessons.task: Design tests for a function that sends a birthday greeting SMS to all customers whose birthday is today. Identify every dependency (customer list, clock, SMS sender), decide which kind of double you would use for each and why, and write out four test cases including one for the case where the SMS service fails for one customer.

quiz.q: A test passes an object to a constructor only because the parameter is required; the object is never used. What kind of double is it?
quiz.explain: A dummy only fills a parameter list and is never actually used by the test.

quiz.q: An in-memory database used in tests instead of the real database is an example of a:
quiz.explain: A fake is a working but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository.

quiz.q: Which double is pre-programmed with expectations about calls and verifies them?
quiz.explain: Mocks are set up with expected interactions and fail the test if the calls do not match.

quiz.q: A test about OTP expiry waits 2 minutes using real time and sometimes fails on slow machines. What is the best fix?
options: Inject a clock and use a fake clock in the test
Run the test only on weekends
quiz.explain: Injecting a controllable clock makes the test instant, deterministic and able to check exact boundaries.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of over-mocking?
options: Tests become coupled to implementation details and fail when code is refactored without behaviour change
Mocks cannot be used with dependency injection
quiz.explain: Verifying every internal call mirrors the implementation, so harmless refactoring breaks many tests.

lessons.title: The Test Automation Pyramid and UI Automation
lessons.content:
Think of a garments factory. The thread, buttons and fabric are checked in bulk by quick machines and simple gauges as they arrive. Each stitched panel gets a fast check at the sewing line. Only a sample of finished shirts goes to the final inspection table, where a person puts the shirt on a mannequin, checks the fit, the folding and the packaging. If the factory tried to catch every problem only at that final table, it would need a hundred inspectors and would still be slow. Test automation works the same way, and the picture that captures it is called the test automation pyramid.

Why automate at all: Automated tests are scripts that execute tests and check results without a human doing each step. They are fast, tireless, and perfectly consistent, which makes them ideal for regression testing: confirming that everything that worked yesterday still works today after many changes. They let teams release often with confidence. But automation is not free. Scripts must be written, maintained when the product changes, and investigated when they fail. Automation is an investment that pays back only when tests run many times.

Return on investment: A simple way to think about it: if a manual regression run takes 20 hours and the team runs it once per release, ten releases cost 200 hours. If automating it costs 120 hours plus 4 hours of maintenance per release, ten releases cost 160 hours, and the suite can also run every night for free. If the product changes so fast that maintenance becomes 15 hours per release, automation costs 270 hours and loses. Good candidates for automation are stable, repetitive, high-value checks that run often; poor candidates are one-off tests, rapidly changing screens, and checks that need human judgement, such as whether a design looks good.

What automation cannot do: Automated tests only check what they were told to check. They do not notice a misaligned logo, a confusing message or a slow, annoying flow unless someone wrote an assertion for it. Exploratory and usability testing remain human activities. A healthy strategy combines automated checks for known risks with human testing for the unknown.

The test automation pyramid: Mike Cohn described the test automation pyramid in his book Succeeding with Agile. At the wide base are many unit tests: fast, cheap, precise about where a fault is. In the middle are fewer service or API tests, which check business logic and integrations without the user interface. At the narrow top are a small number of UI or end-to-end tests that drive the real interface like a user. The message: push each check down to the lowest level where it can be done, and keep the expensive top layer thin.

Why the shape matters: As you move up the pyramid, tests become slower (milliseconds for a unit test, seconds or minutes for a UI flow), more expensive to write and maintain, more likely to break for reasons unrelated to real defects, and less precise about the cause of a failure. A failing unit test points at one function; a failing end-to-end test says only that something somewhere in a 15-step journey went wrong. A suite of 2,000 unit tests may run in under a minute, while 200 UI tests might take an hour.

The ice-cream cone anti-pattern: Many teams end up with the pyramid upside down: a huge number of manual and UI tests, a few API tests and almost no unit tests, drawn as an ice-cream cone with manual testing as the scoop on top. Such suites are slow, flaky and expensive, so they run rarely and give feedback late. The cure is gradual: write unit tests for new code, move business rule checks from the UI to API level, and keep only key user journeys as UI tests.

Other shapes: The pyramid is a guideline, not a law. Some teams describe a "testing trophy" that puts more weight on integration tests, especially for front-end applications where much logic lives in the connection between components. The exact shape matters less than the principle: prefer the fastest, most reliable test that gives you the confidence you need.

What UI automation is: UI automation drives the application through its user interface: open the browser or app, find elements, type, click, swipe, and then check what appears. It is the only automated way to confirm that the whole system works together from the user's point of view, including the front end, the back end and their wiring. That is why a thin layer of it is valuable, typically covering the most important journeys: sign up, login, search, add to cart, pay.

Locators: To act on an element, a script must find it. Locators are the ways to identify elements: by id, by name, by CSS selector, by XPath, by visible text, or by accessibility label or role. Stable locators are the single biggest factor in UI test reliability. An XPath like the third div inside the second section breaks the day a designer adds a banner. Good teams add dedicated test attributes such as data-testid="pay-button", or use accessible roles and labels, which also encourages accessible design.

Waits and synchronisation: Modern apps load data asynchronously, so an element may not exist yet when the script looks for it. A fixed sleep of five seconds is both slow and unreliable. Explicit waits instead wait until a condition is true, such as the element is visible or clickable, up to a timeout. Several modern tools wait automatically before acting. Missing or wrong waits are the most common cause of flaky UI tests.

The Page Object Model: If fifty tests each contain the locator for the login button, a single design change breaks fifty tests. The Page Object Model puts each page or screen behind a class that exposes meaningful actions, such as loginPage.loginAs(phone, pin), and hides the locators inside. Tests then read like user stories and changes are fixed in one place. A related idea, the Screenplay pattern, models actors performing tasks, but Page Objects remain the most widely taught.

Data-driven and keyword-driven frameworks: In data-driven testing, the same script runs with many rows of data from a table or file, for example twenty login combinations. In keyword-driven testing, tests are written as sequences of keywords such as OpenApp, Login, SearchProduct, AddToCart, each implemented once in code, so non-programmers can compose tests from a table. Robot Framework is a well-known keyword-driven tool. Both approaches separate what is tested from how it is automated.

Record and playback: Many tools can record a tester's clicks and replay them. Recording is a quick way to learn a tool or prototype a script, but raw recordings are brittle: they capture fragile locators, fixed waits and duplicated steps. Treat recordings as drafts to refactor into Page Objects, not as finished tests.

Assertions and evidence in UI tests: A UI test should check something meaningful at the end of the journey, such as the order confirmation number appearing and the order status being Paid, not just that the last click did not crash. Checking the result through an API or database query, as well as on screen, makes the test stronger. When a UI test fails, the framework should save evidence automatically: a screenshot, the page source, browser console logs and, where supported, a video or trace of the run. Good evidence turns a mysterious red build into a five-minute diagnosis.

Setting up state quickly: A UI test for checkout does not need to sign up, verify a phone and browse the catalogue through the screen every time. It can create the user and fill the cart through API calls or test data scripts, then use the UI only for the part being tested. This shortcut makes UI tests shorter, faster and less flaky, and it keeps the journey focused on what the test is really about.

Popular web tools: Selenium WebDriver is the long-established, open-source standard for driving browsers, with bindings for Java, Python, C#, JavaScript and other languages, and it underlies the W3C WebDriver standard. Cypress runs tests inside the browser with fast feedback and automatic waiting, mostly for JavaScript web apps. Playwright, from Microsoft, drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit with one API, has automatic waiting and supports several languages. All three can run headless (without a visible window) in CI.

Mobile tools: Appium applies the WebDriver idea to mobile apps on Android and iOS, and can drive native, hybrid and mobile web apps. Platform frameworks such as Espresso for Android and XCUITest for iOS run faster and more reliably but are tied to one platform. Flutter has its own integration testing support. Mobile testing was covered in the mobile app development course; the same pyramid and Page Object ideas apply there.

Flakiness in UI tests: UI tests are flaky more often than other tests, because they depend on timing, animations, test data, network and the environment. Cures: stable locators, proper waits, independent test data created per test, resetting state between tests, disabling animations in test builds, and running against a stable environment. Teams also track flaky tests and quarantine them so they do not block the pipeline, while someone fixes them promptly. A UI suite that is red for random reasons soon stops being trusted.

Real-life example, rebalancing an e-commerce suite: A Bangladeshi online grocery had 600 Selenium tests that took four hours and failed randomly about one run in three. Most checked pricing and discount rules through the UI. The team moved those rules to 900 unit tests and 150 API tests, which ran in eight minutes, and kept 40 UI tests for core journeys like search, cart, checkout with cash on delivery and with mobile wallet. The full suite now ran on every merge, failures pointed at the right place, and testers spent their freed time on exploratory testing before campaigns.

Real-life example, a fragile locator: An exam result portal's UI tests located the "Show result" button by XPath position. Before results day, a notice banner was added at the top of the page and every test failed, minutes before a release meeting. After the incident, developers added data-testid attributes to key elements and the tests were rewritten using a Page Object for the result page. The next layout change broke nothing.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include automating everything through the UI, automating unstable features too early, using fixed sleeps, copying locators across tests, ignoring flaky tests, and measuring success by the number of automated tests instead of the value of their feedback. Exams ask you to draw and explain the automation pyramid, describe the ice-cream cone anti-pattern, list what to automate and what not to, explain the Page Object Model, compare data-driven and keyword-driven approaches, and name tools for web and mobile UI automation.

Recap: Automation pays back when stable, valuable tests run often. The automation pyramid recommends many fast unit tests, fewer API or service tests and a thin layer of UI tests; the ice-cream cone is its costly opposite. UI automation needs stable locators, proper waits and the Page Object Model to stay maintainable, and frameworks can be data-driven or keyword-driven. Selenium WebDriver, Cypress and Playwright drive browsers; Appium, Espresso and XCUITest drive mobile apps. Next we move to the middle of the pyramid with API testing.
key_points: Automation pays back for stable, repetitive, valuable tests that run often; it does not replace human exploratory testing.
The test automation pyramid: many unit tests, fewer API or service tests, few UI or end-to-end tests.
Higher layers are slower, costlier, more fragile and less precise about where faults are.
The ice-cream cone (mostly manual and UI tests) is a common anti-pattern.
Stable locators (test ids, accessible roles) and explicit waits are key to reliable UI tests.
The Page Object Model hides locators behind page classes so changes are fixed in one place.
Selenium WebDriver, Cypress and Playwright automate browsers; Appium, Espresso and XCUITest automate mobile apps.
lessons.tip: Before writing any UI test, ask: could this check be done at API or unit level? If yes, put it there and save the UI test for the journey itself.
lessons.task: Pick a website you use (for example a news or shopping site). List ten checks you would want automated. Place each on the pyramid (unit, API or UI) with a reason, then sketch a Page Object for its login or search page: the class name, three actions it exposes, and the locators you would hope developers provide.

quiz.q: According to the test automation pyramid, which kind of test should be most numerous?
quiz.explain: The wide base of the pyramid is fast, cheap and precise unit tests.

quiz.q: What is the "ice-cream cone" in test automation?
options: A pyramid with many unit tests
An inverted shape with mostly manual and UI tests and few unit tests
quiz.explain: The ice-cream cone is the anti-pattern where the expensive top layers dominate and fast unit tests are scarce.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of the Page Object Model?
options: It removes the need for assertions
Locators and page actions live in one place, so UI changes are fixed once
It makes tests run without a browser
quiz.explain: Page Objects encapsulate locators and actions, so a layout change updates one class instead of many tests.

quiz.q: A UI test uses a fixed 5-second sleep before clicking a button and sometimes fails. What is the better approach?
options: An explicit wait until the button is clickable
Run the test twice and take the better result
quiz.explain: Explicit waits are faster and reliable because they wait only as long as needed for a real condition.

quiz.q: Which tool is designed for automating native mobile apps on both Android and iOS using the WebDriver approach?
quiz.explain: Appium brings the WebDriver idea to mobile apps across Android and iOS.

lessons.title: API Testing
lessons.content:
In a busy restaurant, customers never enter the kitchen. They give their order to a waiter, who carries a written slip to the kitchen and brings back the food. If you wanted to check that the kitchen cooks the right dish every time, you would not sit at every table and watch the plates arrive. You would stand at the kitchen window, hand in order slips directly, and inspect what comes out. An API is that kitchen window. Mobile apps, websites and partner systems all talk to the back end through it, and testing at the API is often the fastest, most reliable way to check the business logic.

What an API is, for testers: An application programming interface is a contract that says which requests a system accepts and what responses it returns. Most modern web and mobile back ends expose HTTP APIs, commonly in a REST style with JSON data; others use GraphQL, gRPC, or older SOAP services with XML. This lesson focuses on HTTP and REST, which you met in the web engineering course, and looks at them through a tester's eyes.

Why API testing matters: API tests sit in the middle of the automation pyramid. They are much faster and more stable than UI tests, because they skip the screen entirely, yet they exercise real business logic, databases and integrations. One API often serves several clients, such as an Android app, an iOS app and a website, so a defect caught at the API is caught for all of them. Many back-end features, such as webhooks or partner integrations, have no UI at all and can only be tested through the API.

Anatomy of a request: An HTTP request has a method, a URL (with a path and maybe query parameters, such as /orders?status=paid), headers (such as Content-Type and Authorization), and sometimes a body, usually JSON. The common methods: GET reads a resource, POST creates one or triggers an action, PUT replaces a resource, PATCH changes part of it, and DELETE removes it. A tester designs requests by varying each of these parts.

Anatomy of a response: A response has a status code, headers and usually a body. Status code families: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirection, 4xx client errors (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized meaning not authenticated, 403 Forbidden meaning authenticated but not allowed, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests), and 5xx server errors (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable). A 500 in response to bad input is almost always a defect: the server should reject bad input with a 4xx and a clear message.

What to check in an API response: Do not stop at the status code. Check the body: required fields are present, types are correct (a price is a number, not a string), values are correct (the total equals the sum of items plus delivery fee), and nothing sensitive leaks, such as password hashes or other users' data. Check important headers, such as content type and caching. Check the response time against expectations. And check side effects: after a POST that creates an order, a GET should return it, and the database or downstream systems should reflect it.

Schema validation: Many APIs are described in an OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) specification, or have a JSON Schema for their bodies. Tests can validate every response against the schema automatically, catching missing fields, wrong types and unexpected nulls without writing an assertion for each field. The specification is also a test basis: each endpoint, parameter, constraint and error response it lists suggests test cases.

Positive and negative tests: Positive tests send valid requests and check correct results. Negative tests send invalid ones and check that the API refuses them gracefully: missing required fields, wrong types, empty strings, values just outside boundaries, very long strings, special characters, malformed JSON, unknown fields, wrong content type, and unsupported methods. All the black-box techniques apply: equivalence partitions and boundary values for each parameter, decision tables for combinations of rules, state transition for resources with life cycles.

Authentication and authorisation tests: Authentication answers "who are you?" and authorisation answers "what may you do?". Test that requests without a token get 401, that expired or tampered tokens are refused, and that a user cannot access another user's resources by changing an id in the URL, such as /orders/1043 to /orders/1044. That last defect, broken object level authorisation, is one of the most common and damaging API security flaws. Also test role rules: a customer must not call admin endpoints.

Idempotency and retries: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent; POST usually is not. Mobile networks drop connections, and apps retry requests, so payment and order APIs often accept an idempotency key: if the same key arrives twice, the server returns the original result instead of charging twice. Testers check this deliberately: send the same payment request twice with the same key and confirm only one charge exists.

Other things worth testing: Pagination (first page, last page, empty page, page size limits), sorting and filtering, rate limiting (does the API return 429 when a client sends too many requests?), concurrency (two requests updating the same resource at the same time), versioning (old clients still work after a new version), error message quality (clear, consistent, without stack traces), and time zones and date formats in fields.

Worked example, a create-order endpoint: POST /orders accepts customerId, a list of items with productId and quantity, and a paymentMethod. Rules: quantity is 1 to 10 per item, at most 20 items, payment method is cod or wallet. Tests: a valid order returns 201 with an order id, status Pending and a correct total; quantity 0 and 11 return 422 while 1 and 10 succeed; 21 items return 422; an unknown product returns 404 or 422 as the specification says; paymentMethod card returns 422; no token returns 401; another customer's id in the body returns 403; missing body returns 400; and the same request with the same idempotency key twice creates one order. Finally, GET /orders/{id} returns what was created.

Chaining requests in a flow: Many API tests follow a short business flow rather than a single call. Log in and capture the token from the response; create a cart and capture its id; add items using that id; place the order; then fetch it and check its status. Each step reads values from the previous response and passes them on. Tools such as Postman support this with variables, and code-based tests do it naturally. Flow tests catch defects in how endpoints work together, such as an order created with a cart that has already been checked out, which single-call tests miss.

GraphQL in brief: A GraphQL API has a single endpoint, and clients send queries that say exactly which fields they want. Testing ideas carry over, with a few additions: queries can ask for deeply nested data, so test depth and complexity limits; errors are often returned inside a 200 response with an errors field, so assertions must check the body, not only the status; and authorisation must be checked per field, not only per endpoint.

Contract testing: When a mobile team and a back-end team work separately, the API contract between them can break silently. In consumer-driven contract testing, the consumer (the app) writes down the requests it makes and the responses it relies on, and the provider (the back end) runs those expectations as tests in its own pipeline. If a back-end developer renames a field the app uses, the provider's build fails before release. Pact is a well-known tool for this approach. Contract tests are much cheaper than full end-to-end tests across both systems.

Tools for exploring APIs: Postman is a popular application for sending requests, organising them into collections, writing test scripts in JavaScript and running collections from the command line with Newman. curl is the command-line tool for quick requests, and every tester should be able to read and write a curl command. Insomnia and the "Try it out" panels of Swagger UI are other common choices. Browser developer tools show the API calls a web page makes, which is a quick way to learn an unfamiliar API.

Tools for automating API tests: In code, testers use HTTP libraries with a test framework: REST Assured for Java, requests with pytest for Python, and supertest with Jest for JavaScript, among others. Karate combines API testing with a Gherkin-like syntax. Such tests live in the repository, run in CI, and are faster and more maintainable than equivalent UI tests.

Test data and environments for APIs: API tests need data they control: create a customer and products at the start, use unique ids, and clean up or use a disposable database. Avoid depending on data that someone else may change in a shared environment. When a dependency, such as an SMS gateway or a partner bank, is not available in the test environment, use service virtualisation or stubs, as discussed in the test doubles lesson, and keep a few tests that touch the real sandbox.

Real-life example, a ride app's fare API: A ride-hailing company in Dhaka built a fare estimate API used by the rider app, the driver app and the call centre tool. Testers wrote 120 API tests covering distance boundaries, surge multipliers, promo codes and invalid locations, running in under two minutes. One negative test sent a pickup point outside the service area and received a 500 with a stack trace showing internal class names. The fix returned 422 with a friendly message, and removed an information leak that a security review later confirmed would have been reported.

Real-life example, an id that exposed other users: During API testing of a telemedicine app, a tester logged in as patient A, fetched /prescriptions/5581, then changed the number to 5582. The API returned patient B's prescription. The UI never showed such links, so no UI test could have found it. The defect was fixed by checking ownership on every request, and the team added an authorisation test for every endpoint that takes an id.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include checking only status codes, testing only happy paths, hard-coding data that changes, ignoring authorisation, sharing state between tests, and treating 500 errors as acceptable for bad input. Exams ask you to list HTTP methods and status codes with meanings, distinguish 401 from 403, design positive and negative tests for an endpoint, explain idempotency, describe contract testing, and explain why API tests are faster and more stable than UI tests.

Recap: API testing checks the back end directly through its contract, sitting in the middle of the automation pyramid. Design tests by varying methods, paths, parameters, headers and bodies; check status codes, bodies, schemas, headers, timing and side effects. Include negative tests, authentication and authorisation checks (especially access to other users' objects), idempotency, pagination, rate limits and concurrency. Use Postman and curl to explore, code-based tools such as REST Assured or pytest with requests to automate, and contract testing to keep separately built clients and services in step. Next we ask how the system behaves under heavy load.
key_points: API tests check business logic directly, faster and more stably than UI tests, and cover all clients at once.
Requests vary method, URL, query parameters, headers and body; responses have status code, headers and body.
Check status codes, response body values and types, schema, headers, response time and side effects.
401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not allowed; a 500 for bad input is usually a defect.
Test authorisation by trying to access other users' resources, a very common API flaw.
Idempotency keys stop retried requests from creating duplicate orders or charges.
Consumer-driven contract testing (for example with Pact) catches breaking API changes before release.
lessons.tip: Learn to read and write curl commands fluently. When you report an API defect, include the exact curl command that reproduces it: developers can run it in seconds.
lessons.task: Choose a free public API with documentation, or the API of a project you built. Using Postman or curl, write and run ten tests for one endpoint: three positive, five negative (missing field, wrong type, boundary, bad auth, unknown id) and two that check side effects or idempotency. Record expected and actual status codes and one body check per test.

quiz.q: A logged-in customer requests another customer's order and the API correctly refuses. Which status code best fits?
quiz.explain: The user is authenticated but not allowed to access that resource, which is 403; 401 means not authenticated.

quiz.q: Sending a malformed JSON body to an API returns 500 with a stack trace. What should a tester conclude?
options: The test is wrong because 500 is always expected for bad input
It is likely a defect: bad input should get a 4xx with a clear message, and stack traces leak information
quiz.explain: Invalid client input should be rejected with a 4xx; a 500 and a stack trace indicate unhandled errors and an information leak.

quiz.q: Why are API tests usually placed in the middle of the automation pyramid?
options: They are faster and more stable than UI tests while still testing real business logic and integration
They are slower than UI tests
quiz.explain: API tests skip the UI, so they are faster and less fragile, yet they exercise real logic, databases and integrations.

quiz.q: A payment request is sent twice because of a network retry, with the same idempotency key. What should happen?
options: The customer is charged once and the original result is returned
quiz.explain: An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and return the original result without charging again.

quiz.q: What does consumer-driven contract testing mainly protect against?
options: A provider changing the API in a way that breaks what a consumer relies on
quiz.explain: Consumers record their expectations, and the provider runs them in its pipeline, so breaking changes are caught before release.

lessons.title: Performance Testing: Load, Stress and Beyond
lessons.content:
Every year, on the day public exam results are published, millions of students and parents try to open the results website at the same minute. Some years the site slows to a crawl or shows errors, and the news reports frustrated families refreshing their phones. The site worked perfectly the day before, with a few hundred visitors. Nothing in its features changed; only the number of people did. Performance testing exists to find out, before the big day, how a system behaves when many people use it at once, and where it breaks.

What performance testing is: Performance testing is a family of non-functional tests that measure how fast, how stable and how scalable a system is under a given workload. It answers questions like: how quickly do pages and APIs respond with 5,000 users? How many orders per second can checkout handle? What happens when traffic doubles suddenly? Does the system stay healthy after running for two days? Where is the bottleneck: database, application server, network or a third-party service?

Key metrics, response time: Response time is how long a request takes from the user's point of view, from sending it to receiving the full response. It is reported in milliseconds or seconds and should be measured for each important transaction separately: login, search, add to cart, pay. Response time alone is meaningless without the load at which it was measured: 300 milliseconds with 10 users says little about the morning of a flash sale.

Why averages lie, percentiles: Suppose ten requests take 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 180, 200, 250, 400 and 1,500 milliseconds. The average is 323 milliseconds, which describes no real user: nine were faster and one waited one and a half seconds. The median (50th percentile) is 170 milliseconds: half the requests were faster. The 90th percentile, using the nearest-rank method, is the 9th value in sorted order, 400 milliseconds: 90 percent of requests finished within that time. Performance goals are therefore written as percentiles, such as "95th percentile under 800 milliseconds", because the slow tail is where users get angry, and at high traffic even 1 percent is many people.

Key metrics, throughput and errors: Throughput is the amount of work done per unit time, such as requests per second or transactions per minute. Error rate is the percentage of requests that fail, through error responses or timeouts. Concurrency is how many users or requests are active at the same time. Resource utilisation covers CPU, memory, disk, network, database connections and thread pools on each server. A good test reports all of these together, because they explain each other.

Little's law: A simple and very useful relationship from queueing theory says that the average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends in it: N = X x R. If an API handles 200 requests per second and each takes on average 0.5 seconds, about 200 x 0.5 = 100 requests are in progress at any moment. That tells you roughly how many threads or connections the server needs. Testers use Little's law to sanity-check results: if the numbers do not fit, the test or the measurement is probably wrong.

Users, think time and throughput: Real users pause between actions to read and decide. This pause is called think time. With think time Z, the law becomes N = X x (R + Z). If 1,000 active users each take 1 second of response time and 9 seconds of think time per action, they generate about 1,000 / (1 + 9) = 100 requests per second. Leaving think time out of a script makes 1,000 virtual users behave like a much larger crowd and gives misleading results; including realistic think time is part of designing a valid test.

Load testing: Load testing checks behaviour under the expected workload, usually the expected peak: for example 3,000 concurrent users during an evening sale. The aim is to confirm that response time, throughput and error rate meet their goals at that load. It is the most common performance test and should be repeated whenever significant changes are made.

Stress testing: Stress testing pushes beyond the expected load, or squeezes resources such as memory or database connections, to find the breaking point and see how the system fails. Does it slow down gracefully, return clear "please try again" errors, and recover when load drops? Or does it crash, corrupt data or lock up until someone restarts it? Knowing the breaking point lets the team plan capacity and design graceful degradation.

Spike testing: A spike test applies a sudden, sharp jump in load, such as results being published at exactly 12:00 or a flash sale opening at 8 pm, then drops back. Systems that cope with gradual growth can fail under spikes, because auto-scaling takes time to add servers, caches are cold, and connection pools fill instantly. Spike tests show whether queues, rate limiting and warm-up plans work.

Endurance or soak testing: A soak test runs a realistic load for a long time, such as 8, 24 or 48 hours. It reveals problems that grow slowly: memory leaks, connection leaks, log files filling the disk, growing queues, and performance that degrades as database tables grow. A system that is fine for one hour may fall over on the third day of a festival campaign.

Scalability and volume testing: Scalability testing checks how performance changes as resources are added: if servers double, does throughput nearly double, or does a shared database cap it? Volume testing checks behaviour with large amounts of data rather than many users: a search over 50 million products, a report over five years of transactions, an import of a 2 GB file. Some texts also mention capacity testing, which finds the maximum users or transactions the system can support while still meeting its goals.

Defining goals: Performance testing needs measurable goals, ideally agreed with the business before testing. Good goals name the transaction, the load and the percentile: "With 2,000 concurrent users and realistic think time, the 95th percentile response time for search is under 1 second and for payment under 2 seconds, error rate under 1 percent, and CPU under 70 percent on application servers." Vague goals such as "the system should be fast" cannot be passed or failed.

Workload modelling: A test is only as good as its workload model: which user journeys are simulated, in what mix, at what rates, with what data. Sources include production analytics and server logs, business forecasts for campaigns, and the risk analysis. For example, an online shop might model 60 percent browsing, 25 percent searching, 10 percent adding to cart and 5 percent checking out. Test data must be varied and large enough: if every virtual user searches for the same word, the database cache answers everything and the results are falsely good.

The test environment: Ideally performance is tested in an environment like production in size and configuration. That is often too expensive, so teams test on a smaller copy and extrapolate carefully, or test in production at quiet hours with care. Whatever the choice, record the environment precisely, generate load from machines that are not themselves the bottleneck, and monitor every tier during the test. A load test without server monitoring tells you that something is slow but not why.

Performance testing tools: Apache JMeter is a long-established open-source tool with a graphical interface and many protocols. Gatling uses code-based scenarios and produces detailed HTML reports. k6 uses JavaScript scripts and suits developers and CI pipelines. Locust lets you write user behaviour in Python. Commercial tools such as LoadRunner are used in large organisations. Cloud services can generate load from many regions. Monitoring and application performance management tools show what happens inside the servers while the load runs.

Analysing results and finding bottlenecks: Plot response time and throughput against the number of users. Typically throughput rises with load until a resource saturates; after that, throughput flattens and response times climb steeply. Look at which resource hit its limit first: CPU on one server, database connections, a slow query, a lock, garbage collection pauses, a third-party API. Fix the biggest bottleneck, rerun, and look again; there is always a next bottleneck. Changes must be made one at a time, or you will not know which helped.

Performance in the delivery pipeline: Full-scale load tests are expensive, so they often run before major releases or campaigns. Between them, teams can run small performance checks automatically: a short load test of key APIs on every merge to the main branch, with a rule that fails the build if the 95th percentile gets more than, say, 20 percent worse than the previous run. Such checks catch a slow new query the day it is written, when the cause is still obvious, rather than weeks later in a big test.

Real-life example, an exam results portal: Before results day, a team estimated 300,000 visitors in the first 30 minutes with a sharp spike at publication time. A spike test with k6 showed 95th percentile response times of 12 seconds and many timeouts at 4,000 requests per second; the database CPU was at 100 percent because every request ran the same results query. The fix: results were pre-generated into a cache keyed by roll number, static pages were served by a content delivery network, and a lightweight queue page appeared above capacity. A repeat test met the goal of under 1 second at the 95th percentile.

Real-life example, a slow leak: A logistics company's tracking API passed a 1-hour load test easily. A 24-hour soak test showed memory on each server growing steadily until, after about 19 hours, servers restarted. The cause was an in-memory cache of tracking lookups that never evicted old entries. With a size limit and expiry added, memory stayed flat for 48 hours. Without the soak test, the failure would have appeared in production during the Eid delivery rush.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include using averages instead of percentiles, no think time, unrealistic or repeated test data, testing in a tiny environment and trusting the numbers, load generators that are themselves overloaded, no server monitoring, vague goals, and testing only at the end of the project. Exams ask you to define and distinguish load, stress, spike, soak, scalability and volume testing; to explain response time, throughput and percentiles; to apply Little's law; to design a workload model; and to interpret a graph of throughput and response time against users.

Recap: Performance testing measures speed, stability and scalability under a workload. Measure response time as percentiles, together with throughput, error rate and resource use, and use Little's law, N = X x R, to sanity-check results. Load testing checks expected peaks, stress testing finds breaking points, spike testing checks sudden jumps, soak testing reveals slow leaks, and scalability and volume testing check growth in resources and data. Define measurable goals, model realistic workloads with think time, monitor every tier, and remove bottlenecks one at a time with tools such as JMeter, Gatling, k6 and Locust. Next we look at another vital non-functional area: security testing.
key_points: Performance testing measures response time, throughput, error rate and resource use under a defined workload.
Report response time as percentiles such as the 95th, because averages hide the slow tail.
Little's law: users or requests in the system N = throughput X x response time R; with think time, N = X x (R + Z).
Load = expected peak; stress = beyond limits to find the breaking point; spike = sudden jumps; soak = long duration for leaks.
Scalability testing adds resources; volume testing uses large amounts of data.
Goals must name the transaction, the load and the percentile; workloads must be realistic, with varied data and think time.
JMeter, Gatling, k6 and Locust generate load; monitoring every tier is needed to find bottlenecks.
lessons.tip: Whenever someone tells you a response time, ask two questions: at what load, and which percentile? Without both, the number cannot be compared to anything.
lessons.task: For an online exam registration site expecting 50,000 students in the last two days before the deadline, write a performance test plan of one page: goals with percentiles, a workload model with three journeys and their mix, think time, which test types you would run (load, spike, soak) and why, and what you would monitor on the servers.

quiz.q: Which test applies a sudden, sharp increase in load, such as the moment results are published?
quiz.explain: A spike test checks how the system copes with abrupt jumps in load, which gradual load tests may not reveal.

quiz.q: Why are performance goals usually written using percentiles rather than averages?
options: Averages hide the slow tail of requests that many users actually experience
Averages cannot be calculated by tools
Percentiles do not depend on load
quiz.explain: A few very slow requests barely move the average, but percentiles such as the 95th show what most users experience.

quiz.q: An API handles 400 requests per second with an average response time of 0.25 seconds. By Little's law, about how many requests are in progress at once?
A system works well for one hour, but memory grows until servers restart after about 19 hours. Which test reveals this?
quiz.explain: Soak tests run realistic load for long periods to expose leaks and slow degradation.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a stress test?
options: To check the system at normal daily load
To check spelling in error messages
To test with a huge database only
To go beyond expected limits to find the breaking point and see how the system fails and recovers
quiz.explain: Stress testing pushes past expected load or squeezes resources to find limits and check graceful failure and recovery.

lessons.title: Security Testing Basics
lessons.content:
A house can have strong walls, a beautiful kitchen and perfect plumbing, and still be robbed in an hour if one window latch is broken. The family living there uses the front door every day and never notices the window. A burglar walks around the house looking only for the weak point. Functional testing is like the family: it checks that doors open for the right people. Security testing is like walking around the house with a burglar's eyes, looking for the one way in that nobody intended.

Why security testing is different: Most testing asks "does the system do what it should for legitimate users?" Security testing also asks "can someone make it do what it must never do?" Attackers do not follow user journeys. They send unexpected input, change ids in URLs, replay old requests, and chain small weaknesses into large breaches. A single overlooked flaw can expose millions of records, empty accounts, or take a service offline. In Bangladesh, as everywhere, mobile financial services, e-commerce, health records and government portals hold sensitive data that attackers target.

The CIA triad: Security goals are often summarised as confidentiality (only authorised people can see data), integrity (data and transactions cannot be altered improperly), and availability (the service is there when legitimate users need it). Related goals include authentication (proving who you are), authorisation (controlling what you may do), and non-repudiation (a user cannot deny an action they performed, supported by logs and signatures). Each security test targets one or more of these goals.

Vulnerabilities, threats and risk: A vulnerability is a weakness, such as unchecked input or a missing access check. A threat is a potential cause of harm, such as an attacker or a malicious insider. Risk combines the likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability with the impact if it does, exactly the risk thinking from earlier in the course. Threat modelling, done during design, asks what we are building, what can go wrong, what we will do about it, and whether we did a good job; it guides where security testing should focus.

The OWASP Top 10: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a non-profit community that publishes free security guidance. Its best-known document, the OWASP Top 10, lists the most critical web application security risk categories and is updated every few years. Categories it has included are broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures, insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable and outdated components, identification and authentication failures, and logging and monitoring failures. Testers use it as a checklist and a common language; OWASP also publishes a Web Security Testing Guide and an API Security Top 10.

Injection and SQL injection: Injection happens when untrusted input is treated as part of a command or query. Imagine a login query built by joining strings: SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 'input'. If an attacker types a value containing a quote followed by OR '1'='1, the query's meaning changes and may return every user. Testers probe input fields and API parameters with special characters such as quotes and check whether errors or unexpected results appear. The defence is parameterised queries (prepared statements), which keep data separate from the command, plus input validation and least-privilege database accounts.

Cross-site scripting: Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when an application includes untrusted input in a web page without proper encoding, so a browser runs an attacker's script. For example, a product review containing a script tag might run in every visitor's browser, stealing session tokens. Stored XSS saves the payload in the database; reflected XSS bounces it from a request, such as a search term, back into the page. Testers enter harmless test payloads in every field that is displayed back and check whether they are shown as text or executed. Defences are context-aware output encoding, frameworks that escape by default, and a Content Security Policy.

Broken access control: Access control flaws let users act outside their permissions. Examples: changing /accounts/1001 to /accounts/1002 to see another person's account (the API lesson's example), calling an admin function as a normal user, skipping a payment step by going directly to the confirmation URL, or modifying a hidden price field in a form. Testers use two or more accounts with different roles and try every action and object id with the wrong account. These tests are simple, but they find some of the most serious defects.

Authentication and session tests: Check password rules, account lockout or rate limiting after repeated failed logins and OTP attempts, that OTPs expire and cannot be reused, that password reset links are single-use and expire, that session tokens are long and random, that logout really invalidates the session on the server, that sessions time out after inactivity, and that cookies carry the Secure and HttpOnly flags. For mobile money and banking apps, check that sensitive actions require re-authentication, such as entering the PIN again before a transfer.
