Sensitive data and configuration: Check that all traffic uses HTTPS with valid certificates, that passwords are stored with a strong, salted, slow hashing algorithm rather than plain text, that error messages and logs do not reveal stack traces, secrets or personal data, that debug endpoints and default admin accounts are disabled in production, that API keys are not embedded in mobile apps or public repositories, and that third-party libraries have no known vulnerabilities. Many real breaches come from such configuration mistakes rather than clever attacks.

Mobile app security checks: Mobile apps add their own risks, because the app runs on a device the attacker controls. Testers check that sensitive data such as tokens and PINs is kept in the platform's secure storage rather than plain files, that the app does not log personal data, that screenshots of sensitive screens are blocked where appropriate, that certificate validation cannot be bypassed easily, and that all security decisions are made on the server, never only in the app. OWASP's Mobile Application Security project provides a checklist for this area.

Static and dynamic security testing: Static application security testing (SAST) analyses source code without running it, looking for patterns such as string-built SQL queries or hard-coded passwords. It finds issues early and points to exact lines, but can produce false positives. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) attacks the running application from outside, like a black-box tester, sending crafted requests and observing responses. It finds real, exploitable issues in the deployed configuration but cannot see the code. Software composition analysis (SCA) checks third-party libraries against databases of known vulnerabilities. Mature teams run all three in their pipelines.

Vulnerability scanning versus penetration testing: A vulnerability scan is an automated sweep for known weaknesses, such as outdated software, missing patches or common misconfigurations. It is broad, fast and repeatable. A penetration test is a focused, mostly manual attempt by skilled testers to exploit weaknesses and chain them together, as a real attacker would, within an agreed scope and time. Penetration tests find logic flaws and combinations that scanners miss. Organisations typically scan often and commission penetration tests periodically and before major releases.

Fuzzing: Fuzz testing sends large volumes of random, malformed or unexpected inputs to a program to see whether it crashes, hangs or behaves strangely. Simple fuzzers mutate valid inputs; smarter ones understand the input format or use code coverage to guide which inputs to try next. Fuzzing is particularly effective at finding memory safety bugs in code that parses files and network protocols, and many serious vulnerabilities have been found this way.

Security testing tools: OWASP ZAP is a free, open-source tool that acts as a proxy between the browser and the application, records traffic, scans automatically for common issues and lets testers modify requests by hand. Burp Suite is a widely used proxy and testing toolkit with a free community edition and a commercial professional edition. Nmap discovers hosts and open ports. sqlmap automates detection of SQL injection. SAST tools and dependency scanners run in CI. Tools support testers; they do not replace understanding.

Security in the development life cycle: Security is cheapest when built in early, the same shift-left idea as all testing. Requirements include security and privacy needs; design includes threat modelling; code is checked by SAST and by reviewers who know common flaws; builds run dependency scans; test environments get DAST and manual tests of access control; and production is monitored for attacks. Writing abuse cases, such as "as an attacker I want to see other users' orders", next to user stories helps testers design negative tests.

Ethics and the law: Security testing must only be done with explicit, written permission from the owner of the system, within an agreed scope. Testing someone else's website or app without permission can be illegal in Bangladesh and many other countries, however good the intention. Test data should not be real personal data where avoidable. When you find a vulnerability in a system you do not own, follow responsible disclosure: report it privately to the owner, often through a published security contact or bug bounty programme, and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly.

Real-life example, a hidden price: During testing of a Dhaka-based online electronics shop, a tester used OWASP ZAP to intercept the checkout request and noticed the item price was sent from the browser. Changing 85,000 to 850 in the intercepted request created a paid order at the lower price. The UI never allowed editing prices, so functional tests passed. The fix was to ignore any price from the client and recalculate everything on the server. The team added an API test that tampers with prices and quantities for every checkout change.

Real-life example, OTP brute force: A wallet app used 4-digit OTPs for login on a new device. A tester's script tried all OTPs in sequence against the test environment and found no limit on attempts; with 10,000 possibilities, a determined attacker could guess the OTP within the time it was valid. The team added a limit of a few attempts per OTP, a cool-down period, and alerts for repeated failures. A simple boundary-style question, what happens on the sixth wrong attempt, would have caught it in design.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include testing only through the UI, trusting client-side validation, testing access control with only one account, treating a clean scanner report as proof of security, leaving security to the end of the project, and testing systems without permission. Exams ask you to explain the CIA triad, describe SQL injection and XSS with examples and defences, distinguish SAST from DAST and scanning from penetration testing, explain fuzzing, describe the OWASP Top 10's purpose, and discuss the ethics of security testing.

Recap: Security testing looks at the system through an attacker's eyes to protect confidentiality, integrity and availability. Use the OWASP Top 10 as a guide; test injection, cross-site scripting, broken access control, authentication and sessions, sensitive data and configuration. Combine SAST, DAST and dependency scanning in the pipeline, scan often and commission penetration tests for depth, and use fuzzing for parsers. Tools such as OWASP ZAP and Burp Suite help, but permission, scope and responsible disclosure are non-negotiable. Next we look at testing for people: usability, accessibility and compatibility.
key_points: Security testing asks whether the system can be made to do what it must never do, from an attacker's point of view.
The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability, with authentication, authorisation and non-repudiation alongside.
The OWASP Top 10 lists critical web risk categories, such as broken access control and injection, and is a common testing checklist.
SQL injection is prevented by parameterised queries; XSS by output encoding; broken access control is tested with multiple accounts.
SAST analyses code, DAST attacks the running app, and SCA checks third-party libraries for known vulnerabilities.
Vulnerability scans are broad and automated; penetration tests are focused, skilled attempts to exploit and chain weaknesses.
Only test with written permission and agreed scope, and report vulnerabilities through responsible disclosure.
lessons.tip: For every feature you test, write one abuse case next to the user story: "As an attacker, I want to..." It turns security from a separate phase into a habit.
lessons.task: Using a practice application built for learning security, such as OWASP Juice Shop running on your own machine, and OWASP ZAP, find and document three issues: one injection or XSS issue, one access control issue, and one sensitive data exposure. For each, write a defect report with steps, impact on the CIA triad and a suggested fix. Never use these techniques on real sites.

quiz.q: Which security goal is violated when an attacker reads other customers' medical records?
quiz.explain: Confidentiality means only authorised people can see data; reading others' records breaks it.

quiz.q: What is the primary defence against SQL injection?
options: Parameterised queries that keep data separate from the SQL command
quiz.explain: Prepared statements with parameters stop input from changing the meaning of the query.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between SAST and DAST?
options: SAST runs only in production, DAST only on paper
SAST analyses source code without running it, while DAST tests the running application from outside
SAST is manual and DAST is always manual too
quiz.explain: Static testing reads the code; dynamic testing attacks the deployed, running system.

quiz.q: A tester changes /accounts/1001 to /accounts/1002 and sees another user's account. What type of flaw is this?
quiz.explain: The server failed to check that the logged-in user owns the requested object, which is broken access control.

quiz.q: You discover a vulnerability on a company's website while browsing. What is the ethical course of action?
options: Exploit it to prove it is real, then post about it publicly
Report it privately to the company through its security contact and allow time to fix it
Ignore it and test other sites
quiz.explain: Responsible disclosure means reporting privately and giving the owner time to fix, without exploiting the flaw.

lessons.title: Usability, Accessibility and Compatibility Testing
lessons.content:
Imagine a new government service app for applying for a trade licence. Every function works: forms submit, payments go through, certificates download. Yet in the first month, the help line is flooded. Shop owners in Sylhet cannot find where to upload documents, an older user who relies on a screen reader cannot get past the first screen, and the app crashes on a popular low-cost Android phone with an older operating system. None of these problems is a broken calculation. All of them stop real people from using the service. This lesson covers three kinds of testing that focus on people and their devices: usability, accessibility and compatibility.

Where this lesson fits: The human-computer interaction course (deep-cse-5-5) teaches how to design for people, including user research, design principles and evaluation methods in depth. Here we take the tester's view: how to plan and run these checks as part of quality assurance, how to report the findings as defects, and how to fit them into a test strategy. If you have studied HCI, treat this as a recap with a testing focus.

Usability, the definition: ISO 9241-11 defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use. Effectiveness asks whether users complete the task correctly; efficiency asks how much time and effort it takes; satisfaction asks how users feel about it. The words "specified users" and "context" matter: an app that is easy for a young software engineer in an office may be hard for a farmer on a bright field with a cracked screen.

Usability testing in practice: In a usability test, representative users try realistic tasks while observers watch and record where they struggle, without helping. A facilitator gives scenarios such as "you want to send 500 Taka to your brother; please do that now" and asks participants to think aloud. Observers note task success, time on task, errors, hesitation and comments. Jakob Nielsen has argued that small rounds with about five users reveal most major problems, so several small rounds with fixes in between work better than one large study at the end.

Measuring usability: Common measures are task completion rate, time on task, error count and satisfaction questionnaires. The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a widely used ten-item questionnaire answered on a 1 to 5 scale. For odd-numbered items, which are positively worded, subtract 1 from the answer; for even-numbered items, which are negatively worded, subtract the answer from 5; add the ten results and multiply by 2.5 to get a score from 0 to 100. A participant who answers 4 to every odd item and 2 to every even item scores (5 x 3 + 5 x 3) x 2.5 = 75. A SUS score is not a percentage; it is useful for comparing versions or products over time.

Heuristic evaluation and checklists: Testers and experts can also review an interface against usability heuristics, such as Nielsen's ten heuristics: visibility of system status, match with the real world, user control and freedom, consistency, error prevention, recognition rather than recall, flexibility, minimalist design, helping users recover from errors, and help and documentation. Such reviews are fast and cheap, and a tester can apply them during ordinary functional testing, but they do not replace observing real users.

Reporting usability defects: Usability findings should be reported like any defect, with evidence: the task, what the user expected, what happened, how many participants struggled, and a severity based on impact (did it block the task, slow it, or merely annoy?). "The button is confusing" is weak; "4 of 5 participants did not find the document upload, because it appears only after scrolling past the payment section; 2 abandoned the task" is actionable.

Accessibility, why it matters: Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with the product. This includes people who are blind or have low vision, are deaf or hard of hearing, have motor impairments, or have cognitive or learning disabilities, and also older users and people with temporary limitations such as a broken arm. Bangladesh has millions of people with disabilities, and accessible design also helps everyone, for example captions in a noisy bus or large touch targets on a moving rickshaw. Many countries have laws requiring accessibility for public services.

WCAG and the POUR principles: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), are the main international standard, and their ideas apply to mobile apps as well. WCAG is organised around four principles, remembered as POUR. Perceivable: information can be perceived, for example images have text alternatives and videos have captions. Operable: everything can be operated, for example with a keyboard, with enough time and nothing that flashes dangerously. Understandable: text is readable and behaviour predictable, with clear error messages. Robust: content works with assistive technologies, through correct structure and roles.

Conformance levels and contrast: WCAG success criteria are grouped into three levels: A (minimum), AA (the level most laws and organisations target), and AAA (the highest, not required for whole sites). A well-known AA criterion is colour contrast: normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, and large text at least 3:1. Light grey text on a white background often fails. Testers check contrast with tools rather than by eye.

How to test accessibility: Use automated checkers such as axe, Lighthouse or WAVE for web pages and the platform accessibility scanners for mobile apps; they quickly find missing alternative text, low contrast, missing form labels and wrong roles, but they detect only part of the possible issues. Then test manually: navigate the whole flow using only the keyboard and check that focus is visible and in a logical order; use a screen reader, such as NVDA or JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on Apple devices or TalkBack on Android, and check that every control is announced meaningfully; zoom text to 200 percent; and check that nothing relies on colour alone, such as a form showing errors only in red.

Including people with disabilities: The best accessibility testing includes users with disabilities themselves. A screen reader user who uses it every day navigates very differently from a sighted tester trying it for the first time, and will find problems that checklists miss. Organisations working with people with disabilities can help recruit participants, and their time should be paid like any expert's.

Accessibility in mobile apps: The same principles apply on phones, with a few extra checks. Touch targets should be large enough to tap without hitting neighbours, content should work in both portrait and landscape where sensible, the app should respect the system font size setting without cutting off text, and every icon button needs a content description or accessibility label so TalkBack or VoiceOver can announce it. Gestures such as swipes should have a simple alternative, such as a button, for users who cannot perform them.

Compatibility testing: Compatibility testing checks that the product works correctly across the environments its users have: browsers and browser versions, operating systems and versions, device models and screen sizes, screen densities and orientations, and network conditions. It also covers compatibility with other software, such as printers, payment apps or older versions of the product's own data. Its cousin, interoperability testing, checks that systems exchange data correctly.

Choosing a device and browser matrix: Nobody can test every combination. Build a matrix from data: analytics showing which devices, operating system versions and browsers real users have, market data for the target country, and risk. In Bangladesh that usually means giving priority to Android phones, including low-cost models with small memory and older operating system versions, and to mobile browsers. Test fully on the most common configurations, run smoke tests on the next group, and use cloud device services such as BrowserStack or Firebase Test Lab to reach the long tail. Pairwise selection from the combinatorial lesson helps keep the matrix small.

Network and environment conditions: Many users switch between Wi-Fi, 4G and weak 3G or 2G signals, pass through areas with no coverage, and use data packages carefully. Test on throttled networks, with high latency and packet loss, and in airplane mode mid-transaction. Check that the app shows clear progress and errors, retries safely, does not lose data, and does not download huge images on a slow connection. Also test with low battery saver modes, low storage, and interruptions such as a phone call during payment.

Localisation and Bangla: Localisation testing checks that the product works correctly in each language and region. For Bangla, check that text renders correctly with conjuncts and vowel signs on all target devices, that Bangla digits and English digits are handled consistently in inputs and displays, that dates, times and currency follow the expected format, that text expansion or longer words do not break layouts, that sorting and search work with Bangla text, and that translations are accurate and natural rather than literal. Internationalisation, building the product so it can be localised, is what makes this possible.

Real-life example, a farmers' advisory app: An agriculture advisory app tested with five farmers in Rangpur before launch. Testers observed that icons for "weather" and "market price" were misunderstood by three participants, the Bangla font was too small to read outdoors, and two participants did not notice that a long text needed scrolling. Bigger fonts, labels under icons and a voice playback option fixed most problems. The second round showed task completion rising from about half to nearly all participants.

Real-life example, an inaccessible payment step: A university fee payment portal passed all functional tests. An accessibility audit with a screen reader found that the CAPTCHA had no alternative, the "Pay" button was an image without a label and announced only as "button", and error messages appeared in red with no text. Blind students could not pay their fees without help. The team added an accessible alternative, labels and text errors, and added automated accessibility checks to their pipeline, plus a manual screen reader pass before each release.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include treating usability as a matter of taste, testing usability only with team members, relying only on automated accessibility checkers, ignoring keyboard and screen reader use, testing only on the team's own new phones, and forgetting slow networks and localisation. Exams ask you to define usability with its three components, describe how to run a usability test, compute a SUS score, explain WCAG's POUR principles and levels A, AA and AAA, describe manual accessibility checks, and explain how to choose a compatibility matrix.

Recap: Usability, accessibility and compatibility testing make sure real people can use the product on their real devices. Usability combines effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction, and is tested by observing representative users on realistic tasks and measuring with tools such as SUS. Accessibility follows WCAG's POUR principles, usually at level AA, with automated checks plus keyboard, screen reader and contrast testing, ideally with disabled users. Compatibility testing covers a data-driven matrix of devices, systems, browsers and networks, and localisation testing makes Bangla and other languages work properly. For deeper design methods, see the HCI course. Next we look at how all testing fits into continuous integration and DevOps.
key_points: Usability is effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users in a specified context (ISO 9241-11).
Usability tests observe representative users doing realistic tasks; small repeated rounds of about five users find most major issues.
SUS scores range from 0 to 100 and are useful for comparing versions; they are not percentages.
WCAG principles are Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust; AA is the usual target level, with 4.5:1 contrast for normal text.
Automated accessibility checkers find only part of the issues; keyboard and screen reader testing are essential.
Compatibility testing uses a data-driven matrix of devices, OS versions, browsers and network conditions.
Localisation testing checks Bangla rendering, digits, dates, currency, layout and translation quality.
lessons.tip: Once a week, use the product you are testing for ten minutes with the screen off and a screen reader on, or with only the keyboard. You will find problems no checklist mentions.
lessons.task: Pick a Bangladeshi public service or shopping website. Run an automated accessibility checker on two pages, then try the same pages with only the keyboard and with a screen reader. List five problems with the WCAG principle each breaks, and write one usability task scenario you would give a test participant for that site.

quiz.q: According to ISO 9241-11, which three components make up usability?
quiz.explain: Usability is the extent to which specified users achieve goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a context of use.

quiz.q: What does the "O" in WCAG's POUR principles stand for?
quiz.explain: POUR is Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust; operable means all functions can be operated, for example by keyboard.

quiz.q: A participant answers 4 to every odd SUS item and 2 to every even item. What is the SUS score?
quiz.explain: Odd items give 4 - 1 = 3 each, even items give 5 - 2 = 3 each; 10 x 3 = 30, and 30 x 2.5 = 75.

quiz.q: Which statement about automated accessibility checkers is correct?
options: They find only part of the issues, so manual keyboard and screen reader testing are still needed
They are only for performance testing
quiz.explain: Automated tools catch issues like missing labels and low contrast, but many problems need human testing.

quiz.q: How should a team choose which devices and browsers to test on?
options: Use analytics and market data about real users, plus risk, to build a prioritised matrix
Test only on the developers' own phones
Choose the newest flagship phones only
quiz.explain: A data-driven, risk-based matrix focuses effort on the configurations real users have, with lighter checks on the long tail.

lessons.title: Testing in Continuous Integration and DevOps
lessons.content:
A busy Dhaka sweet shop does not wait until the end of the week to taste the roshogolla. Every batch is checked as it comes out of the syrup: the texture, the sweetness, the size. If one batch is wrong, the cook knows within minutes, while he still remembers exactly what he changed. If the shop tasted only on Friday, a whole week of bad sweets would already be sold. Continuous integration and DevOps bring the same rhythm to software: small changes, checked automatically within minutes, all day long.

From big releases to continuous flow: Traditional projects integrated code from many developers rarely, sometimes after weeks, and then spent painful days fixing conflicts and defects before a big release. Continuous integration (CI) means every developer merges small changes into a shared main branch frequently, at least daily, and each merge triggers an automated build and test run. Continuous delivery (CD) extends this so that every change that passes the pipeline is in a releasable state. Continuous deployment goes one step further and releases every passing change to production automatically, with no manual approval.

What DevOps adds: DevOps is a culture and set of practices that bring development and operations together, sharing responsibility for building, releasing and running software. For testing, it means quality is everyone's job throughout the life cycle, feedback loops are short, automation is essential, and learning from production is part of testing. Testers in DevOps teams spend less time executing scripted test cases by hand and more time designing automated checks, exploring risks, improving the pipeline and analysing production signals.

The deployment pipeline: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that a change passes through. A typical pipeline: the commit stage compiles the code, runs static analysis and linting, and runs unit tests, aiming to finish in about ten minutes or less; the acceptance stage deploys to a test environment and runs API, integration and a small set of UI tests; further stages may run performance, security and compatibility checks; then the change is deployed to staging and finally production. Each stage gives more confidence and costs more time, so fast checks run first.

Tools for pipelines: Common CI/CD tools include Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Azure Pipelines, CircleCI and Bitrise for mobile apps. Pipelines are usually written as code, in configuration files stored in the repository, so they are reviewed and versioned like everything else. Docker containers give every stage the same environment, ending "it works on my machine" problems, and infrastructure as code creates test environments on demand.

Quality gates: A quality gate is a rule that a change must satisfy before it can move to the next stage or merge. Examples: all unit and API tests pass; no new critical findings from static analysis or security scanning; code coverage on new code is at least an agreed value; no known vulnerable dependencies with high severity; the performance smoke test shows no regression beyond a threshold; at least one reviewer approved the pull request. Gates make quality expectations explicit and automatic, so they do not depend on someone remembering to check.

Keeping the pipeline fast: Feedback is only useful if it arrives while the developer still has the change in mind. Slow pipelines encourage people to batch changes and skip checks. Techniques: follow the test pyramid so most checks are fast unit tests; run tests in parallel across machines; cache dependencies and build outputs; split suites so that a quick subset runs on every commit and the full regression runs nightly; and use test impact analysis, which selects only the tests affected by the files that changed.

Test selection and prioritisation: With thousands of tests, running all of them on every commit may be too slow. Regression test selection chooses tests related to the changed code, using coverage maps or dependency analysis. Prioritisation orders tests so that those most likely to fail, such as recently failing tests or tests of high-risk areas, run first and fail fast. The full suite still runs regularly, such as nightly, to catch anything selection missed.

Dealing with flaky tests in CI: In a pipeline, a flaky test is worse than useless: it blocks merges randomly and teaches people to click "rerun" without thinking. Good practice: detect flakiness automatically by tracking tests that both pass and fail on the same code; quarantine flaky tests into a separate, non-blocking job; create a ticket with an owner and a deadline for each; and fix the root cause as discussed in the test doubles lesson. Automatic retries can hide real intermittent defects, such as race conditions, so use them cautiously and always record that a retry happened.

Test environments on demand: A shared test server that everyone deploys to becomes a bottleneck and a source of confusing failures, because one team's half-finished change breaks another team's tests. Containers and infrastructure as code let pipelines create a fresh, isolated environment for each pull request, often called an ephemeral or review environment, run the tests, let reviewers try the change, and destroy it afterwards. Test data is loaded by scripts, so every run starts from a known state. This makes results reproducible and lets many changes be tested at the same time.

What testers do in a DevOps team: The tester's role shifts rather than disappears. Typical work includes pairing with developers on acceptance criteria and test design, building and maintaining automated suites at the right pyramid level, reviewing tests in pull requests, keeping the pipeline healthy and fast, running focused exploratory sessions on risky changes, defining monitoring and alerts with operations, and analysing production incidents to find gaps in testing. The skills from this whole course stay essential; they are simply applied continuously instead of in one phase at the end.

Shift-left testing: Shift-left means moving testing activities earlier in the life cycle: reviewing requirements and writing acceptance criteria before coding, threat modelling during design, TDD and unit tests during coding, static analysis on every commit, and API tests before the UI exists. Defects found early are cheaper to fix, as the first lesson showed. In DevOps, shift-left is built into the pipeline and the team's daily habits rather than being a separate phase.

Shift-right testing: Shift-right means continuing to test and learn in production, where real users, data and scale exist. No test environment perfectly matches production, so some defects only appear there. Shift-right practices include monitoring and alerting, synthetic monitoring (automated scripts that regularly run key journeys against production, such as logging in and checking a balance every five minutes), canary releases, feature flags, A/B testing and chaos engineering. Shift-left and shift-right complement each other.

Canary releases and blue-green deployment: In a canary release, a new version goes first to a small share of users, say 5 percent, while its error rates, latency and business metrics are compared with the old version. If the canary is healthy, the share grows step by step; if not, it is rolled back with few users affected. In blue-green deployment, two identical production environments exist; the new version is deployed to the idle one, tested, and traffic is switched over at once, with the old one kept ready for instant rollback.

Feature flags: A feature flag (or toggle) lets a team deploy code with a feature switched off, then turn it on for testers, staff, a region or a percentage of users without a new deployment. Flags separate deployment from release, allow quick switch-off when something goes wrong, and support testing in production with real data. They also add risk: every flag doubles the number of possible combinations, so teams must test both states of important flags and remove old flags promptly.

Monitoring and observability: Production monitoring watches the system's health through metrics (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, resource use), logs, and traces that follow a request across services. Business metrics, such as successful payments per minute, often reveal defects faster than technical ones. Alerts tell the team when something crosses a threshold. Testers help define what "healthy" means, check that important failures are logged and alerted, and use production data to find untested paths and real user behaviour.

A/B testing: In A/B testing, two versions of a feature are shown to randomly split groups of users, and their behaviour is compared statistically to see which performs better, for example which checkout design leads to more completed orders. It is mainly a product experiment rather than a defect hunt, but it relies on correct implementation, so testers check that users are assigned correctly, that each variant works, and that events are recorded accurately.

Chaos engineering: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures into a system to test its resilience: shutting down a server, adding network delay, making a dependency return errors. It started at Netflix, whose Chaos Monkey tool randomly terminated production instances to make sure services could survive. Experiments start with a hypothesis ("if one payment service instance dies, checkout success stays above 99 percent"), begin small in test environments, and limit the blast radius. The aim is to find weaknesses before real incidents do.

Real-life example, a fintech pipeline: A Bangladeshi digital lending startup moved from monthly releases to several deployments a day. Its pipeline runs linting, 3,000 unit tests and a dependency scan in eight minutes, then deploys to a test environment and runs 400 API tests and 25 UI tests in fifteen minutes, with quality gates on test results, coverage of new code and security findings. Production releases go out as canaries to 5 percent of users, with automatic rollback if loan application errors rise. In the first year, the time from a defect report to a fix in production fell from weeks to under a day.

Real-life example, a feature flag that saved a sale: An e-commerce company launched a new recommendation widget behind a feature flag the day before a big sale. Synthetic monitoring showed product page latency rising sharply in one region as traffic grew. The team switched the flag off in seconds, without a redeployment, and latency recovered. The widget was fixed and re-enabled after the sale, after a load test that reproduced the problem.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include slow pipelines that people bypass, ignoring flaky tests, quality gates that everyone overrides, treating CI as only "running the build", deploying without monitoring, leaving old feature flags forever, and believing shift-right means testing less before release. Exams ask you to distinguish continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment; draw a deployment pipeline with test stages; explain quality gates; define shift-left and shift-right with examples; and explain canary releases, feature flags, A/B testing and chaos engineering.

Recap: Continuous integration merges small changes often and tests each one automatically; continuous delivery keeps every passing change releasable; continuous deployment releases it automatically. A deployment pipeline runs fast checks first and slower ones later, guarded by quality gates, and stays fast through the pyramid, parallelism and test selection, with flaky tests quarantined and fixed. Shift-left brings testing earlier; shift-right continues it in production through monitoring, synthetic checks, canaries, feature flags, A/B tests and chaos engineering. Next we learn how to measure all this with test metrics.
key_points: CI merges small changes often with automated build and tests; continuous delivery keeps changes releasable; continuous deployment releases them automatically.
A deployment pipeline runs fast checks first (build, static analysis, unit tests) and slower ones later (API, UI, performance, security).
Quality gates are explicit, automatic rules a change must meet before moving on.
Keep pipelines fast with the test pyramid, parallel runs, caching, test selection and prioritisation.
Quarantine flaky tests with an owner and fix them; careless retries can hide real intermittent defects.
Shift-left tests earlier in the life cycle; shift-right learns in production through monitoring, canaries, feature flags and A/B tests.
Chaos engineering injects controlled failures to test resilience, starting small with a hypothesis.
lessons.tip: Measure how long your pipeline takes from push to result, and treat anything over about ten minutes for the first feedback as a defect in the pipeline itself.
lessons.task: For a small web or Flutter project of your own, set up a free CI pipeline (for example with GitHub Actions) that installs dependencies, runs a linter and your unit tests on every push, and fails the build if any test fails. Then write down three quality gates and two shift-right checks you would add if the project went live.

quiz.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
options: In continuous delivery every passing change is releasable but release may need approval; continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically
Continuous delivery has no automated tests
Continuous deployment only applies to mobile apps
quiz.explain: Both keep changes releasable; continuous deployment removes the manual step and releases automatically.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a quality gate?
options: A rule that blocks merging if any unit test fails or a high-severity vulnerability is found
quiz.explain: Quality gates are explicit, automated rules that a change must pass before it moves on.

quiz.q: A new version is released to 5 percent of users first, and its error rates are compared with the old version before rolling it out further. What is this called?
quiz.explain: Canary releases expose a small group to the new version and expand only if it is healthy.

quiz.q: Which practice is an example of shift-right testing?
options: Synthetic monitoring that runs key journeys against production every few minutes
quiz.explain: Shift-right continues testing and learning in production, for example through synthetic monitoring.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of chaos engineering?
options: To make the code harder to read
To test the user interface colours
To deliberately inject failures and learn whether the system stays resilient
quiz.explain: Chaos engineering runs controlled failure experiments to find weaknesses before real incidents do.

lessons.title: Test Metrics and Measuring Quality
lessons.content:
A doctor does not judge a patient's health from one number. Blood pressure, temperature, pulse and blood sugar each tell part of the story, and the doctor watches how they change over weeks, not only today's reading. A doctor who looked only at temperature might send home someone with dangerously high blood pressure. Software quality is the same: no single metric tells you whether a product is good or whether testing is effective. Used together, and watched over time, a few well-chosen measures help teams decide and improve. Used carelessly, they mislead and can even make quality worse.

Why measure: Metrics answer questions that matter to decisions. Is the product ready to release? Is testing progressing as planned? Is quality improving from release to release? Where do defects come from, and where should we invest in prevention? Without measurement, these answers rest on feelings and on whoever argues loudest. With good measurement, a test manager can say "we are on track, the remaining risks are these", and support it with evidence.

Goal-Question-Metric: A useful way to choose metrics is the Goal-Question-Metric (GQM) approach associated with Victor Basili. Start with a goal, such as "reduce defects reaching customers". Ask questions that show progress towards it, such as "how many defects escape to production?" and "in which phase were they introduced?". Only then choose metrics that answer those questions, such as defect leakage and defect origin by phase. Starting from goals prevents the common habit of collecting whatever a tool happens to report.

Kinds of metrics: Process metrics measure how testing is done, such as test case execution progress and defect fix time. Product metrics measure the software itself, such as defect density or code coverage. Project metrics measure schedule, effort and cost. Another split is between leading indicators, which warn early (coverage of high-risk requirements, trends in new defects), and lagging indicators, which confirm outcomes later (defects reported by customers after release).

Test progress metrics: During test execution, teams track tests planned, executed, passed, failed and blocked, usually per day and per risk area. Suppose 520 tests are planned and 500 executed, of which 470 passed: execution progress is 500 / 520, about 96.2 percent, and the pass rate is 470 / 500 = 94 percent. Blocked tests deserve special attention, because they hide untested areas. Progress should be shown by risk: 100 percent of low-risk tests executed means little if half the high-risk ones are blocked.

Coverage metrics: Requirements coverage measures how many requirements or acceptance criteria have at least one test, and how many of those pass; traceability makes it measurable. Risk coverage does the same for the risk register. Code coverage from the white-box lessons, statement and branch, measures how much code the tests execute. Remember the limits: coverage shows what was not tested, but high coverage does not prove good tests, because tests without strong assertions can execute code without checking it. Mutation score from lesson 13 is a stronger measure of test quality.

Defect density: Defect density is the number of defects found divided by the size of the software, often per thousand lines of code (KLOC) or per function point. If a module of 30 KLOC has 45 confirmed defects, its density is 45 / 30 = 1.5 defects per KLOC. Comparing densities across modules points to defect clusters, which may need refactoring, more reviews or more testing. Comparing across teams or languages is dangerous, because counting rules and coding styles differ.

Defect removal efficiency: Defect removal efficiency (DRE), also called defect detection percentage, measures how good the whole quality process was at catching defects before release: DRE = defects found before release / (defects found before release + defects found after release) x 100. If testing and reviews found 180 defects before release and customers reported 20 in the first 90 days, DRE = 180 / 200 = 90 percent. A fixed period after release must be agreed, otherwise the number keeps changing. DRE can also be computed per phase to see how well each review or test level catches defects.

Defect leakage: Defect leakage is the complementary view: the share of defects that escaped a phase or reached production. In the example, 20 / 200 = 10 percent of defects leaked to customers. Analysing each leaked defect is one of the most valuable improvement activities: why did our tests not catch it? Was it a missing requirement, a missing test technique, an untested configuration, or data that only production had? Each answer suggests a specific fix.

Defect trend and arrival metrics: Plotting new defects found per day or per week, alongside defects fixed, shows whether a release is stabilising. Early in testing, arrivals usually rise as more of the system becomes testable; near release they should fall, and the curve of open defects should flatten towards zero for high-severity ones. A curve that is still rising a week before release is a warning, whatever the pass rate says. Breakdowns by severity, module and root cause make the trends actionable.

Defect origin and phase containment: Recording the phase in which each defect was introduced and the phase in which it was found produces a simple but revealing table. If 40 percent of defects are introduced in requirements but only a few are found in requirement reviews, most of them travel all the way to system testing or production, where they cost far more. Phase containment, the share of defects caught in the same phase that introduced them, shows which reviews and test levels are pulling their weight. It turns the abstract idea of shift-left into numbers a team can track.

Rejected and reopened rates: Two small metrics say a lot about communication. A high rate of rejected defect reports suggests that testers misunderstand requirements or that the requirements are unclear, both worth fixing. A high rate of reopened defects suggests fixes are rushed, not reviewed, or not covered by regression tests. Neither number should be used to blame a person; both are prompts for a conversation in the retrospective.

Defect age and fix time: Defect age measures how long defects stay open; mean time to fix measures the average time from report to verified fix, often split by severity. Long-lived critical defects signal a process problem: unclear ownership, overloaded teams, or defects that nobody can reproduce. Many teams set targets, such as critical defects fixed within two days, and track how often they are met.

Production reliability metrics: In DevOps teams, testing metrics are complemented by operational ones. Mean time to detect (MTTD) is how long problems in production go unnoticed; mean time to restore or recover (MTTR) is how long it takes to restore service. If four incidents in a month took 30, 90, 45 and 75 minutes to restore, MTTR is 240 / 4 = 60 minutes. The DORA research programme popularised four delivery metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service; together they describe both speed and stability.

Automation metrics: Teams with large automated suites track how long the pipeline takes, how many tests are automated at each pyramid level, how often builds fail and why (real defects, environment problems, flaky tests), the flaky test rate, and the maintenance effort spent on test code. A suite where most failures are false alarms needs attention more urgently than one with lower coverage.

Cost of quality: Cost of quality groups spending into prevention (training, reviews, good design), appraisal (testing and inspection), internal failure (fixing defects before release) and external failure (fixing defects after release, support calls, refunds, lost customers, reputation damage). Investing in prevention and early appraisal usually reduces the expensive failure costs, which is the economic case for testing and QA. This model comes from manufacturing quality management and is useful when arguing for budgets.

Goodhart's law and gaming: Goodhart's law is often summarised as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure". If testers are rewarded for the number of defects reported, they split one defect into five and argue over trivial issues. If developers are punished for defects, they argue that defects are "features" or avoid reporting their own. If a coverage target of 90 percent is imposed, people write tests that execute code without meaningful assertions. Metrics should inform conversations and improvement, not rank individuals.

Measuring with small numbers: Many teams have only a few dozen defects per release, so percentages can jump wildly by chance. Six leaked defects out of twenty is 30 percent, but one more or one fewer changes it by five points. Look at several releases together, show the raw counts next to percentages, and avoid drawing strong conclusions from tiny samples.

Presenting metrics well: Show trends, not single snapshots; show metrics together with context, such as test progress next to risk coverage and open high-severity defects; keep dashboards small, with a handful of numbers that answer the stakeholders' real questions; explain what each number means and what it does not; and always accompany metrics with the tester's judgement. A one-page test summary report with five meaningful numbers and three clear sentences about residual risk is worth more than a forty-chart dashboard.

Real-life example, a bank's leakage analysis: A bank's mobile app team computed DRE for three releases: 82, 85 and 78 percent. Analysing the leaked defects of the third release showed that 9 of 14 came from one area: transactions crossing midnight and month-end, which the test environment never simulated because test runs happened in office hours with a real clock. The team added a controllable clock to the test environment and boundary tests for date changes. The next two releases reached DRE of 91 and 93 percent.

Real-life example, a metric that backfired: A software company in Dhaka set a target that every tester must log at least 25 defects per sprint. Within two months the defect count doubled, but customers saw no improvement. Triage meetings were flooded with duplicates and cosmetic issues, and developers grew resentful. When management replaced the target with leakage analysis and risk coverage reviews, the number of reported defects fell, collaboration improved, and production incidents dropped the following quarter.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include collecting metrics without goals, judging people by defect counts, trusting coverage as proof of quality, comparing defect density across unlike projects, reporting single numbers without trends, and ignoring Goodhart's law. Exams ask you to compute defect density, DRE, defect leakage, pass rate and execution progress; explain the GQM approach; distinguish process, product and project metrics; describe cost of quality categories; explain MTTR and the DORA metrics; and discuss the dangers of metrics.

Recap: Metrics turn testing into evidence for decisions and improvement when chosen from goals with GQM. Track test progress and pass rate by risk, requirements and risk coverage, code coverage with its limits, defect density, DRE and leakage, defect trends, age and fix time, and, in DevOps, MTTD, MTTR and the DORA metrics. Cost of quality explains why prevention pays. Beware Goodhart's law: never use metrics to rank individuals, and always present trends with context and judgement. In the final lesson we look at process quality models and at careers in software testing.
key_points: Choose metrics from goals using Goal-Question-Metric, not from whatever tools report.
Execution progress = executed / planned; pass rate = passed / executed; show both by risk area.
Defect density = defects / size, such as defects per KLOC; use it to find defect clusters, not to compare unlike teams.
DRE = defects before release / (before + after release) x 100; leakage is the share that escaped.
Coverage reveals untested areas but high coverage does not prove good tests.
MTTD, MTTR and the DORA metrics measure delivery speed and production stability.
Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure; never rank individuals by defect counts.
lessons.tip: Every time you present a metric, add one sentence that starts with "This means..." and one that starts with "This does not tell us...". It keeps numbers honest.
lessons.task: A project found 240 defects during reviews and testing, and customers reported 60 in the first three months after release. The code is 80 KLOC. Compute DRE, defect leakage and defect density. Then write three GQM entries (goal, question, metric) for improving the next release, and name one way each metric could be gamed.

quiz.q: Testing found 160 defects before release and 40 were found in production during the agreed period. What is the DRE?
What does Goodhart's law warn about?
options: When a measure becomes a target, people optimise the number and it stops reflecting quality
quiz.explain: Turning a measure into a target invites gaming, so the number no longer means what it used to.

quiz.q: A module of 8 KLOC has 24 confirmed defects. What is its defect density?
quiz.explain: Defect density = 24 / 8 = 3 defects per KLOC.

quiz.q: In the Goal-Question-Metric approach, what comes first?
quiz.explain: GQM starts with a goal, derives questions that show progress, and only then selects metrics.

quiz.q: Why is high code coverage alone not proof of good testing?
options: Tests can execute code without meaningful assertions, so coverage shows what ran, not what was checked
quiz.explain: Coverage reveals what was not executed; it cannot show whether the executed code was actually verified.

lessons.title: Process Quality, Standards and Careers in Testing
lessons.content:
Two tea stalls stand on the same corner. At the first, the tea is wonderful on some days and terrible on others, depending on who is making it and how busy they are. At the second, the owner has a routine: the same measure of leaves, water boiled the same way, milk added at the same moment, and every evening he thinks about what went wrong that day and adjusts. His tea is reliably good, and slowly gets better. The difference is not talent; it is process. This final lesson looks at how organisations improve the process that produces software, at the standards and models behind that, and at how you can build a career in software testing and quality.

Product quality and process quality: Most of this course has been about product quality: testing the software to find defects and measure quality characteristics. Process quality is about the way the software is produced: if the process is defined, followed, measured and improved, good products become more likely and more predictable. Quality assurance in its full sense, as lesson 2 explained, is about the process; testing is one of its most important tools.

The PDCA cycle: The Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, popularised by W. Edwards Deming and often called the Deming cycle, is the basic engine of process improvement. Plan: identify a problem and plan a change, with a way to measure its effect. Do: try the change, ideally on a small scale. Check: measure the results and compare with the plan. Act: if it worked, make it standard; if not, learn and plan again. Sprint retrospectives in Scrum are a small, frequent PDCA loop.

ISO 9001: ISO 9001 is the international standard for quality management systems, used across all industries, not only software. It requires an organisation to define its processes, understand customer requirements, control documents and records, manage risks, measure performance, handle nonconformities with corrective action, conduct internal audits and management reviews, and continually improve. Organisations can be certified by external auditors. ISO 9001 does not prescribe how to write or test software; it requires that whatever the organisation does is defined, followed and improved. At this level of detail it is enough to know its purpose and its process approach.

CMMI and its maturity levels: Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI), which grew out of work at the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon University, describes how organisations mature their processes. Its staged representation has five maturity levels. Level 1, Initial: processes are ad hoc and success depends on individual heroes. Level 2, Managed: projects are planned, tracked and controlled, with requirements and configuration managed. Level 3, Defined: the organisation has standard processes, tailored for each project, including verification and validation. Level 4, Quantitatively Managed: processes are controlled using statistical and quantitative data. Level 5, Optimizing: the organisation continually improves processes based on quantitative understanding and innovation.

What maturity levels mean for testers: At level 1, testing is often a rushed phase at the end, done however each project chooses. At level 2, testing is planned and tracked per project. At level 3, the organisation has a standard test process, templates, techniques and training. At levels 4 and 5, test metrics such as DRE and defect density are used with statistical control to predict and improve quality. Some Bangladeshi software companies serving international clients have pursued CMMI appraisals, because some clients use maturity levels in vendor selection. A maturity level is a statement about process capability, not a guarantee that every product is good.

TMMi, maturity for testing: The Test Maturity Model integration (TMMi) applies the same idea specifically to testing and is designed to complement CMMI. It also has five levels, from Initial, where testing is chaotic and not distinguished from debugging, through Managed, Definition and Measured, to Optimization, where test processes are continuously improved and defect prevention is a focus. Organisations use TMMi assessments to see what their test process lacks and to plan improvement in steps rather than trying to fix everything at once.

Other improvement approaches: Lean thinking focuses on removing waste, such as waiting for test environments, handoffs and rework. Six Sigma, from manufacturing, uses data and statistics to reduce variation, with the DMAIC cycle (Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control) and the well-known target of 3.4 defects per million opportunities. In software, these ideas appear in value stream mapping of the delivery pipeline and in data-driven defect prevention. Agile and DevOps teams improve through retrospectives, small experiments and metrics such as the DORA measures rather than heavy models, but the PDCA logic is the same.

Testing standards: The ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 series defines international standards for software testing: concepts, test processes, test documentation and test techniques. It replaced older standards such as IEEE 829 for test documentation, whose document types, such as the test plan and test summary report, are still widely recognised. Standards give a shared vocabulary and checklists; teams should tailor them sensibly rather than produce documents nobody reads. Safety-critical domains have their own standards that demand specific testing, such as the MC/DC coverage you met in lesson 12.

Audits and reviews of the process: A quality audit is an independent examination of whether the organisation follows its own defined processes and whether those processes are effective. Internal auditors check, for example, that test plans exist and are approved, that defects are tracked through their life cycle, that exit criteria were met before release, and that corrective actions were taken after major incidents. Audit findings feed PDCA. For testers, good habits such as traceability, clear test reports and recorded decisions make audits straightforward.

Root cause and prevention at organisation level: Mature organisations do not stop at fixing defects; they ask why each class of defect happens and change the process to prevent it. Examples: a checklist for requirement reviews after many ambiguity defects; mandatory API authorisation tests after an access control incident; a static analysis rule after repeated null pointer crashes; a controllable clock in test environments after date defects. This is defect prevention, the highest-value quality activity, and it is fed by the metrics and root cause analysis from earlier lessons.

Careers in testing and quality: Testing offers many paths. A software tester or QA engineer designs and runs tests, explores, and reports defects. A test automation engineer or software development engineer in test (SDET) builds automated suites and frameworks and works closely with developers. Specialists focus on performance engineering, security testing, accessibility or mobile testing. A test lead or QA manager plans testing, manages people and risks, and reports to stakeholders. Quality engineers in DevOps teams own pipelines and quality gates. Many testers move into product management, business analysis, site reliability engineering or development, carrying a valuable habit of questioning.

Skills that matter: Strong testers combine technical and human skills. Technical: test design techniques from this course, programming in at least one language such as Python, Java or JavaScript, SQL, HTTP and APIs, Git, a test framework, an automation tool, CI basics, and enough knowledge of operating systems and networks to diagnose problems. Human: curiosity, scepticism without cynicism, clear writing, careful observation, the courage to deliver bad news politely, and understanding of the business domain, whether banking, e-commerce, health or telecom.

Certification: The International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB) offers widely recognised certifications, starting with the Foundation Level and continuing to advanced and specialist levels such as test automation, performance, security, agile and test management. Many concepts in this course, such as the seven principles, test levels and types, static testing and black-box techniques, match the Foundation syllabus closely. A certificate shows shared vocabulary; employers still look for practical skills, so combine certification with real projects.

Building a portfolio: You do not need a job to show testing skill. Build a public portfolio: a GitHub repository with a small UI automation project using Page Objects, an API test suite for a public API, and a CI pipeline that runs them; well-written sample bug reports and a test plan for an app you use; an accessibility audit of a website; a short performance test with k6 or JMeter and an analysis of results. Contribute tests or bug reports to open-source projects. Write short articles about what you learned. These show employers exactly what you can do.

Growing in your first job: In your first testing role, learn the product and domain deeply, ask why requirements exist, read the code you test, pair with developers, volunteer for automation and pipeline work, and keep a log of defects you found that others missed and the techniques that found them. Read widely: classic books on testing, the OWASP guides, and blogs by practitioners. The best testers keep learning, because technologies change but the craft of asking good questions remains.

Real-life example, a process improvement journey: A mid-sized software company in Dhaka delivering projects for European clients had frequent late releases and angry clients. A TMMi-style assessment found no standard test process, no risk analysis and no defect metrics. Over eighteen months, using PDCA in small steps, they introduced a test strategy, risk-based test planning, defect tracking with root cause fields, review checklists and a CI pipeline with automated regression. DRE rose from about 70 to above 90 percent over the following releases, and two clients extended their contracts, citing predictable quality.

Real-life example, from manual tester to SDET: A graduate from a Bangladeshi university joined a fintech company as a manual tester. She learned Python and pytest in the evenings, automated the team's most painful regression checks at the API level, and later built their Playwright suite with Page Objects. She presented leakage analysis in retrospectives and proposed quality gates. Within three years she led the company's quality engineering team. Her advantage was not one tool; it was combining testing fundamentals with steady technical growth.

Course wrap-up: Across these lessons you have learned why software fails and what testing can and cannot prove; how quality, QA and QC relate; the test levels and types; static testing and reviews; black-box techniques from partitions to pairwise and exploratory testing; white-box coverage up to MC/DC and mutation; test processes, planning, estimation, test cases, defects and risk; unit frameworks, TDD, BDD and test doubles; the automation pyramid, UI and API automation; performance, security, usability, accessibility and compatibility testing; CI, DevOps and metrics; and, finally, process quality and careers. Together they form a craft: the disciplined, creative work of finding out the truth about software so that people can trust it.

Common exam questions: Exams ask you to distinguish product and process quality; explain the PDCA cycle; describe the purpose of ISO 9001; list and explain CMMI's five maturity levels; explain what TMMi adds; outline Six Sigma's DMAIC; name the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 series and its scope; explain the role of quality audits; and describe defect prevention. Career questions in interviews often ask how you would test a common object or app, how you would report a defect, and how you decide what to automate.

Recap: Process quality is about how software is produced; better processes make good products more predictable. PDCA drives improvement; ISO 9001 defines quality management systems; CMMI's five levels describe organisational maturity, and TMMi applies the idea to testing; Lean and Six Sigma reduce waste and variation; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 standardises testing. Audits and defect prevention close the loop. Careers range from QA engineer to SDET, specialist and manager; build skills, certification and a portfolio, and keep learning. Thank you for completing this course.
key_points: Process quality concerns how software is produced; defined, measured and improved processes make good products more predictable.
PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) is the basic improvement cycle; retrospectives are a small PDCA loop.
ISO 9001 specifies quality management systems for any industry, focused on defined processes and continual improvement.
CMMI maturity levels: 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitatively Managed, 5 Optimizing.
TMMi applies maturity levels to testing; Six Sigma uses DMAIC; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 standardises software testing.
Testing careers include QA engineer, SDET or automation engineer, performance and security specialists, and test lead or manager.
ISTQB certification plus a practical portfolio of automation, API tests and bug reports shows real skill.
lessons.tip: Keep a personal "defect diary": for every interesting defect you find, write one line about the technique or question that found it. In a year it becomes both your best interview material and your own testing handbook.
lessons.task: Create a one-page plan for your testing portfolio: three projects you will build (for example UI automation with Page Objects, an API test suite, and a performance test), the tools and language for each, how you will run them in a CI pipeline, and one sample bug report you will publish. Then map your current skills against the list in this lesson and pick two to improve in the next month.

quiz.q: In CMMI, which maturity level describes an organisation with standard processes tailored for each project?
quiz.explain: At level 3 the organisation has standard processes that projects tailor; level 2 manages projects individually.

quiz.q: What do the letters PDCA stand for?
quiz.explain: PDCA is Plan-Do-Check-Act, the Deming cycle for continual improvement.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of ISO 9001?
options: To specify requirements for a quality management system that can apply to any industry
quiz.explain: ISO 9001 is about defined processes, customer focus, measurement and continual improvement, not about any specific technology.

quiz.q: Which model applies maturity levels specifically to test processes?
quiz.explain: TMMi, the Test Maturity Model integration, applies the maturity level idea to testing and complements CMMI.

quiz.q: Which role mainly builds automated test suites and frameworks and works closely with developers?
options: Software development engineer in test (SDET) or automation engineer
quiz.explain: SDETs and automation engineers combine programming and testing skills to build and maintain automated suites.
